messages.content: I want to characterize sharp policy-value bounds for clinical decision policies when outcomes are selectively observed and there is bounded unmeasured confounding. The sensitivity assumptions need to be explicit. I also want to know when the bounds certify improvement over the historical policy, with at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the stated sensitivity model.

A useful starting point is to separate three objects: the value of a candidate policy, the value of the historical policy, and their difference. The data may not identify any of these exactly when treatment decisions are confounded and outcomes are observed selectively. Instead, explicit sensitivity assumptions define which full-data distributions remain possible given the observed data. The sharp lower and upper bounds are the smallest and largest values attained across that feasible set.

For improvement, the most direct object is the policy-value difference. Its sharp lower bound being greater than zero means every distribution allowed by the stated sensitivity model favors the candidate policy over the historical one. A confidence-based claim needs an additional step: a lower confidence limit for that difference must be greater than zero, with coverage controlled uniformly over the sensitivity model. Neither conclusion can be inferred without specifying the model and evaluating it against data.
What would count as specifying the sensitivity assumptions, rather than merely saying that confounding and selective observation are bounded?

The assumptions need to say what may be unobserved, which dependencies are allowed, and exactly what quantity is bounded. For example, one could introduce an unobserved prognostic factor and place a numerical bound on how much treatment-assignment odds can vary with that factor among otherwise comparable patients. Separately, one could bound how much the odds of observing an outcome can vary with the unobserved factor or with the outcome itself. Those are two distinct restrictions: a bound on treatment selection does not automatically bound outcome observation.

The specification should also state the policy-value target, the range of possible outcomes if bounded outcomes are being used, and relevant support conditions. No numerical confounding or observation-sensitivity limit, outcome range, or support condition has been supplied here, so these would have to be stated as assumptions rather than treated as known features of the clinical setting.
Can you express the target and the sharp bounds without choosing those numerical limits yet?

Yes. Let X denote information available to a policy, A a decision, and Y(a) the outcome that would occur under decision a. Write π(a|X) for a candidate policy and π₀(a|X) for the historical policy. Under a specified target population, their values can be written abstractly as V(π) = E[Σₐ π(a|X)Y(a)] and V(π₀) = E[Σₐ π₀(a|X)Y(a)]. The improvement contrast is Δ(π,π₀) = V(π) − V(π₀).

Let F denote the set of full-data distributions that agree with the observable distribution and satisfy the explicitly chosen consistency, sensitivity, and other identifying assumptions. Then the sharp bounds for the contrast are LΔ = inf_{P∈F} Δ_P(π,π₀) and UΔ = sup_{P∈F} Δ_P(π,π₀). Analogous infima and suprema define the bounds for either policy’s value. ‘Sharp’ means these extrema describe the range actually permitted by the assumptions and observable distribution, rather than a convenient but unnecessarily wide range.
Does taking a lower bound for the candidate policy and subtracting an upper bound for the historical policy give the sharp improvement bound?

It gives a valid conservative lower bound if both value bounds are valid, but it need not be sharp for the difference. The candidate and historical values are evaluated under the same possible full-data distribution. A distribution that minimizes the candidate’s value may not be one that maximizes the historical policy’s value. Optimizing V(π) − V(π₀) jointly over F retains that connection and is the appropriate way to characterize the sharp contrast bound.
Could you give a concrete form for the sensitivity restrictions while keeping it clear that no particular parameter values have been chosen?

One possible formulation, for a binary decision purely as an illustration, uses two parameters, Γ≥1 and Λ≥1. At a fixed observed covariate value X, a treatment-confounding restriction could say that the treatment-assignment odds for any two admissible values of an unobserved factor differ by no more than a factor Γ. For a fixed X and treatment, an observation restriction could say that the odds of the realized outcome being observed across admissible latent prognostic states or realized outcome values differ by no more than a factor Λ. The latter permits selective observation while limiting its strength.

That illustration is not a claim that decisions here are binary or that an odds-ratio model has already been selected. A complete specification would define the admissible comparisons and conditional probabilities precisely, along with any needed positivity conditions. In particular, it should not silently treat outcomes as missing at random: whether observation may depend on the unseen outcome is central to the sensitivity model.
Why keep the treatment and observation parameters separate?

They address different routes by which the observed outcomes can misrepresent a policy’s value. Unmeasured confounding concerns which decisions patients receive, even before asking whether their outcomes are recorded. Selective observation concerns which realized outcomes enter the available outcome data. A small allowance for one mechanism does not imply a small allowance for the other.

Keeping the restrictions separate also makes the conclusion interpretable: any improvement certificate would be conditional on the stated limits for both mechanisms. If either limit is changed, the feasible set of full-data distributions may change, and the bounds must be reconsidered.
What exactly should ‘certify improvement’ mean in this setting?

At the population identification level, it means LΔ>0: even the least favorable full-data distribution consistent with the observed distribution and every stated sensitivity assumption gives the candidate policy a higher value than the historical policy. If LΔ≤0≤UΔ, the bounds do not certify improvement; they leave improvement and non-improvement compatible with the model. An upper bound below zero would instead establish that the candidate has lower value throughout the feasible set.

Because the bounds must be estimated, a statistical certificate is more demanding. The lower endpoint of a suitably covered confidence set for Δ must exceed zero. A positive estimate, or even a positive estimated sharp lower bound, does not by itself provide that confidence-based certificate.
Is a positive sharp lower bound the same thing as a 95% confidence statement?

No. A sharp lower bound is a population-level consequence of the observable distribution and assumptions; an estimated bound is subject to sampling uncertainty. The confidence procedure must account for that uncertainty. For example, one can seek a confidence set that contains the entire population identified interval for Δ with probability at least 95%. That is stronger than merely covering one possible true value, and it would also cover the true contrast whenever the stated model holds.

If such a set’s lower endpoint is above zero, the confidence-set statement and the sensitivity-model statement work together to support a 95%-level improvement certificate. This describes the required guarantee, not an assertion that a particular procedure has achieved it.
The coverage requirement says ‘uniformly over the stated sensitivity model.’ How is that different from checking 95% coverage at one distribution?

Pointwise coverage addresses one particular data-generating distribution. Uniform coverage asks for the guarantee across all distributions admitted by the stated model, including difficult cases near its boundaries. For a confidence set Cₙ for the contrast, a finite-sample version of the target would be inf_{P∈M} Pr_P{Δ_P∈Cₙ}≥0.95, where M is the stated sensitivity model. If the objective is coverage of the whole identified interval I(P), the corresponding requirement is inf_{P∈M} Pr_P{I(P)⊆Cₙ}≥0.95.

An asymptotic uniform guarantee has a different form, such as liminfₙ inf_{P∈M} Pr_P{I(P)⊆Cₙ}≥0.95. It is important to say which guarantee is intended. A method that attains 95% coverage separately at each fixed distribution does not, without further justification, establish the uniform requirement.
Do I need to distinguish a confidence set for the candidate value from one for improvement?

Yes. A confidence set for V(π) alone does not establish whether π improves on π₀. That comparison needs the uncertainty in both values and their dependence to be handled. A confidence set constructed directly for Δ is naturally aligned with the improvement question; a jointly valid set for the two values can also be used to derive a valid comparison.

Likewise, separate marginal 95% sets for the two values do not automatically give 95% coverage for a comparison obtained by combining them. The coverage claim must apply to the object used for the certificate.
What if an outcome is never recorded for a group relevant to the candidate policy?

Then the stated assumptions have to carry more of the identification burden. With no relevant observation support, the observed data alone cannot reveal that group’s outcome distribution under the decision of interest. A known bounded outcome range might still give bounds, but they could be too wide to certify improvement. Without an outcome-range restriction or other suitable constraint, finite informative bounds may not be available.

That is why observation support and the scope of the sensitivity restrictions should be stated explicitly. One should not interpret a narrow result as data-driven if it actually depends on an unstated restriction on outcomes that are never seen.
And if the candidate policy assigns a decision rarely or never made historically?

The same principle applies on the decision side. Bounds for the candidate policy require information or assumptions about its potential outcomes under decisions it may assign. If relevant decisions lack support in the observed setting, an unmeasured-confounding limit alone need not supply that missing information. The resulting bounds may rely heavily on an outcome range or other explicitly declared restrictions.

This does not rule out defining the policy value. It does mean that claims of sharpness and improvement must be relative to the full set of assumptions used to handle that lack of support.
Could the sensitivity model itself fail to fit the observed distribution?

Yes. For a particular choice of restrictions, there could be no full-data distribution that both reproduces the observable distribution and satisfies the assumptions. In the abstract notation, F would be empty. An empty feasible set is not a certificate that the candidate improves on the historical policy; the value bounds and comparison would need to be interpreted only after the model’s compatibility is addressed.
Suppose the lower bound just touches zero. Can I still describe the candidate policy as certified to improve?

Not under a strict improvement criterion. If the sharp lower contrast bound equals zero, the stated model allows a full-data distribution with no improvement, or allows contrasts arbitrarily close to zero if the infimum is not attained. The bound therefore does not certify Δ>0. With sampling uncertainty, the lower confidence endpoint would likewise need to be strictly above zero for a confidence-based strict-improvement claim.
Does the at-least-95% requirement apply only at whichever sensitivity values look favorable?

No. The coverage statement should match the sensitivity model actually stated for the analysis. If that model includes a range of allowed confounding and observation mechanisms, the guarantee must hold uniformly across that range, not just at a favorable member of it. An improvement claim must also be read relative to the particular stated limits: it cannot be presented as robust to mechanisms outside them.

The main distinction is between a mathematical conclusion conditional on specified sensitivity assumptions and a statistical coverage guarantee over all data-generating distributions satisfying those assumptions. Both are needed for the requested confidence-based certification.

Let’s make the proposed approach concrete: optimize policy-minus-historical value over latent-outcome tables, impose Γ-bounded assignment and recording odds ratios, and project exact 95% multinomial confidence regions. How do those pieces fit together?

The latent-outcome tables represent possible full-data distributions, including outcomes that the observed records do not reveal. Each admissible table must reproduce a possible distribution of the observable cells and satisfy the stated Γ bounds on both assignment and recording odds ratios. For a fixed observable distribution, minimize and maximize the *same* contrast—candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value—over those tables. Those extrema are the proposed sharp population bounds.

Sampling uncertainty enters through an exact 95% confidence region for the observable multinomial cell probabilities. Projecting that region means considering every admissible latent table compatible with at least one observable distribution in the region, then taking the range of policy-value contrasts across them. This joins the sensitivity analysis and the confidence calculation without treating an estimated observable distribution as known.
When you say ‘latent-outcome table,’ are you claiming that the unrecorded outcomes have been reconstructed?

No. A table is a possible completion of what the records leave unknown, not a recovered patient-level dataset. Its entries can describe probabilities of potential-outcome patterns, assignments, and recording events at whatever level the model explicitly defines. Many tables may agree with the same observed cell probabilities. The optimization ranges across all that satisfy the assumptions; it does not select one completion and call it the truth.
What does the Γ restriction need to say in this proposal?

It needs to define the relevant odds, the comparisons to which the bound applies, and the conditioning variables. The proposed restriction is that specified assignment-odds ratios and specified recording-odds ratios lie within a factor Γ of one, with the reciprocal lower limit where appropriate. Γ is a sensitivity limit, not an estimate of confounding or selective recording obtained merely from the observed outcomes.

Saying only ‘Γ-bounded’ would be incomplete without specifying, for example, which latent states may be compared and what happens when an odds denominator is zero. The proposal uses Γ to bound both mechanisms, but a complete model must state each restriction separately: assignment concerns which decision is received, whereas recording concerns whether a realized outcome becomes observable.
Does the proposal require recording to be unrelated to the outcome?

No. Selectively observed outcomes are the reason to include a recording sensitivity restriction. Subject to the precisely stated Γ bound, recording may depend on information that is unavailable in the observed records, potentially including the outcome that would otherwise be missing. The model should say exactly which such dependencies its recording-odds comparison permits. It should not quietly substitute a missing-at-random assumption for the proposed bounded-selectivity analysis.
Why optimize the policy-minus-historical contrast directly instead of bounding each value and subtracting?

The two policy values depend on the same latent table. Directly optimizing their difference respects that shared dependence. Subtracting a separately optimized upper bound for the historical value from a separately optimized lower bound for the candidate value can pair extrema that cannot occur under one admissible table, producing a needlessly wide lower bound.

For an observable probability vector q, if T(q,Γ) denotes the latent tables consistent with q and the fully specified Γ restrictions, the proposed contrast bounds are inf_{t∈T(q,Γ)} Δ(t) and sup_{t∈T(q,Γ)} Δ(t), where Δ(t) is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value under table t. This notation states the optimization target; it does not assume that the extrema have already been computed.
What would make those population bounds sharp rather than merely conservative?

The feasible tables must describe exactly the full-data possibilities allowed by the observable distribution and every stated assumption, without dropping feasible tables or enlarging the set through a relaxation. Then the infimum and supremum delimit the contrasts compatible with that model. If the tabulation omits possible latent configurations, or the computation substitutes an outer approximation, the resulting extrema need not be the sharp bounds for the stated model.

Sharpness is always relative to the specified sensitivity and support assumptions. It does not mean the assumptions themselves are verified by the optimization.
How is the exact multinomial confidence region used? Do we just calculate bounds at its center?

No. Let C₉₅ be an exact 95% confidence region for the observable cell-probability vector q under the proposed multinomial sampling model. Projection considers the full region, not only a center or a point estimate. One way to express the projected contrast set is {Δ(t): q∈C₉₅, t∈T(q,Γ)}. Its lower and upper endpoints, if an interval is reported, optimize over q and t together, subject to both the confidence-region constraint and the latent-table constraints.

Observable vectors in C₉₅ for which no admissible latent table exists contribute nothing to that projection. The construction should not interpret such incompatibility as evidence of policy improvement.
What does ‘exact 95%’ guarantee here, and what does it not guarantee?

For the observable multinomial probabilities, an exact 95% confidence region is constructed to contain the true probability vector with probability at least 95% under the specified sampling model, rather than relying solely on a pointwise large-sample approximation. Discreteness can make actual coverage greater than 95%.

That guarantee does not mean the projected contrast set has exactly 95% coverage at every distribution, nor that it is the narrowest possible confidence set. Projection can be conservative. It also does not repair a misspecified sensitivity model or an incorrect observable sampling model.
Can you spell out why projection gives the uniform coverage requirement for the policy contrast?

Suppose the true data-generating distribution belongs to the stated sensitivity model, with observable multinomial probabilities q*. Its true latent table is then in T(q*,Γ). On every sample for which q*∈C₉₅, that table is among those considered in the projection, so its policy-minus-historical contrast is in the projected set. If C₉₅ contains q* with probability at least 0.95 for every observable multinomial distribution allowed by the model, the projected set covers the true contrast with probability at least 0.95 uniformly over the stated sensitivity model.

The same event also ensures that the projected set contains the entire population identified set at q*, provided the projection includes *all* tables in T(q*,Γ). That stronger inclusion is useful when presenting confidence limits for sharp bounds. These statements depend on the region’s exact coverage and on carrying out the proposed projection over the full feasible set.
So when would this approach certify that the candidate policy improves on the historical policy?

At the population level, the sharp lower bound on candidate-minus-historical value must be strictly above zero. For a confidence-based certificate using this proposal, the lower endpoint of the projected 95% contrast set must be strictly above zero. Then every contrast retained by both the multinomial confidence region and the Γ-constrained latent tables is positive.

If that projected lower endpoint is zero or negative, this construction does not give a 95%-level certificate of strict improvement, even if a point estimate favors the candidate. No such endpoint or conclusion has been supplied here; this is the criterion the proposed analysis would apply.
Does the 95% statement apply to a single favorable candidate policy only?

The coverage argument I described applies to the contrast whose projected set is constructed. If several policies are examined using the same observable confidence region and each contrast is projected over its appropriate full feasible set, the event that the true observable probability vector lies in that one region can support simultaneous inclusion of their true contrasts. But any claim about selecting a policy after examining results should be stated in terms of the actual joint construction used, not inferred from separate, unrelated 95% calculations.

The present proposal specifies the projection principle, not a set of candidate policies or a selection rule.
What if I want to see how the answer changes as Γ changes?

For each stated Γ, the assignment and recording restrictions define an admissible latent-table set, and the contrast can be optimized and projected against the multinomial region for that set. A conclusion should identify the Γ restriction under which it holds. If a common exact region is used, its event of covering the true observable probabilities does not depend on which Γ is inspected; nevertheless, any claimed simultaneous statement across sensitivity settings must be formulated for the settings actually included and must still use their correctly specified feasible sets.

There is no Γ value, range, or improvement threshold specified in the proposal, so it would be premature to report how far a certificate persists.
Could an exact region still give an uninformative projected interval?

Yes. Exact coverage addresses sampling reliability, not informativeness. If the data and Γ restrictions permit latent tables with substantially different unrecorded outcomes, the projected contrast set can be wide. Limited assignment or recording support can likewise leave important policy outcomes weakly constrained. A wide set may correctly reflect uncertainty and fail to certify improvement; that is distinct from a coverage failure.
Do we need to decide the observable cells and outcome scale before treating this as a completed analysis?

Yes. The multinomial region requires a defined set of observable categories and a sampling model for their counts. The latent tables require a defined outcome and policy-value scale, a mapping from latent entries to those observable categories, and precise assignment- and recording-odds restrictions. Those definitions also determine whether the proposed finite table captures every permitted full-data distribution.

The current proposal identifies the route—joint contrast optimization under Γ restrictions, followed by projection of exact 95% multinomial confidence regions—but it does not supply those definitions, data, computed bounds, or a demonstrated improvement certificate.
Does optimizing the candidate policy’s value and the historical policy’s value separately destroy sharpness of the improvement bounds when they share latent confounding?

It can. Each separately optimized value bound may be sharp for its own target, yet subtracting those bounds need not give a sharp bound for improvement. Both values must be evaluated under the same admissible latent-outcome table, including the same latent confounding structure. The table that makes the candidate value smallest may differ from the one that makes the historical value largest.

If F is the feasible set of tables, the sharp lower improvement bound is infₜ∈F[Vₜ(π) − Vₜ(π₀)]. Separately optimizing gives infₜ∈F Vₜ(π) − supₜ∈F Vₜ(π₀), which is no greater than that sharp lower bound. It is a valid conservative bound, but it may be unnecessarily low.
Why is the separately calculated lower bound still valid?

For every single feasible table t, its candidate value is at least the candidate’s separate lower bound, and its historical value is at most the historical policy’s separate upper bound. Their difference is therefore at least the difference of those two separate bounds. The problem is not validity; it is that the two separate extrema may come from incompatible tables.
Can you illustrate that without assuming anything about the clinical data?

As a purely mathematical illustration, suppose the only feasible pairs of candidate and historical values were (0, 0) and (1, 1). Improvement is zero under either pair, so its sharp bounds are both zero. Separately, the candidate’s minimum is 0 and the historical policy’s maximum is 1. Subtracting them gives a lower bound of −1—even though no feasible pair has improvement of −1. The separate upper bound would likewise be 1. The example illustrates the loss of the shared-table constraint; it is not a claim about the clinical setting.
Does that mean separate optimization is always non-sharp for the contrast?

No. The separate lower bound is sharp if a feasible table can simultaneously attain the candidate’s minimum and the historical policy’s maximum, or, when extrema are not attained, if feasible tables can approach both extrema together. The analogous condition for the separate upper bound requires the candidate’s maximum and the historical policy’s minimum to be jointly attainable or approachable. Shared confounding makes incompatibility possible, not inevitable.
Would the issue disappear if both optimizations used exactly the same sensitivity assumptions?

Not necessarily. Using the same assumptions gives both optimizations the same feasible set, which is essential for a coherent comparison. But separate optimizations can still choose *different members* of that set. Optimizing the difference directly requires one feasible table to determine both values at once.
So is the question about dependence between the estimated values?

There are two related but distinct issues. Sharpness is an identification issue: which pairs of policy values can coexist under one admissible latent table? Sampling dependence is an inference issue: how uncertainty in the estimated observable distribution affects the two values and their difference. Accounting for sampling dependence alone does not restore a shared-table constraint lost during separate population optimizations.
How should I state the answer for both endpoints of the improvement interval?

Write the sharp contrast bounds as infₜ∈F[Vₜ(π) − Vₜ(π₀)] and supₜ∈F[Vₜ(π) − Vₜ(π₀)]. Subtracting separate value bounds instead yields an outer interval: its lower endpoint can be below the sharp contrast lower bound, and its upper endpoint can be above the sharp contrast upper bound. Either endpoint may coincide with its sharp counterpart if the relevant extrema are compatible. Thus separate optimization does not necessarily destroy sharpness, but it cannot establish it without that compatibility.
Why does this matter specifically for certifying improvement?

A conservative lower bound may remain at or below zero even when the sharp lower bound for candidate-minus-historical value is positive. In that case, subtracting separate value bounds would fail to certify an improvement that joint optimization could certify under the same assumptions. Conversely, if even the conservative lower bound is strictly positive, it does establish improvement at the population-bound level. Any confidence-based certificate must also account for sampling uncertainty with the stated coverage guarantee.

My working hypothesis is that joint optimization gives sharp improvement bounds under shared latent confounding, and that those bounds are sometimes strictly tighter than subtracting separate marginal value intervals. Is that the right way to frame it?

Yes, as a hypothesis about the stated model, with one important condition: joint optimization gives sharp bounds only if its feasible set represents every latent configuration allowed by the observed distribution and the sensitivity assumptions, without adding configurations the model excludes. Optimizing candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over that set keeps both values tied to the same latent configuration. Subtracting separately optimized marginal intervals does not necessarily keep that tie, so it can produce a wider improvement interval.

“Sometimes strictly tighter” is appropriately qualified. The two approaches may also give identical bounds when the marginal extrema are jointly attainable.
Can you state the comparison precisely without treating strict tightening as an observed result?

Let F be the common feasible set of latent configurations. Write C(t) for candidate-policy value and H(t) for historical-policy value under t. The proposed joint lower and upper improvement bounds are

L_joint = infₜ∈F [C(t) − H(t)] and U_joint = supₜ∈F [C(t) − H(t)].

The interval obtained from separate marginal bounds has endpoints

L_sep = infₜ∈F C(t) − supₜ∈F H(t) and U_sep = supₜ∈F C(t) − infₜ∈F H(t).

For any nonempty F where these quantities are defined, L_sep ≤ L_joint ≤ U_joint ≤ U_sep. These inequalities show why strict tightening is possible; they do not say whether either inequality is strict for a particular clinical policy or sensitivity model.
Where exactly does shared latent confounding enter that comparison?

It enters through F and through the fact that C(t) and H(t) are calculated from the same t. A latent configuration compatible with a low candidate value also determines a historical value; the historical value cannot be independently replaced by its maximum under some other configuration. Assignment and recording restrictions, if included in F, constrain those possibilities jointly as well.

The separate calculation retains the attainable range of each value but discards information about which candidate and historical values can occur together. Joint optimization retains that information.
Is it accurate to say separate bounds assume two different confounders, one for each policy?

That would overstate it. The separate optimizations can each use the same latent-confounding model and the same feasible set. The loss occurs when their independently chosen extrema are combined: the resulting pair may correspond to two different feasible latent configurations rather than one. It is more precise to say that subtracting marginal intervals can ignore *compatibility between extrema*, not that the underlying analysis necessarily assumes different confounders.
What would make the improvement bounds strictly tighter at the lower endpoint?

The lower endpoint is strictly tighter when L_joint > L_sep. Intuitively, that happens if feasible configurations that drive the candidate value toward its minimum cannot, at the same time, drive the historical value toward its maximum closely enough to attain the separately calculated difference. If both marginal extrema can be approached together by feasible configurations, the lower endpoints coincide. The corresponding question for the upper endpoint is whether the candidate maximum and historical minimum can be approached together.
Could just one endpoint tighten?

Yes. Compatibility of the extrema relevant to the lower endpoint and compatibility of those relevant to the upper endpoint are separate questions. Joint and separate lower bounds could coincide while the upper bounds differ, or the reverse. The hypothesis of ‘sometimes strictly tighter’ does not require both endpoints to tighten in every case.
Could the two value intervals look wide even though the improvement interval is narrow?

In principle, yes. If admissible latent configurations move candidate and historical values together, each value can vary substantially while their difference varies much less. Marginal intervals describe each coordinate’s range; the joint contrast describes the range along the candidate-minus-historical direction. Whether that pattern occurs here is a question for the specified feasible set, not something established by the hypothesis alone.
What if the marginal extrema are attained by different tables but their subtraction still equals the joint bound?

Attainment needs careful wording. If both marginal extrema are attained and the separate lower bound equals the joint lower bound, some feasible configuration must attain the candidate minimum and historical maximum together, assuming the joint minimum is attained. Merely finding two different tables that separately attain those extrema does not rule out a third that attains both.

When extrema are infima or suprema that need not be attained, equality can instead come from a sequence of feasible configurations approaching the two relevant marginal extrema together. The substantive test is joint attainability or joint approachability, not whether the first optimizers found happen to be different.
Does joint optimization alone establish sharpness?

No. Joint optimization addresses the correct *target*—the difference evaluated under one latent configuration—but sharpness also depends on an exact characterization of F. If F excludes possibilities that the stated sensitivity model permits, the result may be too narrow. If it includes configurations that the model rules out, the result may be too wide. Numerical optimization must also find the actual extrema of the specified problem rather than only a relaxation or a local solution. The working hypothesis therefore has a model-representation and optimization qualification.
Would accounting for correlation between two estimated value bounds recover the same improvement interval?

Not by itself. Correlation describes sampling variation in estimates; compatibility of latent values is an identification constraint. A statistical method can account for correlation while still starting from separate population extrema that cannot occur together. Conversely, a sharp joint population bound still needs a valid treatment of sampling uncertainty before it supports a confidence-based statement.
How should this hypothesis bear on a claim that the candidate policy improves on the historical one?

If the hypothesis holds for the fully specified model, a joint lower improvement bound could be positive even when the lower bound formed by subtracting marginal intervals is not. That is the potential practical consequence of strict tightening. It does not imply that the joint bound *is* positive in this setting; the sign must come from the actual optimization.

A population improvement claim would require the sharp joint lower bound to exceed zero. A confidence-based claim would additionally require an appropriately covered lower confidence limit to exceed zero. Tighter identification bounds and at-least-95% uniform confidence-set coverage are distinct requirements.
So the hypothesis is not that marginal value bounds are themselves wrong?

Correct. Marginal bounds can be sharp for the candidate and historical values individually. The hypothesis concerns the additional information needed to bound their *difference*: which pairs of values are jointly feasible under shared latent confounding. Separate marginal intervals may discard that information, while direct optimization of policy-minus-historical value is designed to preserve it.

I want to turn the joint-versus-separate comparison into a plan: derive the joint Γ-constrained latent-table extrema, compare them with marginal subtraction, and certify improvement only when the projected exact-95% lower bound exceeds zero. How should I keep those steps distinct?

First, define the latent-table feasible set under the stated Γ restrictions and, for a fixed observable distribution, minimize and maximize candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over that *same* table. Those are the proposed population improvement bounds. Second, compute the marginal value extrema over that same feasible set and subtract them to see whether the joint bounds are tighter. Third, incorporate sampling uncertainty by projecting an exact 95% confidence region for the observable multinomial probabilities through the Γ-constrained table model. The improvement rule applies to the lower endpoint of that projected contrast set, not merely to a population bound evaluated at estimated probabilities. These are planned derivations and comparisons; none of their numerical outcomes is given.
What exactly must stay shared in the joint optimization?

One admissible latent table must determine both policy values in each evaluation of their difference. Its latent outcomes, assignment mechanism, recording mechanism, and implied observable probabilities must jointly satisfy the specified constraints. The candidate value cannot be evaluated at one table while the historical value is evaluated at another and then called a feasible improvement contrast. That shared-table requirement is the point of optimizing the difference directly.
How would you write the derivation target compactly?

Let q represent the observable cell-probability vector, and let TΓ(q) be all latent tables compatible with q and the fully specified Γ-bounded assignment and recording odds-ratio restrictions. If Vπ(t) and V₀(t) are the candidate and historical policy values at table t, set Δ(t)=Vπ(t)−V₀(t). The population targets are LΓ(q)=inf_{t∈TΓ(q)}Δ(t) and UΓ(q)=sup_{t∈TΓ(q)}Δ(t).

Writing these expressions is not yet deriving their values. The derivation must characterize TΓ(q) accurately and establish that the reported extrema are attainable, or approachable when the bounds are infima and suprema.
Where does marginal subtraction enter without changing the model?

Use the *same* TΓ(q) to bound each value individually. For a lower comparison bound, subtract the historical value’s marginal supremum from the candidate value’s marginal infimum. For an upper comparison bound, subtract the historical value’s marginal infimum from the candidate value’s marginal supremum. Both calculations use the stated Γ-constrained model; their difference from joint optimization is that each marginal extremum may be reached at a different table.

The planned comparison is between these outer bounds and LΓ(q), UΓ(q). It should not mix different sensitivity restrictions or observable distributions without explicitly saying so.
Can we know the direction of that comparison before solving anything?

Yes, the direction follows from optimization over a common feasible set. Marginal subtraction gives a lower endpoint no greater than the joint lower endpoint and an upper endpoint no less than the joint upper endpoint, whenever the quantities are defined. What requires derivation is whether either inequality is strict for the specified model and observable distribution. The plan does not presuppose strict tightening.
Does Γ have to be applied to both assignment and recording in the latent-table step?

The proposed Γ-constrained table step must spell out both restrictions if both are part of the stated sensitivity model. Assignment and recording have different roles, so each needs its own defined odds comparison, conditioning information, and treatment of probabilities at a boundary. Using the symbol Γ does not by itself make the constraints precise or imply that either mechanism has been measured directly. No numerical Γ value is specified in this plan.
What has to be shown before describing the joint extrema as sharp?

The table representation must include every full-data distribution allowed by the observable information and stated Γ restrictions, and must not include distributions they exclude. The objective must be the requested policy-minus-historical value on each table, and the optimization must reach the global infimum and supremum, or otherwise justify them. If those conditions hold, the resulting extrema are sharp *relative to that model*. Simply labeling an optimization ‘joint’ would not establish sharpness if its feasible set were incomplete or relaxed.
Now where does the exact 95% region enter? I do not want to mistake a point-estimate bound for a confidence bound.

Let C₉₅ be an exact 95% multinomial confidence region for q under the stated observable sampling model. Rather than insert just an estimated q into LΓ(q), consider every q in C₉₅ and every table in TΓ(q). The projected lower endpoint can be expressed as inf{Δ(t): q∈C₉₅, t∈TΓ(q)}; the upper endpoint uses the corresponding supremum.

That projected lower endpoint reflects both the permitted latent uncertainty and the sampling uncertainty represented by C₉₅. It is the quantity specified in the planned improvement rule.
Would it be equivalent to calculate sharp joint bounds at the center of C₉₅ and then widen them afterward?

Not without a separately justified widening rule. The proposed projection ranges over the entire exact region. A center may omit observable probability vectors in the region whose compatible latent tables yield a lower contrast. Any shortcut would have to be proved to preserve the intended coverage; it is not part of this plan merely because it starts from a sharp bound at one vector.
What is the coverage argument for that projection?

For any data-generating distribution in the stated sensitivity model, let q* be its true observable probabilities and t* its true admissible latent table. On the event q*∈C₉₅, the projection includes t*, and hence includes Δ(t*). If the multinomial region covers q* with probability at least 95% for every distribution allowed by the stated model, the projected contrast set covers the true contrast with probability at least 95% uniformly over that model. On the same event, projecting *all* of TΓ(q*) includes its entire population identified interval.

This is a conditional argument for the planned construction: the exact-region guarantee, the observable sampling model, and the completeness of the feasible-table projection all matter. The plan alone is not evidence that a particular computed region meets them.
Suppose the projected lower endpoint is positive. What can the certification say?

If it is strictly greater than zero, every contrast in the projected set favors the candidate policy over the historical policy. Under the stated sensitivity model and a valid uniformly covering exact-95% projection, that supplies the planned at-least-95%-coverage basis for a strict-improvement certificate. The statement is conditional on those assumptions and on the realized projected endpoint actually exceeding zero; this plan does not say that it does.
And if that lower endpoint equals zero?

Then the rule does **not** certify strict improvement. A lower endpoint of zero can still leave positive contrasts in the projected set; it does not mean improvement is impossible. The same failure to certify applies if the lower endpoint is negative. The criterion is a lower endpoint *strictly above* zero, not a requirement that every conceivable contrast be zero or negative when the criterion fails.
Could marginal subtraction be used for the 95% comparison too?

It could be calculated as a conservative comparator if the marginal confidence bounds are formed from the same projected, Γ-constrained possibilities. Its lower endpoint would subtract the largest feasible historical value across the projection from the smallest feasible candidate value across the projection, potentially combining values from different tables or different q vectors. Directly projecting the contrast retains their joint compatibility and can yield a tighter lower endpoint.

That comparison does not imply that a tighter projected contrast set is itself the narrowest possible confidence set. Population sharpness and the conservatism of a confidence construction are different questions.
Should the comparison be made before projection or after projection?

They answer related but distinct questions. At a fixed q, comparing joint extrema with marginal subtraction tests what is gained by retaining shared latent-table constraints in the population bounds. After projection, the analogous comparison shows what the distinction means for the proposed confidence sets, where both tables and observable probabilities vary over their permitted sets. The plan can report both comparisons, keeping their targets clearly labeled rather than treating a fixed-q result as an already established 95% result.
Is a projected positive lower endpoint possible even if a marginal-subtraction lower endpoint is not positive?

It is possible in principle: the joint projection could exclude the incompatible pairing of a very low candidate value and a very high historical value that marginal subtraction uses. Whether that happens under the specified Γ constraints and confidence region must be established by the planned derivation and calculation. It should not be assumed from the direction of the bounds alone.
What if a probability vector inside the exact region has no Γ-admissible latent table?

It contributes no contrast to the projection because there is no compatible table to optimize over at that vector. The projection is over pairs (q,t) with q in the region *and* t in TΓ(q). If no such pair exists anywhere in the region, an empty projected set should not be described as a positive improvement certificate; compatibility and the construction would need to be addressed.
Can I claim the planned certificate applies uniformly just because the confidence region is called exact?

The coverage property must be stated and verified for the observable multinomial model being used. If ‘exact 95%’ means at-least-95% coverage for every admissible observable probability vector, and the Γ-constrained projection retains every true admissible table whenever that vector is covered, the uniform contrast-coverage argument follows. The label alone does not establish correct cell definitions, a valid sampling model, or a faithful latent-table representation.
What would be a careful one-sentence statement of the plan, without presenting it as a result?

We will derive sharp candidate-minus-historical value extrema over jointly Γ-constrained latent tables, compare them with bounds obtained by subtracting marginal value intervals, and use projection of an exact 95% multinomial confidence region to certify strict improvement only if the projected lower contrast bound exceeds zero, subject to uniform coverage over the stated sensitivity model.

For the implementation activity, I want to benchmark joint versus marginal Γ-constrained extrema with exact-95% projection on two-stratum treatment-outcome-recording tables. What should the implementation actually compare?

It should compare two ways of bounding the *same* candidate-minus-historical policy value on the same admissible tables. The joint calculation optimizes that difference directly. The marginal calculation bounds each policy value separately and then subtracts the resulting endpoints. Run the comparison both at a fixed observable probability table, to examine the population bounds, and through the exact-95% confidence-region projection, to examine the resulting confidence bounds.

The benchmark should report the endpoints side by side. It should not treat a narrower joint interval as evidence of correct coverage or sharpness by itself; those require separate checks of the table representation, optimization, and projection.
What belongs in a two-stratum treatment-outcome-recording table?

At the observable level, each cell needs to distinguish the stratum, the treatment received, and whether the outcome was recorded. For recorded outcomes, it also distinguishes the observed outcome category. Outcomes in unrecorded cells are not observed; the latent table represents the possible outcome information behind those cells, together with whatever additional latent distinctions are needed to express the Γ restrictions and policy values.

The number of treatment and outcome categories, the policy rules, and the target-population stratum weights have not been specified here. Those definitions must be fixed before cell probabilities and value objectives can be implemented; ‘two-stratum’ alone does not determine them.
Should I solve a separate optimization in each stratum and add the answers?

Only if the fully specified model makes that decomposition valid. If the target value is a weighted sum of stratum-specific values and every constraint separates by stratum, the optimization may decompose, with the stated target weights. But a constraint shared across strata, an uncertain common quantity, or a confidence region that couples their observable probabilities can prevent a simple sum of separately computed extrema from being the desired joint result.

The implementation should therefore define the complete feasible set and objective first, then use stratum-wise decomposition only if it preserves exactly that optimization problem. Two strata do not, by themselves, imply independent latent mechanisms or separate confidence guarantees.
What is the shared object for the joint and marginal runs?

For any fixed observable probability vector q, use one set TΓ(q) of admissible two-stratum latent tables. Each table must map to q and satisfy the specified Γ-bounded assignment and recording odds ratios. Both policy values are functions of that same table. The joint run minimizes and maximizes their difference over TΓ(q); the marginal runs optimize each value over TΓ(q) and then combine their extrema.

Holding q, Γ, the policy definitions, the target population, and all other constraints fixed makes the comparison about joint versus marginal optimization—not about changing the sensitivity model between runs.
How should the Γ-bounded parts be represented without assuming that assignment and recording are the same mechanism?

Represent them as distinct constraints on the latent table. The assignment constraint limits the specified odds-ratio comparisons governing treatment receipt; the recording constraint limits the specified comparisons governing whether an outcome is recorded. Both use the proposed Γ sensitivity limit, but they have different events and may involve different conditioning and latent states.

The implementation needs explicit formulas for those comparisons, including how zero probabilities are handled. A single label saying ‘Γ-constrained’ cannot substitute for those formulas, and no numerical Γ value has been supplied for the benchmark.
What are the four marginal extrema I would need?

For each fixed q, you need the infimum and supremum of candidate-policy value, and the infimum and supremum of historical-policy value, over TΓ(q). The marginal-subtraction lower endpoint is the candidate infimum minus the historical supremum; its upper endpoint is the candidate supremum minus the historical infimum. The joint endpoints instead optimize candidate value minus historical value under one table at a time.

With a common, nonempty feasible set and well-defined values, the marginal interval contains the joint interval. Equality or strict inclusion in a particular benchmark remains to be determined by the calculations.
Would a strict gap between those endpoints prove that the joint optimization was implemented correctly?

No. A strict gap is compatible with the expected mathematical ordering, but an incorrect feasible set or optimization result could produce one too. A useful implementation check is that the joint lower endpoint is not below the marginal-subtraction lower endpoint and the joint upper endpoint is not above the marginal-subtraction upper endpoint, subject to numerical tolerances. Passing that check is necessary for a coherent comparison, not a proof that the extrema are global or sharp.

The reported bounds should also come from tables that satisfy the observable mapping and both Γ restrictions, or be accompanied by a justified limiting argument when an extremum is not attained.
How can the benchmark distinguish numerical failure from genuine equality between joint and marginal bounds?

It should treat a small reported gap as a numerical question until the optimization accuracy is established. One can check constraint satisfaction and objective values at returned feasible tables, and compare them with valid global bounds on each optimization problem. If those checks pin the endpoints down closely enough to resolve the gap, equality or strictness can be assessed at that precision. Merely obtaining similar printed numbers from two runs does not establish that the underlying population bounds coincide.
Does the benchmark have to claim a faster algorithm for either formulation?

No such claim follows from the activity. Benchmarking can compare computational behavior as well as bound widths, but any speed or scaling conclusion would require specified problems, measurement conditions, and actual results. Joint optimization addresses the appropriate contrast; that does not alone say whether it is faster or slower than the marginal calculations on the two-stratum tables.
For exact-95% projection, can I build one 95% region for each stratum and simply intersect the two?

Not without a joint-coverage argument. Two separate regions that each cover their own stratum’s probabilities with probability at least 95% do not automatically cover *both* true stratum vectors together with probability at least 95%. The projection needs a region with the stated at-least-95% guarantee for the full observable probability vector relevant to the two-stratum analysis, whether constructed jointly or through another procedure whose simultaneous coverage is justified.

The exact region must also match the sampling model used for the observable treatment-outcome-recording counts. The presence of two strata does not specify that model by itself.
What gets projected once that joint exact region is available?

For each observable probability vector q in the exact-95% region, consider every Γ-admissible two-stratum latent table in TΓ(q). Evaluate candidate-minus-historical value at each such table. The projected lower and upper endpoints are the infimum and supremum across all those compatible pairs (q,t).

For the marginal benchmark, take the extrema of each policy value across the *same projected feasible pairs*, then subtract the relevant endpoints. That keeps the confidence-level comparison aligned: both methods use the same exact region and sensitivity constraints.
If q varies across the confidence region, does the marginal subtraction lose more than just the shared latent table?

Potentially. Its candidate minimum and historical maximum can come from different latent tables *and* different observable probability vectors within the region. Directly projecting the contrast keeps the values associated with one compatible (q,t) pair in each evaluation. Thus the projected comparison can reflect both sources of compatibility. Whether either causes a strict gap is an output of the benchmark, not something established in advance.
What should happen if some probability vectors in the exact region have no compatible latent table?

Those vectors contribute no feasible (q,t) pair to the projection. If compatible pairs remain elsewhere in the region, optimize over those pairs. If the projected feasible set is empty, the implementation should flag that condition rather than return an improvement certificate from an empty optimization. It also matters for interpretation: a constraint violation or empty set is not a positive policy-value result.
How does the implementation activity connect to uniform at-least-95% coverage?

The intended coverage argument is that, for any true distribution in the stated Γ sensitivity model, its observable probability vector q* is in the exact region with probability at least 95%, uniformly over the applicable multinomial probabilities. When that happens, every true admissible latent table compatible with q* remains in the projection. The projected contrast set therefore includes the true improvement contrast—and, with complete projection, the entire identified contrast interval at q*—on that event.

Implementing the projection is necessary to realize that argument, but benchmarking widths or runtimes does not itself demonstrate coverage. The region’s exact simultaneous guarantee and the correctness of the projection have to be established separately.
Where should the improvement decision appear in the benchmark output?

After the projected contrast bounds, not after the fixed-q or marginal calculations alone. The criterion is whether the joint projected exact-95% *lower* bound on candidate-minus-historical value is strictly greater than zero. The benchmark can show how that lower bound compares with the marginal-subtraction counterpart, but no improvement decision follows until an actual projected endpoint and its coverage justification are available. This activity does not supply such an endpoint.
What if the marginal projected lower bound is positive too?

Then, provided the projection and coverage conditions hold, that more conservative lower bound would also support strict improvement. Joint optimization might still change the width of the reported contrast interval, or the two intervals might coincide. The point of comparing them is to determine what retaining shared-table compatibility contributes, not to assume marginal subtraction must fail.
And if the joint projected lower bound is positive but the marginal one is not?

That would be a consequential strict difference: the joint projection would meet the stated improvement criterion while marginal subtraction would not. It is a possible benchmark outcome, not a reported finding for these two-stratum tables. Before making that claim, the implementation would need to establish the Γ constraints, both global extrema, the exact-95% region, and the correctness of its projection.
Can I use the same two-stratum tables to check both sharpness and confidence coverage empirically?

They can support checks, but the two claims require different justifications. For sharpness, the issue is whether the latent-table formulation exactly represents all distributions allowed by the assumptions and whether the global contrast extrema are obtained. For coverage, the issue is whether the observable confidence region has its exact 95% guarantee uniformly under the sampling model and whether projection preserves all compatible contrasts. Computational examples may expose implementation errors or illustrate the resulting bounds, but they cannot replace those general arguments.

The restrictions must also cover the relevant conditioning and boundary cases.

Merely saying ‘bounded recording odds’ would leave open whether selective recording can depend on latent prognosis, the realized outcome, or both. The proposal permits an explicit sensitivity analysis of selective observation; it does not silently assume that unrecorded outcomes are missing at random.
Does a binary outcome also mean the treatment decision must be binary?

No. ‘Binary-outcome’ restricts the outcome to two categories. It does not, by itself, specify how many treatment choices there are or what decisions the candidate and historical policies may assign. Those policy and treatment definitions would have to be supplied to make the optimization concrete.
How would you define a positive policy gain with a binary outcome?

Define the value of each policy using a stated outcome coding and target population, then set Δ equal to candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value. If the binary outcome is coded 1 for the desirable event and 0 otherwise, Δ>0 means the candidate increases the probability of that event in the target population. If 1 instead denotes an undesirable event, a higher raw outcome probability would not mean a clinical improvement; the value or utility definition must account for that.

‘Positive gain’ therefore means Δ>0 on the explicitly chosen value scale. The proposal does not specify which outcome is favorable or give a particular policy’s value.
Why use the historical policy as part of the optimization instead of evaluating its observed outcomes directly?

The comparison has to put the candidate and historical policies on a common target and value scale. Selective recording can affect what is known about outcomes under historical decisions, and unmeasured confounding can affect policy-value identification. The proposed contrast evaluates both policy values under each admissible full-data distribution, so the improvement bound respects their common latent structure.

An average of recorded outcomes under historical decisions is not automatically the historical policy’s target value when recording is selective. The precise historical policy must also be defined; its name alone is not an identifying assumption.
What is being optimized in the linear-fractional program?

For each admissible full-data representation consistent with an observable probability vector, evaluate Δ: the candidate policy’s value minus the historical policy’s value. Minimize Δ for a lower improvement bound and maximize it for an upper bound, subject to the treatment, recording, and observable-data constraints.

A linear-fractional formulation represents the relevant objective or conditional quantities as ratios of linear functions of suitable nonnegative variables. Whether the *entire* problem can be handled as a particular linear-fractional program depends on the precise parameterization and constraints. The proposal calls for developing that formulation; it does not supply its variables or prove that a generic linear-fractional algorithm already solves every version of the model.
Would it be sufficient to solve separate programs for the candidate and historical values, then subtract their endpoints?

That would give a conservative comparator if both programs use the appropriate common feasible set, but it need not give sharp improvement bounds. The candidate minimum and historical maximum might require different full-data distributions. Directly optimizing their difference requires one admissible distribution to determine both values in each evaluation. A conclusion about *positive gains* is particularly sensitive to the lower endpoint, so discarding that compatibility can make the certificate unnecessarily difficult to obtain.
How does binary outcome information help without identifying the missing outcomes?

If the outcome is coded 0 or 1, each unrecorded outcome is constrained to those possibilities rather than an unspecified numerical range. The distribution of unrecorded outcomes is still unknown. The Γ and Λ restrictions, together with the observable cell probabilities and any other explicitly stated assumptions, limit which completions are admissible. Optimizing across those completions yields a range rather than treating an unobserved binary response as recovered.
What would make the resulting policy-gain bounds sharp?

The optimization must range over all and only the full-data distributions permitted by the observed probabilities and the precisely stated sensitivity model, with both policies evaluated under each distribution. A feasible configuration attaining an endpoint—or an admissible sequence approaching it—shows that the endpoint cannot be tightened under those assumptions. A valid global bound shows nothing more extreme is feasible.

Simply obtaining an optimum from a convenient relaxation is not enough. Nor does calling the formulation linear-fractional establish that its feasible variables represent every compatible treatment, recording, and binary-outcome configuration.
Do Γ and Λ odds restrictions necessarily make that feasible set convex?

Not necessarily. It depends on the variables and the exact form of the odds comparisons. Ratios of conditional probabilities and restrictions coupling latent assignment with recording can yield constraints that need careful reformulation. A linear-fractional objective does not by itself guarantee convexity, global solvability by a single linear program, or attainment of an endpoint. Those properties would have to be proved or otherwise justified for the proposed formulation.
Could one transform a linear-fractional objective into a linear one?

Under suitable conditions, such as a denominator with a known positive sign over the relevant feasible set, a linear-fractional objective can sometimes be transformed or handled through equivalent feasibility problems. But whether an equivalent tractable formulation exists here depends on the coupled Γ and Λ constraints and on how policy values and observable probabilities are represented. The transformation must preserve the feasible distributions and both global extrema; a transformation of the objective alone would not address a relaxed sensitivity model.
What happens if an odds denominator can vanish?

Then an odds ratio may be undefined, and the model must explicitly say whether such boundary distributions are excluded, interpreted through limiting constraints, or handled another way. The same issue matters for any linear-fractional expression: its denominator must be defined over the configurations at which it is evaluated. These conventions affect the feasible set and possibly whether endpoints are attained, so they cannot be left implicit while claiming sharp bounds.
Are the treatment and recording constraints independent once we give them separate parameters?

No. Γ and Λ specify distinct sensitivity limits, but the two mechanisms still have to coexist in one full-data distribution. An optimization must not combine an assignment pattern from one latent population with a recording pattern from an incompatible one. Separate parameters do not authorize separate, independently chosen confounder mixtures for a single candidate-minus-historical contrast.
Where does multinomial sampling enter this proposal?

The observable categories—for example, the treatment and recording distinctions and the outcome category when recorded—would define a vector of cell probabilities under a stated multinomial sampling model. Observed counts provide uncertainty about that vector. Exact test inversion builds a confidence region for the possible observable probability vectors, instead of substituting the observed proportions as though they were the population probabilities.

The categories and sampling structure must be defined before a particular multinomial test can be specified. Binary outcomes alone do not uniquely determine the observable table.
What exactly does it mean to invert an exact multinomial test?

For each proposed observable probability vector q, test whether the observed multinomial counts are compatible with q. Keep the vectors whose tests do not reject; their collection is the inverted confidence region. To obtain at least 95% coverage, the rejection probability for a *true* q must be no greater than 5% at every q in the stated observable parameter space. The proposal does not prescribe a particular test statistic or acceptance rule, so the word ‘exact’ must be supported by the actual test construction.
Is a 95% region for observable probabilities already a 95% region for the policy gain?

Not by itself. It must be projected through the Γ-and-Λ-constrained full-data model. For every q in the inverted multinomial region, consider every admissible full-data distribution that maps to q, evaluate its candidate-minus-historical value contrast, and collect the resulting contrasts. The projected lower endpoint is the infimum across all those compatible pairs. Optimizing only at the observed proportions or at a center of the region would not be that projection.
How does exact test inversion yield uniform coverage after projection?

Suppose P is any data-generating distribution in the stated sensitivity model, q_P its observable multinomial probability vector, and Δ_P its policy gain. If the exact inverted region contains q_P, then a complete projection also contains P’s admissible full-data configuration and hence Δ_P. Therefore the projected set covers Δ_P whenever the observable region covers q_P.

If that observable event has probability at least 0.95 for every allowed P, the projected set covers the true gain with probability at least 0.95 *uniformly* over the stated sensitivity model. The argument requires both uniform test-size control and a projection that does not omit admissible configurations. It describes what this proposal must establish, not a verification of a particular implementation.
Could the projection cover the whole population identified interval, not just the true gain?

Yes, if it includes every Γ-and-Λ-admissible full-data distribution compatible with each retained observable vector. On the event that the true q_P lies in the region, the projection then includes every contrast in the population identified set at q_P, not merely the contrast under P’s particular full-data configuration. That is a stronger inclusion statement. It should be distinguished from simply reporting that a procedure covers the true gain.
What if the exact region includes vectors that cannot arise under the sensitivity model?

Those vectors contribute no policy contrasts to the projection because they have no compatible full-data configuration. Projection takes the union over pairs consisting of a retained observable vector *and* an admissible distribution mapping to it. An entirely empty projected set is not evidence of a positive gain; model compatibility or the construction would have to be examined.
Is ‘exact 95%’ a promise that the projected coverage equals precisely 95%?

No. The desired guarantee is **at least** 95% uniformly over the stated model. Multinomial tests can be conservative because of discrete counts, and projection can add conservatism. Exactness concerns controlling the test’s rejection probability under the specified sampling model without relying solely on an unverified asymptotic approximation; it does not force equality of the coverage probability to 0.95 at each distribution.
So what exact numerical condition would certify a positive gain?

The lower endpoint of the *projected* candidate-minus-historical policy-value contrast set must be strictly greater than zero. Then every contrast retained under the observable confidence region and the Γ-and-Λ sensitivity assumptions is positive. With the stipulated uniformly valid exact-95% construction, that yields the proposed confidence-based certification. A positive point estimate or a fixed-q lower bound does not, on its own, meet this condition.
Would a lower endpoint of zero count as a positive-gain certificate?

No. A lower endpoint at zero does not rule out no gain, and a negative lower endpoint does not rule out a loss. Either fails the strict-positive criterion, even if some values in the projected set are positive. Failing to certify is different from establishing that the candidate policy is worse.
If the binary outcome is unfavorable when it equals one, could the same positive-gain rule still be used?

Yes, but only after defining policy *value* so that higher value means the desired clinical direction—for example, by choosing an appropriate utility coding. If value is instead the raw probability of an unfavorable outcome, a positive difference would mean more of that outcome, not an improvement. The proposal needs to specify its value scale before interpreting the sign of the lower bound.
Can we claim that this proposal already yields sharper bounds than the Γ-only formulation?

No comparison result follows from proposing Γ for treatment odds and Λ for recording odds. The feasible set changes with the exact restrictions and their values, and the binary-outcome linear-fractional formulation still needs a sharpness argument. This proposal specifies a way to analyze bounded treatment confounding and selective recording and to seek positive-gain certificates; it supplies no computed bound-width comparison.
Does selecting Γ and Λ after seeing which values produce a positive gain preserve the proposed confidence interpretation?

A claim must identify the sensitivity model to which it applies. If Γ and Λ are selected or reported on the basis of results, the interpretation of any confidence statement must account for the actual selection and the scope of the region or simultaneous procedure being claimed. A confidence region with uniform coverage over a *specified* model does not by itself establish a positive-gain certificate for an unstated or unrestricted collection of sensitivity choices.
What if the candidate policy assigns treatments for which the observable data have little support?

The bounds may then be wide, because the data provide limited information about outcomes relevant to that policy. Binary outcomes still place the outcome on a bounded scale, but that does not create missing treatment-outcome information. The proposal must state its support assumptions and any constraints used where treatment or recording probabilities are at a boundary. Exact confidence coverage does not guarantee that the projected lower bound will be informative or positive.
How should we distinguish the proposed method’s three claims: sharpness, coverage, and improvement?

Sharpness asks whether optimizing over the precisely stated Γ-and-Λ full-data model yields the tightest compatible population contrast bounds. Coverage asks whether exact multinomial test inversion, followed by complete projection, includes the relevant gain or identified set with probability at least 95% uniformly over that model. Improvement asks whether the resulting projected lower contrast bound is strictly above zero. Establishing one does not automatically establish the other two.
What is the most careful compact statement of the proposal?

“For binary outcomes, formulate joint candidate-minus-historical value bounds through linear-fractional optimization under explicitly defined Γ-bounded treatment-assignment odds and Λ-bounded outcome-recording odds; invert exact multinomial tests and project their 95% confidence region through the sensitivity model, certifying a positive policy gain only when the projected lower contrast bound exceeds zero.” The formulation, sharpness, and any actual certification remain to be established.
Can linear-fractional extrema remain sharp when treatment and outcome recording share an unrestricted confounder but have separate Γ and Λ odds bounds?

They can in principle, but the linear-fractional form does not itself guarantee sharpness. The decisive question is whether the program’s feasible set represents exactly the full-data distributions allowed by the two odds restrictions, the observable data, and a *shared* latent confounder. “Unrestricted” cannot mean that treatment and recording may each choose a different confounder distribution: they must still coexist in one distribution. No sharpness result for this formulation is established by posing the question.
What is unrestricted about the confounder, then?

Unless the model says otherwise, its distribution and its relationships with outcomes are not specified beyond the observable constraints and the stated sensitivity restrictions. The Γ bound limits the designated treatment-odds comparisons; the Λ bound limits the designated recording-odds comparisons. Neither, just by being stated, fixes the confounder’s support, its distribution, or every way it may relate to potential outcomes. The exact scope depends on how the two odds comparisons are defined.
If assignment and recording each satisfy their own bound, why might a program still be non-sharp?

Separate inequalities need not guarantee that the probabilities used in the two parts arise from one joint latent distribution. An optimization could combine treatment behavior associated with one mixture of confounder states with recording behavior associated with another. Its objective might then take a value no admissible full-data distribution can produce. That would make an otherwise valid outer bound loose. This is a possibility to check, not a conclusion about every linear-fractional program with Γ and Λ constraints.
Is the problem that Γ and Λ are numerically different?

No. The parameters may differ because they bound different mechanisms. Compatibility concerns the joint probability structure, not equality of the sensitivity limits. A shared confounder can affect treatment and recording differently while the resulting conditional odds satisfy their respective Γ and Λ restrictions.
Would forcing the two mechanisms to have identical conditional probabilities solve it?

That would generally be a different, stronger condition, not what sharing a confounder means. Treatment assignment and outcome recording are different events. The relevant requirement is that their conditional probabilities, along with the outcome quantities needed for policy value, can be assembled under the *same* confounder distribution. One should not obtain a seemingly sharp interval by imposing equality that the stated sensitivity model does not require.
What would be a precise test for sharpness of the lower improvement bound?

First show that every feasible point in the program corresponds to a full-data distribution satisfying the observable constraints and both stated odds bounds; otherwise the calculated infimum might be unattainably low. Then show the converse: every allowed full-data distribution is represented by a feasible point, or at least that the representation captures or approaches every contrast needed to determine the infimum. Finally, establish the global optimum of the correctly represented problem. An admissible distribution attaining the reported lower bound, together with a valid global lower-bound argument, would provide an especially direct endpoint certificate.
Why allow ‘approaches’ instead of insisting on attainment?

A sharp lower bound is an infimum. The feasible set might admit a sequence of distributions with policy gains approaching that infimum without containing a distribution that attains it, depending on the model’s boundary conventions. Sharpness requires that the bound cannot be raised while retaining every admissible or arbitrarily approachable gain; exact attainment is a stronger property. The formulation should distinguish the two.
Does turning the objective into a linear-fractional expression preserve the required joint structure?

Not automatically. It is possible to parameterize a genuine joint distribution and express the relevant quantities in linear-fractional form, but an algebraically convenient transformation could also relax or omit compatibility constraints. The odds ratios themselves require attention to conditional denominators and boundary probabilities. A reformulation must be shown equivalent to the stated feasible set, not merely equivalent to an objective evaluated on a subset of variables.
What if the program has a globally certified optimum?

That certifies the optimum *of the program as written*. It establishes the desired sharp policy-gain bound only if the program’s feasible set is exact for the shared-confounder sensitivity model. A globally solved relaxation can still have a conservative lower endpoint that no permitted distribution can attain or approach.
Can I impose both odds limits independently within each confounder state?

Whether that expresses the intended model depends on the comparisons specified by Γ and Λ.
