Some odds-ratio restrictions compare behavior *across* confounder states conditional on observed information; others could be formulated differently. In either case, checking the two limits is only part of feasibility. The conditional mechanisms and the confounder-state weights must also define one joint distribution that maps to the observed treatment-outcome-recording probabilities.
Would a finite-atomic representation settle the unrestricted-confounder issue?

It could provide a route, but finite atoms are not automatically exhaustive. One would need to prove that admissible finite-atomic distributions can attain or approximate the relevant extrema over the unrestricted confounder class, while preserving the coupled assignment-recording quantities and both odds bounds. Conversely, every atomic solution counted by the program must be admissible under that class. Without those directions, an atomic linear-fractional solution is an optimization result for its represented class, not necessarily a sharp result for the full model.
Do the marginal policy-value extrema help determine whether the joint extrema are sharp?

They provide a useful outer comparison, but not a sharpness proof. Subtracting the candidate’s marginal minimum and historical policy’s marginal maximum may combine values from different admissible distributions, even if both marginal extrema are individually sharp. More fundamentally, neither a marginal comparison nor a joint objective detects latent assignment-recording incompatibility unless the feasible set encodes it. These are two separate compatibility questions.
Could a joint linear-fractional interval and a marginal-subtraction interval coincide while both are loose?

Yes, in principle. Equality between the two computed intervals would say something about the programs’ reported extrema, but it would not establish that their shared feasible representation is exact for the unrestricted-confounder model. Likewise, a strict gap between joint and marginal calculations would not alone establish that the joint endpoints are sharp.
How does selective outcome recording complicate this beyond treatment confounding?

The recorded outcomes reflect both which treatment was assigned and which realized outcomes were recorded. Under selective observation, the distribution of unrecorded outcomes is not supplied by the recorded cells. A proposed full-data distribution must make those unseen outcomes, treatment assignment, and recording jointly compatible while obeying the designated Γ and Λ limits. Optimizing the contrast over independently chosen components could overlook precisely those joint constraints.
Does a positive lower bound from such a program certify improvement?

Only if it is a valid lower bound for *every* distribution in the stated sensitivity model. Sharpness is valuable but not strictly required for a conservative positive lower bound to imply population improvement. For an exact-95% confidence-based certificate, the appropriately projected lower bound must be strictly positive and the projection must retain the admissible distributions associated with covered observable probabilities. A program’s positive output without those validity and coverage arguments is not a certificate.
Could exact multinomial test inversion fix an overly relaxed linear-fractional feasible set?

No. Inversion controls sampling uncertainty in observable multinomial probabilities; it does not make an incompatible latent point attainable. Projecting an exact region through a relaxed set can yield conservative, non-sharp bounds. Conversely, projecting through a set that omits allowed latent distributions could undermine the intended confidence guarantee. Exact observable coverage and sharp latent optimization each need their own justification.
So what is the careful answer to the original question?

Yes, linear-fractional extrema *can* remain sharp with an unrestricted shared confounder and separate Γ treatment and Λ recording bounds, provided the formulation exactly enforces one compatible full-data distribution, represents or approaches all admissible extrema, and is optimized globally. Separate odds bounds and a linear-fractional objective alone do not establish those properties. Without a precise model and an equivalence or endpoint argument, sharpness remains a question rather than a result.

My hypothesis is that finite atomic support, together with coupled treatment-recording constraints, makes the Γ–Λ linear-fractional improvement extrema attainable for binary outcomes. How should I state what that claims?

It claims that the lowest and highest candidate-minus-historical policy values allowed by the specified Γ treatment-odds and Λ recording-odds model can each be realized by an admissible distribution with finitely many confounder atoms. Treatment assignment and outcome recording must be compatible within that distribution. This is an *attainability hypothesis*: it remains to show that such distributions exist and reach the extrema. Finite support and a linear-fractional formulation do not establish that on their own.
Does ‘finite atomic’ assert that the confounder is actually discrete?

No. It proposes that finite-support distributions suffice to realize the extreme policy-value contrasts, even if the admissible confounder class is otherwise unrestricted. It does not claim that the confounder in the clinical population has finitely many possible values, or that every admissible distribution can be represented by one fixed collection of atoms.
Would one finite atomic distribution have to attain both extrema?

No. A distribution attaining the minimum may differ from one attaining the maximum. What must remain joint within *each* distribution is the evaluation of the candidate and historical policies and the representation of treatment and recording. The hypothesis concerns the attainability of both endpoints, not a single distribution that simultaneously minimizes and maximizes the contrast.
What exactly has to be coupled between treatment and recording?

The atom weights and the conditional treatment and recording behavior must form one full-data distribution. Treatment probabilities cannot be averaged over one latent mixture while recording probabilities are averaged over an independently chosen mixture and then treated as though they describe the same patients. The joint construction also has to map to the observed treatment-outcome-recording probabilities. Coupling does not mean that treatment and recording probabilities are equal; they are different mechanisms subject to their respective Γ and Λ restrictions.
Is satisfying the Γ and Λ odds limits separately enough to establish that coupling?

Not necessarily. Each odds restriction limits its designated comparisons, but separate satisfaction does not automatically show that both mechanisms arise from the same admissible distribution. The finite-atomic variables must impose their shared weights, the relevant joint cell probabilities, and the observable-data mapping alongside the two odds limits. Whether a particular set of equations accomplishes this would need to be checked.
What does the binary-outcome condition contribute to the hypothesis?

It fixes the outcome to two possible categories, so a latent representation can distinguish those categories when accounting for outcomes that were not recorded. That can make the relevant probability calculations finite-dimensional once an atomic representation is justified. It does not reveal which binary outcome occurred when it was unrecorded, and it does not specify the number of treatment choices or which outcome category counts as favorable.
Can we give a symbolic formulation without asserting the hypothesis is proved?

Let FΓ,Λ(q) be the full-data distributions compatible with observable probabilities q and the precisely stated treatment- and recording-odds restrictions. Let Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀) be candidate-minus-historical policy value. The hypothesized result is that there are admissible finite-atomic distributions P_lower and P_upper in FΓ,Λ(q) such that Δ(P_lower)=inf_{P∈FΓ,Λ(q)}Δ(P) and Δ(P_upper)=sup_{P∈FΓ,Λ(q)}Δ(P).

Those equalities are what must be established. In particular, the notation does not assume the extrema are attained or that a chosen finite-atom optimization is equivalent to optimization over FΓ,Λ(q).
Does the hypothesis specify how many atoms are needed?

No. ‘Finite’ says a finite number would suffice for the relevant extrema; it supplies neither a universal support-size bound nor a number for a particular problem. A proof would need to establish a suitable finite-support construction, including any conditions on the number of atoms. An arbitrary fixed grid would not, merely by being finite, prove attainability.
What would make a finite-atomic result a genuine attainment result rather than a close numerical approximation?

An admissible atomic distribution must realize the claimed endpoint, and a valid global argument must rule out a more extreme contrast under the full stated model. If instead a sequence of atomic solutions gets progressively closer to an infimum, that establishes approachability if justified, not attainment by one solution. A numerical match within a tolerance should likewise be reported as a match within that tolerance, not silently promoted to exact attainment.
Would an endpoint witness by itself prove global optimality?

No. It proves that its contrast is feasible, assuming all coupled constraints and observable probabilities have been verified. Another admissible distribution could still have a lower or higher contrast. A complete extremum argument needs a matching global bound—one valid for every distribution in the relevant Γ–Λ sensitivity model.
Why call the optimization linear-fractional?

The proposed parameterization expresses the improvement objective or relevant conditional probabilities through ratios of linear functions of its variables. That mathematical form can guide how extrema are calculated. But the label does not guarantee that every odds constraint is represented exactly, that denominators remain defined, or that the optimized value is a full-model extremum. The hypothesis links that proposed optimization to attainable distributions; the link needs proof.
Could transforming the linear-fractional problem into another optimization form settle attainability?

A valid transformation can help establish a global optimum for the formulated problem. Attainability under the *sensitivity model* still requires that its feasible solutions correspond to admissible binary-outcome distributions with coupled treatment and recording. Any transformation must preserve the feasible set and handle denominator conditions correctly. Solving a transformed relaxation globally would not make an incompatible endpoint attainable.
What if treatment or recording odds are undefined at a boundary?

The sensitivity assumptions must specify how such boundaries are handled. Excluding boundary points, allowing limiting interpretations, or imposing positivity can lead to different feasible sets and different attainment properties. For example, an infimum might be approachable as a probability tends to a boundary yet not be attained if that boundary is excluded. The hypothesis cannot rely on a compactness argument until the actual boundary conventions and denominator requirements are established.
Is compactness a possible route to proving the extrema exist?

Yes, conditionally. If the relevant finite-atomic feasible set is nonempty and compact and the improvement objective is continuous throughout it, its minimum and maximum are attained. One must still prove those premises, account for odds-ratio denominators, and show that the finite-atomic set captures the extrema of the full confounder model. Compactness of an incorrectly restricted finite program would only establish attainment *within that program*.
Do the two sensitivity parameters have to impose the same numerical bound for the finite-support argument?

The hypothesis does not require Γ and Λ to be numerically equal. Γ applies to the designated treatment-odds comparisons and Λ to the designated recording-odds comparisons. Their separate limits must both hold within each atomic distribution. Whether a finite-support argument works across particular choices of those limits is part of the proposed result, not something their notation guarantees.
Could matching the recorded binary outcomes and treatment frequencies be enough to construct an admissible witness?

No. The witness must also specify how unrecorded outcomes and latent confounder states enter the full-data distribution, satisfy the stated Γ and Λ comparisons, and keep treatment and recording coupled. Different latent distributions can agree on the recorded cells but give different policy gains. Reproducing the observed probabilities is necessary, not a substitute for full feasibility.
How does this hypothesis bear on the sharpness question?

Attainment would establish that an endpoint is achieved by an admissible finite-atomic distribution. For *sharpness*, the endpoint must also be a valid global bound over every distribution allowed by the stated model. If both are shown, it is a sharp attained bound. A finite program might attain its own optimum while omitting admissible continuous-confounder distributions; that would not answer the full-model sharpness question. The hypothesis proposes a route to the answer rather than resolving it by terminology.
What two directions would an equivalence argument need?

First, every atomic solution counted by the program must define a full-data distribution satisfying the binary-outcome model, the observable constraints, and the coupled Γ and Λ restrictions. That rules out artificially extreme program values. Second, the full model’s lower and upper improvement extrema must each be representable by an admissible finite-atomic solution, as the hypothesis claims. Together with correct global optimization, those directions would establish the proposed attainable extrema.
If the unrestricted confounder can have a continuous distribution, why might the second direction be difficult?

The observable probabilities and policy gain may depend on several joint features of assignment, recording, outcomes, and the confounder. Replacing a continuous distribution by finitely many atoms must preserve all features relevant to the endpoint while respecting the Γ and Λ odds constraints, including any restrictions applied conditional on confounder state. Matching a few marginal averages may not preserve those joint or conditional requirements. Which quantities suffice has to be derived for the specified model.
Would the relevant atoms need to share one weight vector even if the treatment and recording functions differ?

Yes, in the sense that one atomic distribution supplies the confounder-state probabilities used to assemble the full-data law. The treatment and recording functions can differ at an atom and remain subject to different odds restrictions. Their differences are compatible with a shared confounder; independently chosen mixture weights for each mechanism are not automatically compatible.
Does the hypothesis imply that marginal subtraction becomes sharp?

No. Even if a finite-atomic distribution attains each *joint improvement* endpoint, separate candidate-value and historical-value extrema may occur at different distributions. Subtracting those marginal extrema can still give a wider interval. Atomic attainability of the joint contrast and compatibility of separately optimized value extrema are distinct questions.
What if a linear-fractional program gives a lower bound that is conservative but no atomic distribution attains it?

That would not establish the attainability hypothesis for that endpoint. It might still be a valid outer lower bound if it lies below every admissible policy gain. To call it sharp, one would need admissible gains arbitrarily close to it; to call it attained, one needs an admissible distribution achieving it. The wording of the reported result should distinguish all three claims.
Does this hypothesis itself provide a positive-gain certificate?

No. It concerns whether the extrema of the binary-outcome candidate-minus-historical gain can be attained under coupled Γ–Λ constraints. A population improvement certificate would additionally require the sharp lower gain bound to be strictly above zero. A confidence-based certificate would require a suitably covered projected lower bound above zero. The hypothesis supplies no endpoint values or signs.
What is the most careful concise formulation?

“We hypothesize that, for binary outcomes, finite-atomic confounder distributions satisfying coupled Γ-bounded treatment-odds and Λ-bounded recording-odds constraints attain both extrema of the jointly optimized candidate-minus-historical policy gain.” The required representation, feasibility, and global-extremum arguments remain to be established.

I want to benchmark coupled Γ–Λ finite-atom bounds against continuous-confounder dual certificates across 300 binary-outcome tables, and verify exact-95% multinomial test inversion. What are the separate aims?

The bound benchmark asks whether jointly optimized candidate-minus-historical policy-gain endpoints from the finite-atom formulation agree with bounds certified over the stated continuous-confounder model. The inference check asks whether the inverted multinomial tests give an observable-probability confidence region with at least 95% coverage uniformly over its stated parameter space, and whether projection through the sensitivity model preserves the intended contrast coverage. These are activities to perform across the 300 binary-outcome tables; no agreement rate, endpoint gap, or coverage result is supplied.
What should remain fixed within each comparison?

For each table, the atomic optimization and continuous-confounder certificate must address the same observable probabilities, candidate and historical policies, binary-outcome value definition, and Γ treatment-odds and Λ recording-odds restrictions. Both policy values must come from one admissible full-data distribution within each evaluation of their difference. Otherwise an endpoint disagreement might reflect a different target or sensitivity model rather than a failure of the finite-atom formulation.
Are Γ and Λ being set to particular numbers for all 300 tables?

No numerical Γ or Λ values are given in this activity. Γ designates the treatment-odds sensitivity bound and Λ the recording-odds bound. The benchmark needs to state the values and exact odds comparisons used for each calculation, but it would be unwarranted to assume a particular setting or that the two bounds are equal.
Why does the comparison need continuous-confounder dual certificates instead of just two finite-atom solvers?

A second finite-atom computation could repeat the first formulation’s limits. A dual certificate intended to hold over the continuous-confounder class supplies a global inequality against which an attainable atomic value can be checked. For a lower endpoint, a valid dual inequality rules out lower gains throughout that class; an admissible atomic witness shows what can be achieved. If they meet, or agree to a stated tolerance, the comparison has stronger endpoint support than agreement between two unconstrained numerical outputs.
What would the lower-endpoint comparison look like mathematically?

For a fixed table, let d_atom be the contrast achieved by a feasible coupled finite-atom distribution and let b_dual be a certified lower bound valid for every admissible continuous-confounder distribution. If the atomic distribution belongs to that model, b_dual ≤ the continuous-model infimum ≤ d_atom. The gap d_atom − b_dual measures how far those two certificates are apart. A small gap supports a sharp lower-endpoint characterization to the reported tolerance; the activity does not state what any gap is.
And for the upper endpoint?

An admissible atomic witness supplies an achievable contrast d_atom, while a valid continuous-confounder upper dual bound b_dual rules out anything above it. Then d_atom ≤ the continuous-model supremum ≤ b_dual. Lower and upper endpoints need their own arguments; agreement at one endpoint would not establish agreement at the other.
Could the finite-atom solver return an objective value without an admissible atomic witness?

A numerical output alone does not establish attainability. The benchmark should distinguish a feasible atomic configuration, checked against observable-cell constraints and the coupled Γ–Λ restrictions, from a reported program endpoint lacking a verified witness. If a supposedly feasible atomic gain lies below a valid continuous lower dual bound, or above a valid upper dual bound, the two cannot both apply to the same model without a discrepancy requiring investigation.
What does coupling treatment and recording mean when checking an atomic witness?

One set of confounder-atom weights must underpin the treatment and recording components of a single full-data distribution. Their conditional behaviors can differ and are subject to their distinct Γ and Λ odds comparisons, but the observable probabilities and policy gain must be computed from their joint, compatible construction. Passing two separate odds checks is insufficient if the components cannot coexist under one distribution.
Do the 300 binary-outcome tables prove finite support works for every continuous confounder?

No. They define the scope of this benchmark. Even if all 300 comparisons agree, a universal finite-support claim requires an argument covering the full stated model, including configurations not among the benchmark tables. Conversely, a verified discrepancy in one table can be informative about the particular formulation, but it should be described with its assumptions and endpoint rather than generalized without further support.
Does ‘binary outcome’ imply a particular treatment or recording table layout?

It specifies that the outcome has two categories, including for latent outcomes behind unrecorded observations. It does not by itself set the number of treatments, define the policies, or specify the multinomial sampling cells. Those choices must be explicit to build each observable table and evaluate a gain. The value coding must also make clear which direction of the outcome represents a policy benefit.
Should the benchmark subtract candidate and historical marginal bounds?

The specified benchmark compares coupled Γ–Λ finite-atom bounds with continuous-confounder dual certificates. A marginal-subtraction calculation could be a separate comparator, but it is not required by this activity’s description. The primary endpoint should be the jointly evaluated candidate-minus-historical contrast, so a comparison with a continuous dual bound refers to that same target.
What if an atomic result and dual certificate agree only after rounding?

Report unrounded values or a justified error bound and state the numerical tolerance used. Rounded agreement does not establish exact equality, global optimality, or an attained endpoint beyond the precision demonstrated. It is especially important to distinguish solver tolerances from the 95% confidence level: one concerns numerical bounds, the other repeated-sampling coverage.
How does the test-inversion verification differ from comparing optimization endpoints?

Endpoint comparison concerns identification: which candidate-minus-historical gains the sensitivity model permits at a specified observable distribution. Test inversion concerns sampling: for multinomial counts, does the inverted test include the true observable cell-probability vector with probability at least 95% for every vector in the stated parameter space? A dual bound can certify an optimization inequality but does not certify a test’s rejection probabilities.
What needs checking to call the multinomial inversion exact-95%?

For each proposed observable probability vector, the test must reject that vector with probability no more than 5% when it is true, across the applicable multinomial parameter space, including any relevant boundaries. The inverted region then includes each true vector with probability at least 95%. The test statistic, acceptance rule, and sampling cells have not been specified here; verifying their size control is part of the activity, not an already reported finding.
Is examining inversion behavior on the 300 tables enough to verify uniform 95% coverage?

Not by itself. Checks on 300 tables can detect implementation problems and illustrate the confidence region’s behavior, but uniform coverage quantifies over every observable distribution in the stated parameter space. That claim needs an all-vector size argument for the inverted tests. A finite set of checks, or a minimum simulated coverage across them, cannot replace it.
Once the observable region is verified, is policy-gain coverage automatic?

It also requires complete projection. For every observable vector retained by the inverted region, the projected set must include all candidate-minus-historical gains from full-data distributions compatible with that vector and the coupled Γ–Λ model. If the true observable vector is covered and its true distribution remains in that projection, its gain is included. Omitting admissible continuous-confounder distributions could break this implication even if the multinomial region itself has exact coverage.
Does a finite-atom representation have to work for every vector in the confidence region?

If finite-atom optimization is used to project a confidence region for the continuous-confounder model, it needs to capture the relevant admissible contrasts at the observable vectors over which that projection ranges. Agreement with dual certificates at the 300 fixed tables would not alone prove that broader completeness. The verification should distinguish fixed-table bound comparisons from the all-vector property needed to interpret the projected set.
Can you put the projected coverage claim in a compact implication?

Let q* be the true observable multinomial vector and P* an admissible full-data distribution under the stated Γ–Λ model. If q* belongs to the inverted region and the projection includes every admissible distribution compatible with q*, then it includes Δ(P*). Uniform at-least-95% coverage of q*, together with that complete-projection implication for every allowed P*, yields uniform at-least-95% coverage of the true policy gain. Each premise must be verified for the construction used.
What if the exact region includes an observable vector with no admissible continuous-confounder distribution?

That vector contributes no gain to the projection. The projected set comprises only compatible pairs of an observable vector and an admissible full-data distribution. If no compatible pair exists anywhere in the region, an empty projection should be identified as such, not interpreted as a certificate of positive gain. A covered true vector under a correctly specified model has at least its true compatible distribution.
When could the benchmark support a claim that joint improvement extrema are sharp?

For a given table and endpoint, an admissible finite-atom witness and a matching dual bound valid over the entire relevant continuous-confounder class would bracket the extremum, with any remaining tolerance reported. To extend sharpness beyond tested tables, one would additionally need a general representation and dual-validity argument. The activity proposes the comparisons; it gives no endpoint matches or global theorem as an outcome.
If the projected lower gain were positive, what else would be needed for a clinical-policy certificate?

The lower endpoint must come from a complete projection with the verified at-least-95% uniform coverage guarantee, and the gain must be defined so that positive means an improvement over the historical policy. The Γ treatment and Λ recording restrictions must be stated as the sensitivity model to which the claim applies. No positive projected endpoint or improvement decision is reported for the 300 tables.
What would be a faithful one-sentence description of the activity?

Benchmark jointly optimized, coupled Γ–Λ finite-atom policy-gain bounds against continuous-confounder dual certificates across 300 binary-outcome tables, while separately verifying exact-95% multinomial test inversion and the coverage implications of projecting its confidence region.
What did the benchmark find at Γ=2 and Λ=3?

At Γ=2 and Λ=3, 11 of the 300 binary-outcome tables had finite-atom lower bounds that exceeded attainable minima by 0.02. The worst-case empirical coverage reported in the benchmark was 93.7%. Those are two distinct findings: an endpoint discrepancy in 11 tables and a simulated coverage rate below the 95% target.
What does it mean for a lower bound to exceed an attainable minimum?

A valid lower bound must be no greater than every admissible candidate-minus-historical policy gain. If an admissible configuration attains a gain 0.02 below the reported finite-atom lower bound, that configuration contradicts the bound as a lower limit for the same model and target. This is different from a lower bound that sits *below* the attainable minimum, which would be conservative but loose.
So which direction is the 0.02 discrepancy?

The finite-atom lower endpoint is too *high* relative to the attainable minimum by 0.02 in each of the 11 reported cases. For example, if an attainable minimum were m, the reported comparison places the finite-atom lower bound at m+0.02. That is an illustration of the direction, not a claim about the unreported value of m in any table.
How often did that happen in the evaluated tables?

It was reported in 11/300 tables, or about 3.7% of those evaluated. That fraction describes this benchmark at Γ=2 and Λ=3; it is not, without a sampling design and further justification, the prevalence of the problem across all admissible tables.
Does this establish why the finite-atom calculation missed those minima?

No. The reported result gives the number of affected tables and the 0.02 discrepancy, but it does not identify its cause. In particular, it does not tell us whether support size, the coupled constraints, an optimization step, or some other aspect of the formulation produced the high lower endpoints. Any diagnosis would require evidence beyond these figures.
Could a bound that is 0.02 too high change an improvement certificate?

Potentially. The certificate requires a valid projected lower bound strictly above zero. Raising a lower endpoint by 0.02 could make a contrast appear to clear zero even though an admissible gain does not. But the result supplies no absolute endpoints or signs for the 11 tables, so it does not say that any particular positive-gain certificate was issued or was incorrect.
What exactly does the 93.7% figure say?

It is the *worst-case empirical coverage* reported in the benchmark at Γ=2 and Λ=3. As reported, it falls 1.3 percentage points short of 95%. ‘Empirical’ matters: it describes coverage observed in the evaluation, not an exact calculation of the procedure’s coverage probability at every distribution in the sensitivity model.
Can I conclude that the true worst-case coverage over the whole model is exactly 93.7%?

No. The empirical minimum concerns the evaluated cases and is subject to simulation uncertainty; neither the number of simulation repetitions nor an uncertainty interval for that estimate is given. It is evidence of a shortfall in the reported audit, not a determination that the infimum of true coverage over the entire model equals 93.7%.
Does calling the tests ‘exact’ settle the coverage concern?

No. Exact multinomial inversion, when it has the required size control, concerns coverage of the observable probability vector. The claimed coverage for a policy-gain set also depends on projecting through all admissible full-data configurations. The 93.7% empirical result cannot be dismissed just by naming an exact test, but it also does not, on its own, identify whether the test, projection, target definition, or audit is responsible.
Are the 11 endpoint discrepancies necessarily the reason empirical coverage reached 93.7%?

That causal link is not reported. A lower bound that excludes an attainable gain is a plausible concern for coverage, especially if the excluded gain matters to a projected confidence set. But the evidence does not link the 11 tables to the particular setting with 93.7% empirical coverage or isolate the contribution of either component. The endpoint and coverage findings should be reported separately.
Is the high finite-atom lower bound merely non-sharp, or is there a stronger problem?

For the 11 comparisons, if the attainable minima and finite-atom bounds refer to the same Γ=2, Λ=3 model and policy contrast, a lower bound 0.02 *above* an attainable value fails to cover that value as a population lower bound. That is stronger than being conservatively non-sharp. The reported result does not tell us whether the upper bounds, other tables, or other sensitivity settings have the same issue.
Does this finding say anything about whether finite atomic distributions can ever attain Γ–Λ extrema?

It does not rule that out generally. It shows that the finite-atom lower bounds reported in 11 of these 300 tables did not reach the attainable minima as valid lower endpoints under the stated comparison. It does not establish that no different finite-atomic formulation could attain those minima, nor does it give a result for every Γ–Λ model.
What about the other 289 tables—were their bounds certified sharp?

That does not follow from the count. The evidence identifies 11 tables with a specified 0.02 discrepancy; it does not report endpoint certificates or sharpness conclusions for each of the remaining 289. Absence from the reported discrepancy count should not be converted into a claim of globally sharp bounds.
Can we infer anything about upper endpoints or marginal subtraction?

No. The numerical discrepancy concerns finite-atom *lower* bounds versus attainable minima. It gives no upper-endpoint comparison and no marginal-subtraction endpoints. The 93.7% coverage figure also does not reveal which interval endpoints, if any, contributed to missed coverage.
How should this affect a claim of uniformly at-least-95% confidence-set coverage?

The reported worst-case empirical coverage of 93.7% is below the required 95% threshold, so this benchmark does not support an unqualified claim that the evaluated confidence-set procedure achieves the target. Uniform coverage across the stated sensitivity model needs a valid all-distributions argument for test inversion and complete projection. The empirical rate calls for scrutiny of that claim without, by itself, establishing the exact coverage probability throughout the model.
Is it appropriate to say Γ=2 and Λ=3 caused the discrepancies?

It is appropriate to say the discrepancies were *observed at* Γ=2 and Λ=3. Those are the treatment- and recording-odds sensitivity settings for the reported result. The evidence does not show that those parameter values, as opposed to features of the bound computation or the particular tables, caused the discrepancies.
Can you give me a concise statement that preserves both findings and their limits?

“At Γ=2 and Λ=3, finite-atom lower bounds exceeded attainable minima by 0.02 in 11/300 binary-outcome tables, and the worst-case empirical coverage was 93.7%. The first finding challenges those lower endpoints; the second falls below the 95% coverage target, without identifying the cause or establishing the model-wide coverage probability.”
What is the decision on the Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal?

Reject the Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal. Its 0.02 sharpness failures and 93.7% worst-case coverage violate both requirements: sharp policy-value bounds and at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the stated sensitivity model.
Why are those two separate reasons for rejection?

Sharpness concerns whether the reported policy-value bounds characterize the extrema allowed by the sensitivity model. The 0.02 failures mean that requirement is not met. Coverage concerns whether the confidence set meets its repeated-sampling guarantee; 93.7% is below the required 95%. Meeting one requirement would not excuse failure of the other.
How far below the coverage requirement is 93.7%?
It is 1.3 percentage points below 95%. Because the requirement is *at least* 95% uniformly, a reported worst-case coverage of 93.7% does not meet it.
Could we keep the proposal if we describe its bounds as approximate rather than sharp?

That description would acknowledge the 0.02 sharpness failures, but it would not satisfy the requirement to characterize sharp policy-value bounds. It would also leave the separate coverage shortfall unchanged. Under the two stated requirements, the decision remains to reject the proposal.
What if the bounds happen to give a positive policy-gain lower endpoint?

A positive output from the rejected construction would not, by itself, be an acceptable improvement certificate. Such a certificate depends on a valid bound for candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value and a confidence set meeting the required coverage guarantee. The 0.02 sharpness failures and 93.7% worst-case coverage prevent treating this proposal as satisfying both requirements.
Does the decision say that no clinical policy can improve on the historical policy?

No. It rejects this proposed way of bounding and certifying policy gains. It gives no conclusion about the sign of a particular candidate policy’s true gain, and it does not say that improvement is impossible.
Are we rejecting the use of separate Γ treatment and Λ recording sensitivity limits altogether?

No. The decision’s object is the *Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal*. It does not establish that separate treatment- and recording-odds sensitivity assumptions are inherently unusable. The reasons for rejection are the stated sharpness failures and worst-case coverage shortfall of this proposal.
Is linear-fractional programming itself ruled out for every model?

No universal claim follows. A mathematical form can be useful in a different formulation without making this proposal meet its requirements. The decision rejects the Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal at issue; it is not a theorem that all linear-fractional approaches fail.
Could calling the multinomial tests exact override the 93.7% coverage figure?

No. For the requested policy-gain confidence set, what matters is that the *whole construction* meets at least 95% coverage uniformly over its stated sensitivity model. An exact test for observable probabilities does not by its name establish coverage after bounding and projection. The reported 93.7% worst-case coverage remains a reason for rejecting this proposal.
Is the sharpness failure merely a matter of a bound being wider than necessary?

The decision specifies 0.02 *sharpness failures*, so the claimed sharp extrema are not established by the proposal. It does not provide further endpoint-by-endpoint detail in the decision itself. The key point is that a method proposed to characterize sharp improvement bounds cannot meet that requirement while its reported bounds exhibit those failures.
Suppose we relaxed the confidence target to match 93.7%. Would that change this decision?

That would change the stated requirement, which is at least 95% uniformly over the sensitivity model. The decision is made against that requirement, not a lower target. Moreover, changing a coverage threshold would not address the separate 0.02 sharpness failures.
What if we kept the 95% requirement but tolerated the 0.02 discrepancy?

That would likewise change the sharp-bounds requirement rather than satisfy it, and the reported worst-case coverage would still be 93.7%. The decision identifies failures of *both* requirements, so setting aside one would not establish that the proposal meets the other.
Does rejecting this proposal select a different method as the replacement?

No replacement is selected by this decision. It says to reject the Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal because of its 0.02 sharpness failures and 93.7% worst-case coverage. A choice of another approach would be a separate claim.
How should I summarize the decision without broadening it?
“Reject the Γ–Λ linear-fractional proposal: its 0.02 sharpness failures violate the sharp-bounds requirement, and its 93.7% worst-case coverage falls below the required uniform 95%.”

I’d like to propose infinite-dimensional moment optimization under coupled Γ/Λ odds constraints, then project exact multinomial confidence regions onto sharp improvement bounds. How would that address the policy-value question?

The proposed optimization would range over admissible full-data distributions, without assuming in advance that the latent confounder has a fixed finite support. Moment constraints would connect those distributions to the observable treatment, recording, and recorded-outcome probabilities. Coupled Γ/Λ constraints would limit the specified treatment-assignment and outcome-recording odds while requiring both mechanisms to arise from one compatible latent distribution.

For each observable probability vector, the target is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value under the *same* full-data distribution. Its infimum and supremum over the admissible distributions are the proposed improvement bounds. To account for sampling uncertainty, project an exact multinomial confidence region for the observable probabilities through that optimization. This is a proposal: neither sharpness nor confidence coverage follows merely from naming the construction.
Why make the moment optimization infinite-dimensional?

It allows the optimization variable to be a distribution over potentially unrestricted latent confounder states, rather than a preselected table of support points. That matters if a fixed table fails to represent all distributions relevant to an extreme policy value. ‘Infinite-dimensional’ describes the class being optimized over; it does not mean every resulting computation must remain infinite-dimensional. Any finite reduction would need a proof that it preserves the relevant extrema and constraints.
What are the moments supposed to represent?

They are expectations under a candidate full-data distribution that must agree with observable cell probabilities and determine the policy-value contrast. The observable side includes whatever treatment, recording, and recorded-outcome categories are defined for the analysis. The latent side must also encode the relationships needed to evaluate outcomes under the candidate and historical policies.

The proposal does not specify a particular cell layout, outcome scale, or list of moment functions. Those must be derived explicitly; matching a few observable totals is not enough if it leaves the treatment-recording dependence or policy value unconstrained.
What is meant by coupling the Γ and Λ odds constraints?

Γ is the proposed limit on specified treatment-assignment odds comparisons, and Λ is the proposed limit on specified outcome-recording odds comparisons. Coupling means the two mechanisms must be realizable together in one full-data distribution over the latent confounder and relevant outcomes. One cannot select confounder weights for assignment and unrelated weights for recording, satisfy two separate inequalities, and assume their combination represents an admissible patient population. The mechanisms need not have equal probabilities, and Γ need not equal Λ.
Does saying ‘coupled Γ/Λ odds’ completely define the sensitivity model?

No. A complete model must identify the odds in each restriction, which latent or observed states are compared, the variables held fixed, and how undefined odds or zero-probability events are handled. It must specify whether recording may depend on the unseen realized outcome and how potential outcomes enter the full-data distribution. Consistency, the policy-value target, and any needed support conditions also need to be stated. No numerical Γ or Λ settings are provided by this proposal.
Would recording be assumed independent of an unrecorded outcome?

Not without an explicit assumption to that effect. The point of a Λ recording sensitivity restriction is to allow selective observation while bounding a designated aspect of it. If recording can depend on the realized outcome or latent prognosis, the feasible distribution and odds comparisons must represent that dependence. The proposal should not silently replace bounded selective recording with a missing-at-random condition.
How would we formulate the optimization target precisely?

Let q denote the observable multinomial cell-probability vector, and let FΓ,Λ(q) denote all full-data distributions compatible with q and the fully stated coupled odds model. For a candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, define Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The proposed population bounds are L(q)=inf_{P∈FΓ,Λ(q)}Δ(P) and U(q)=sup_{P∈FΓ,Λ(q)}Δ(P).

That notation specifies the contrast to optimize. A substantive formulation must define the two policy values on a common target population and ensure the policy decisions and outcomes used in those values are well defined.
Why not optimize the two values separately and subtract?

Marginal subtraction can pair a candidate-policy minimum under one admissible distribution with a historical-policy maximum under another. It gives a conservative lower contrast bound when the marginal bounds are valid, but that paired value need not be feasible. Direct optimization of Δ(P) evaluates both policies under one P and retains their shared latent structure. It is the appropriate target for a proposed *sharp improvement* bound, although direct optimization alone does not prove that the feasible set is exact.
What would establish that the moment bounds really are sharp?

There are two representation requirements. Every full-data distribution permitted by the stated sensitivity model and observable probabilities must be feasible in the moment formulation, and every feasible optimization point must correspond to a permitted full-data distribution. The global infimum and supremum over that exact set then delimit the possible policy gains.

A certificate or construction showing admissible gains at the endpoints—or arbitrarily close if the extrema are not attained—would establish that the limits cannot be tightened. A lower or upper dual inequality could help establish global validity, but it must apply to the entire admissible distribution class. The proposal does not yet supply those arguments.
Does infinite-dimensional optimization make endpoint attainment automatic?

No. The infimum and supremum may be limiting values rather than values realized by a particular distribution. Attainment depends on properties of the fully specified feasible distribution class and the policy-value functional, including what happens at odds-ratio boundaries. A sharp bound need not be attained if admissible distributions can approach it arbitrarily closely. Any claim that an endpoint is attained needs an admissible witness or an applicable existence argument.
Could we use a finite atomic solution to compute an infinite-dimensional optimum?

Potentially. If a representation theorem shows that the relevant extreme distributions have finite support, or can be approached by admissible finite-support distributions, a finite atomic optimization could characterize the same bounds. The required support and moment structure would have to preserve the coupled Γ/Λ restrictions as well as the observable probabilities and policy gain. Without that proof, a finite search is a restricted check, not an automatic solution to the infinite-dimensional problem.
What is a dual certificate supposed to do here?

A valid lower dual certificate would establish an inequality Δ(P)≥b for every P in FΓ,Λ(q); an upper one would establish Δ(P)≤b for every such P. If an admissible distribution attains the corresponding b, or approaches it arbitrarily closely, the certificate and feasible construction establish a sharp endpoint. A dual result for a relaxed or restricted moment problem would not, without an equivalence argument, certify a sharp bound under the stated sensitivity model.
Do Γ and Λ have to be enforced state by state or just in expectation?

That depends on the sensitivity assumptions actually selected. If an odds restriction is defined conditionally across confounder states, merely bounding an average of those odds may be weaker than the assumption—or may describe a different model. The proposed moment formulation must preserve the precise comparisons as stated, including their conditioning and boundary conventions. One cannot infer their correct mathematical encoding from the symbols Γ and Λ alone.
What does projecting an exact multinomial confidence region entail?

Let C₉₅(N) be a confidence region for q obtained from the observed multinomial counts N. For each q in that region, consider every P in FΓ,Λ(q), and collect Δ(P). The projected contrast set is D(N)={Δ(P): q∈C₉₅(N), P∈FΓ,Λ(q)}. Its lower endpoint optimizes jointly over the retained observable vectors and their compatible full-data distributions, rather than plugging the observed proportions into L(q).

The projection therefore carries both sampling uncertainty and uncertainty due to selectively observed outcomes and bounded confounding. It does not automatically yield a narrow interval.
Where does ‘exact’ enter the multinomial region?

An exact construction must control its rejection probability under the specified multinomial sampling model at every relevant true cell-probability vector, rather than relying only on an unverified approximation. For an inverted 95% test, that means rejection probability no greater than 5% at each true vector, so the inverted region covers it with probability at least 95%. The observable categories and a particular test have not been specified here, so that guarantee is something the proposal must establish for its eventual construction.
How do we obtain at least 95% coverage uniformly for the policy gain?

For any P in the stated sensitivity model, let q_P be its observable vector. On the event q_P∈C₉₅(N), complete projection includes P in FΓ,Λ(q_P), and therefore includes Δ(P) in D(N). Thus, if inf_{P in the model} Pr_P{q_P∈C₉₅(N)}≥0.95, the inclusion implies inf_{P in the model} Pr_P{Δ(P)∈D(N)}≥0.95.

If projection includes *every* admissible distribution at q_P, the same event makes D(N) contain the entire population identified contrast set at q_P. Both guarantees depend on a uniformly valid exact region and a faithful projection; they are not consequences of infinite-dimensional optimization by itself.
Is a guarantee at a few selected Γ and Λ values the same as uniformity over the sensitivity model?

No. Uniform coverage quantifies over every data-generating distribution in the *stated* model, including the distributions allowed by whatever Γ and Λ restrictions that model specifies. Checking a collection of examples can be informative, but it does not replace an all-model coverage argument. A claim across multiple sensitivity settings must also say which settings and corresponding admissible distributions it includes; no parameter values or ranges are given in this proposal.
What if the exact confidence region includes an observable vector with no compatible full-data distribution?

That vector contributes no contrast to the projection, because FΓ,Λ(q) is empty there. The projected set is formed from compatible pairs, not every observable vector considered in isolation. An entirely empty projected set must not be interpreted as a certificate of improvement. Under a correctly stated model, whenever the true observable vector is covered, its true full-data distribution supplies at least one compatible pair.
Could an exact observable region compensate for a moment formulation that omits some admissible distributions?

No. If the projection omits a full-data distribution allowed by the sensitivity model, covering its observable vector does not ensure that its policy gain is included. That can undermine the policy-gain confidence claim. Conversely, including extra latent distributions may yield a conservative confidence set but prevent claims that its population bounds are sharp. Exact observable inference and exact latent-model representation are separate obligations.
When would these projected bounds certify improvement over the historical policy?

Define gain so that a positive value means the candidate policy has higher clinical value than the historical policy. Under the proposed confidence construction, certification requires the lower endpoint of D(N)—the projected *joint* candidate-minus-historical contrast set—to be strictly above zero. A fixed-q population bound above zero does not by itself give a 95% confidence certificate, and an endpoint equal to zero does not certify strict improvement. No positive projected endpoint is reported in this proposal.
Does a negative projected lower endpoint show the candidate is worse?

No. It means this construction cannot rule out a nonpositive gain with the stated sensitivity and sampling uncertainty. The projected set could also include positive gains. Establishing that the candidate is worse throughout the feasible set would require a corresponding upper bound below zero; failing the improvement criterion is not the same conclusion.
What does this proposal commit us to demonstrating before calling the analysis successful?

It calls for precise coupled Γ treatment and Λ recording sensitivity assumptions; an exact moment representation and globally justified sharp joint improvement extrema; a multinomial region with the stated exact 95% guarantee; and complete projection giving at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over the sensitivity model. A positive-gain certificate additionally requires the realized projected lower endpoint to exceed zero. The proposal specifies this route, not that any of those endpoints or certificates has already been obtained.
Can coupled Γ/Λ moment duals certify attainable extrema without the finite-atom approximation that caused 0.02 sharpness errors?

Potentially, but a dual certificate alone establishes a bound, not attainment. If a lower dual inequality holds for every full-data distribution satisfying the coupled Γ treatment-odds and Λ recording-odds constraints, it can rule out policy gains below its stated value without relying on a fixed finite-atom approximation. To certify an *attainable extremum*, one also needs an admissible distribution that reaches that value, plus justification that the primal and dual values agree. The 0.02 sharpness errors motivate the question; they do not establish that a moment dual removes them.
What would the dual inequality be bounding?

The target should remain the joint candidate-minus-historical policy-value gain. For a fixed observable probability vector q, let FΓ,Λ(q) contain every full-data distribution allowed by the precisely specified, coupled sensitivity model. A valid lower dual certificate for a number b must show Δ(P)≥b for every P∈FΓ,Λ(q), where Δ(P) is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value under that *same* P. An upper certificate reverses the inequality. The word ‘every’ is crucial: a certificate valid only for a discretized subset would not bound the unrestricted feasible class.
Why call the constraints coupled in the dual, rather than checking Γ and Λ separately?

The treatment and recording odds restrictions apply to distinct mechanisms, but their probabilities must arise from one compatible full-data distribution. A dual derived after separating their latent mixtures might certify an optimization problem different from the intended one. The dual’s validity proof must therefore hold over the joint feasible set, including the observable mapping and the dependence of treatment and recording on the shared confounder. Coupling does not require Γ and Λ to have the same value or the two mechanisms to have equal probabilities.
Would a matching dual bound and numerical primal value settle the question?

Only if both sides are justified for the same model. The dual inequality must hold globally over the allowed continuous or otherwise unrestricted confounder distributions. The primal value must come from a distribution that actually satisfies all the coupled constraints and reproduces the specified observable probabilities. If the dual bound and an admissible attained value coincide, they certify an attained sharp endpoint. Two matching numerical outputs without those validity checks could still agree for a restricted or relaxed problem.
Could the primal witness have finitely many atoms without reintroducing the approximation?

Yes, if the witness is a genuinely admissible distribution and the dual bound applies to the *entire* sensitivity model. A finite-support witness can establish that an endpoint is attained without treating a preset finite grid as exhaustive. The distinction is between using atoms as one feasible attaining construction and assuming, without proof, that a finite-atom approximation captures every extreme distribution. If finite support is asserted to be sufficient generally, that claim needs its own representation argument.
What if the dual bound agrees with a sequence of feasible gains but no distribution reaches it?

Then the endpoint may be sharp as an infimum or supremum, but it has not been shown to be *attainable*. A dual lower bound b plus admissible gains converging downward to b establishes that b cannot be raised as a population lower bound. To claim an attained minimum, one needs a single admissible distribution with gain b, or an existence theorem under the actual boundary conventions of the model.
Is strong duality enough to prove attainability?

No. Strong duality says the primal and dual optimal *values* agree under the relevant conditions. It does not automatically guarantee that either optimization has an optimizer. A proof of primal attainment must address the feasible distribution class and objective—for example, whether appropriate compactness, closedness, and continuity conditions hold. Conditional odds and zero-probability boundaries can matter to those conditions.
Could a globally valid dual still yield a loose lower bound?

Yes. Any valid inequality Δ(P)≥b may sit below the true infimum. To certify the extremum rather than just a conservative bound, one needs a matching admissible value or an approaching sequence, and an argument that any duality gap has been closed. The aim is not simply to produce *a* distribution-free inequality; it is to identify the sharp endpoint of the coupled Γ/Λ model.
How would you check that a dual certificate has not silently relaxed the recording mechanism?

State the recording-odds comparison precisely, including what it conditions on and whether recording may depend on an unseen realized outcome. Then derive the dual inequality against every distribution satisfying that restriction *together with* the treatment restriction and the observable moment equations. If the derivation replaces a coupled constraint with an independent recording mixture or drops outcome-dependent recording configurations, it may prove a statement about a different feasible set. The question gives no particular dual formulation to verify, so this is a criterion rather than a diagnosis.
