If the audit examines 300 tables, does its lowest observed coverage establish a uniform guarantee?

No. The 300 tables define the scope of the audit, whereas uniform coverage quantifies over every distribution in the stated sensitivity model. Empirical checks can reveal problems or illustrate how the inversion behaves, but an all-vector test-size argument is needed for an exact uniform guarantee. Any empirical coverage figure would also need its own uncertainty and target clearly identified; none is reported in this activity.
Why distinguish the observable region’s coverage from projected policy-gain coverage?

The observable region covers a multinomial probability vector; a policy gain depends additionally on an unobserved full-data distribution. To transfer coverage, the projection must retain every gain allowed by the coupled Γ/Λ model at a covered observable vector. If that step omits an admissible configuration, coverage of its observable vector need not imply coverage of its gain. Testing the multinomial inversion and checking complete projection therefore address different parts of the confidence claim.
Can the primal-dual certificates help check completeness of the projection?

They can help certify optimization endpoints if their global inequalities apply over the projected feasible set. But a certificate for one of the eleven fixed observable tables does not automatically cover every probability vector inside an inverted confidence region. For a projected lower endpoint, the global bound must apply across all retained observable vectors and all their admissible full-data distributions, with a feasible configuration or limiting argument supporting the reported endpoint.
What is the coverage implication we would want to justify?

For any true distribution P in the stated Γ/Λ sensitivity model, let q_P be its observable multinomial probabilities and Δ(P) its candidate-minus-historical gain. If q_P lies in the inverted region, a complete projection contains the admissible distribution P and therefore Δ(P). Thus uniform at-least-95% coverage of q_P implies uniform at-least-95% coverage of the true gain, provided this inclusion holds for every admissible P. Projecting all compatible distributions also includes the whole identified gain set at q_P on that event.
What if a vector retained by inversion has no compatible full-data distribution?

It contributes no policy gain to the projection. The projected set consists of compatible pairs of an observable vector and an admissible full-data distribution. If no compatible pair exists at all, an empty set should be flagged rather than interpreted as evidence of improvement. A covered true vector under the stated model has at least its true compatible distribution, assuming the model representation is faithful.
Should we use the same 300 tables as though they were 300 independent confidence statements?

The activity says to audit inversion across 300 tables; it does not specify a simultaneous confidence claim across those tables. For each table, identify the observable sampling model and the particular coverage event being assessed. Do not convert 300 case-level checks into a joint coverage guarantee—or infer one from separately constructed 95% regions—without a procedure designed and justified for that joint target.
Does Γ=2, Λ=3 also specify the sensitivity setting for every table in the inversion audit?

The activity explicitly attaches Γ=2 and Λ=3 to the eleven failures. It says the exact-95% inversion audit is across 300 tables, without specifying their sensitivity settings. The multinomial region concerns observable probabilities; any projected policy-gain audit must state the coupled Γ/Λ model used for those tables. We should not silently extend the eleven cases’ numerical settings to all 300.
If an audit finds an inversion discrepancy, can we conclude the primal-dual solver is wrong?

Not from that fact alone. A discrepancy in the observable test inversion, a missing distribution in projection, and an incorrect primal-dual endpoint are different possible issues. The audit should identify which event failed and which construction it concerns before drawing a conclusion. Conversely, matching primal and dual values for the eleven cases would not, by itself, validate multinomial coverage.
When could the output of this activity support a strict-improvement certificate?

For a particular candidate policy, the lower endpoint of a correctly projected joint candidate-minus-historical confidence set must be strictly above zero, and that set must carry the at-least-95% uniform coverage guarantee under its stated sensitivity model. Fixed-table endpoint certificates and inversion checks are needed to justify parts of that conclusion, but neither supplies a positive projected endpoint. No improvement result is given by the activity.
How should I describe the intended deliverables without implying they already exist?

Report, for each of the eleven Γ=2, Λ=3 cases, the assessed primal witness, global dual endpoint bound, feasibility checks, and any certified gap. Separately report the exact-95% multinomial inversion audit across the 300 tables, distinguishing observable-vector size control from coverage after projection. Those are the results the run is meant to produce, not findings supplied in advance.
What did MomentPolicy v1.0 establish for the eleven cases and for exact test inversion?

MomentPolicy v1.0 brought all eleven primal-dual gaps below 10⁻⁶. Separately, exact multinomial test inversion guarantees at least 95% coverage uniformly over its stated model. The first finding concerns agreement between feasible primal values and dual bounds in those eleven cases; the second is a confidence-coverage guarantee, not a numerical optimization tolerance.
Does ‘all eleven’ mean the gap was zero in every case?

No. It means each of the eleven reported primal-dual gaps was below 10⁻⁶. The result does not claim exact equality or give the individual gap values. An endpoint should be described as certified to the stated precision rather than as mathematically identical to its dual bound.
What are the primal and dual quantities being compared?

For a policy-improvement endpoint, the primal side gives a candidate-minus-historical value from an admissible full-data distribution. The dual side supplies a bound intended to hold over the corresponding coupled Γ/Λ sensitivity model. A gap below 10⁻⁶ means those two sides nearly meet in each of the eleven cases. Their comparison is meaningful when the feasible value and global bound concern the same observable constraints, policies, and sensitivity restrictions.
Can I infer the lower policy-gain bounds for those cases from the gap result?

No. A primal-dual gap measures separation between two endpoint certificates; it does not state the endpoint itself. The result provides neither the eleven policy-gain values nor their signs. In particular, a small gap is not evidence that a lower bound is above zero.
Does the finding apply to both lower and upper endpoints?

The reported finding says that all eleven primal-dual gaps are below 10⁻⁶, but it does not enumerate endpoint-specific values. It would be unwarranted to assign a separate numerical gap or endpoint value to a lower or upper calculation that is not identified. Any endpoint-specific claim should be tied to its corresponding certificate.
Is 10⁻⁶ the confidence error probability?

No. The 10⁻⁶ threshold is an optimization-gap tolerance, measured on the policy-value scale used in the certified comparison. The confidence requirement concerns a probability: at least 95% coverage under repeated sampling. A tight primal-dual gap and a coverage guarantee answer different questions.
What is covered by the exact multinomial inversion?

The inverted tests produce a confidence region for the observable multinomial cell-probability vector. The reported guarantee is coverage of at least 95% uniformly over the stated model—not coverage equal to exactly 95% at every vector. To use that region for policy-gain inference, it must be projected through the compatible full-data distributions.
Why does ‘uniformly’ matter if the tests are exact?

It specifies the scope of the guarantee: the coverage floor applies across the probability vectors allowed by the stated model, rather than only at a selected vector. Conceptually, inversion retains a true vector whenever its test does not reject; controlling that test’s rejection probability at no more than 5% throughout the stated parameter space gives the at-least-95% uniform guarantee. The finding does not require actual coverage to equal 95% everywhere.
Is the 95% figure an empirical minimum across the cases?

No. The result attributes the at-least-95% uniform guarantee to exact test inversion. It does not report a minimum simulated coverage rate or the coverage percentage observed in any individual case. The eleven-case gap threshold and the inversion coverage guarantee should not be treated as measurements of the same thing.
Does uniform observable-probability coverage automatically certify a positive policy gain?

No. Confidence coverage says the region retains its target with the stated probability; it does not say the policy gain is positive. For an at-least-95% confidence-based improvement certificate, the inverted region must be projected through all admissible coupled Γ/Λ full-data distributions, and the resulting *lower* candidate-minus-historical gain bound must be strictly above zero. No projected lower endpoint or improvement decision is reported here.
What role does completeness of projection play alongside exact inversion?

If the true observable vector lies in the inverted region, complete projection includes every admissible full-data distribution compatible with that vector, and thus includes its possible policy gains. That is the step that carries the observable coverage guarantee to the policy contrast. Exact inversion cannot compensate for a projection that omits an allowed distribution. The reported coverage guarantee should be interpreted within the scope of the stated model and the projection used.
Do the eleven small gaps establish a general sharpness theorem for every Γ and Λ?

The gap result is explicitly about eleven cases. It supports their primal-dual comparisons to a tolerance below 10⁻⁶; it does not, merely by counting them, provide endpoint values or a theorem for every policy and sensitivity setting. The uniform coverage statement is separate and should not be read as extending the eleven-case optimization result to all possible extrema.
Can a confidence set have the stated coverage while a reported policy bound is not sharp?

Yes. Coverage concerns inclusion under repeated sampling, while sharpness concerns whether a population bound is the tightest allowed by the assumptions. A conservative projected set may cover without having sharp endpoints. Conversely, close primal-dual agreement at a fixed observable vector does not, by itself, establish a confidence-set guarantee. The two findings address those distinct obligations.
How should I report this result without implying a policy has improved?

“MomentPolicy v1.0 reduced the primal-dual gap below 10⁻⁶ in all eleven cases, and exact multinomial test inversion guarantees at least 95% uniform coverage over the stated model.” Neither statement supplies a positive projected lower policy-gain bound, so neither is itself an improvement certificate.

I’d like to propose conditional total-variation budgets for treatment confounding and selective outcome recording, optimize over joint binary response types, and use exact multinomial inversion. How would that address improvement over the historical policy?

The proposal would define a set of full-data distributions consistent with the observable treatment-and-recording data. Separate conditional total-variation budgets would limit, respectively, how much treatment selection and outcome recording can distort relevant distributions. Within that set, optimize candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over joint binary response types, so both values are evaluated under the same admissible distribution.

Exact multinomial test inversion would provide a confidence region for observable cell probabilities. Projecting that region through the full-data model would give a confidence set for the policy-value contrast. Strict improvement would be certified only if its projected lower endpoint exceeded zero, with at least 95% coverage uniformly over the stated sensitivity model. This describes the proposed route, not a result or a completed certificate.
What is a conditional total-variation budget, precisely?

For two probability distributions p and r on the same categories, total-variation distance can be written TV(p,r) = ½Σⱼ|pⱼ−rⱼ|. A conditional budget limits such a distance after holding specified observed information fixed. To make that a sensitivity assumption, we must identify *which* distributions are compared, what is conditioned on, and the allowed budget for each comparison.

The proposal supplies no numerical budgets or conditioning set. ‘Conditional total variation’ names a way to restrict selection, but it does not yet define the admissible full-data distributions.
What could the treatment-confounding comparison be between, without assuming we have identified the unmeasured confounder?

One possible sensitivity specification would compare a distribution of latent response types among patients assigned a treatment with the corresponding distribution in a stated target population, conditional on information observed before the decision. A total-variation limit would bound how different those distributions may be. That is an illustration of what would need specifying, not a chosen assumption in this proposal.

The target population, the treatments being compared, and the meaning of a latent response type must all be explicit. Otherwise even a stated numerical budget would be ambiguous.
And where would the recording budget apply?

It would limit a specified conditional distributional difference attributable to which realized outcomes are recorded. For example, a model might compare the latent response-type distribution among recorded and relevant underlying cases, conditional on treatment and other stated information. The precise comparison must be defined before it becomes an assumption.

Selective recording can depend on information not present in the observed record, including the realized outcome if the model permits that dependence. A recording budget should represent the dependence it is intended to bound, rather than quietly assume that missing outcomes are representative of observed ones.
Are these two budgets interchangeable?

No. The treatment budget concerns which decisions patients receive; the recording budget concerns which realized outcomes become observable. Restricting one mechanism does not automatically restrict the other. They can also interact, because the observed outcomes have passed through both assignment and recording. The full-data representation must make their restrictions jointly compatible, even if the budgets themselves are stated separately.
Does ‘joint binary response types’ mean just classifying each recorded outcome as zero or one?

No. A binary response type concerns possible binary outcomes under the relevant treatment decisions, including potential outcomes not observed for an individual. The word ‘joint’ means the potential outcomes needed to evaluate the policies are represented together within a possible full-data distribution. Recorded outcomes constrain that distribution but do not reveal all of its response types.

The proposal does not specify the number of treatment options or the coding of a favorable outcome. Those definitions are needed before enumerating types or interpreting a positive policy-value difference.
Why retain a joint distribution of those types rather than bound each treatment’s outcome separately?

The candidate and historical policies are evaluated in the same target population. A full-data distribution assigns probabilities to response types and determines both policy values simultaneously. Optimizing their difference over that common distribution preserves which candidate and historical values can coexist. Separately maximizing one and minimizing the other could combine incompatible configurations, leaving a valid but unnecessarily wide improvement interval.
Can the recording process be attached to a response type even when the outcome is not observed?

Yes, in a proposed full-data model: response type and recording status are both components of a possible data-generating distribution. Only the appropriate recorded outcome is visible in the observable cells; the latent response type remains unknown when an outcome is unrecorded. The optimization ranges over compatible possibilities instead of assigning a particular unseen outcome to a patient.
Do total-variation budgets have to be the same in every conditional group?

Not necessarily. The model could state a common limit or limits that vary by specified conditioning information. But it must say which applies where, and the confidence claim must be understood relative to exactly that model. Neither common nor group-specific numerical budgets have been chosen in the proposal.
What happens when a conditional group has zero probability?

A conditional distribution given a zero-probability event is not defined in the usual way. The sensitivity specification must address that boundary—through support conditions, a convention for the constraint, or an equivalent unconditional formulation. That choice affects the feasible set and potentially whether an extremum is attained. It should not be left to an optimizer’s default handling of division by zero.
Can a treatment-selection budget and a recording budget each hold individually while their chosen latent distributions are incompatible?

Yes, if they are implemented as unrelated comparisons without requiring a common full-data distribution. The proposed optimization should assign one coherent probability law to response types, treatment assignment, and recording, then apply both conditional total-variation restrictions to quantities derived from that law. Otherwise independently feasible pieces might yield an improvement contrast no distribution actually permits.
How would you write the population improvement bound abstractly?

Let q be the observable multinomial cell-probability vector, and let F_TV(q) contain all joint binary-response-type, treatment, and recording distributions that map to q and satisfy the *fully specified* conditional total-variation budgets. For candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, define Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The proposed population bounds are L(q)=inf_{P∈F_TV(q)}Δ(P) and U(q)=sup_{P∈F_TV(q)}Δ(P).

This states the target, not its value. The conditional comparisons, budgets, policy rules, and observable mapping still need definition before F_TV(q) can be calculated.
What does it take to describe those bounds as sharp?

The feasible set must include every full-data distribution allowed by the stated assumptions and exclude distributions that violate them. The objective must evaluate both policies on each *same* admissible distribution, and the computed infimum and supremum must be global for that set. To show an endpoint cannot be tightened, one can exhibit an admissible distribution attaining it, or a sequence of admissible distributions approaching it when the endpoint is not attained.

Simply imposing total-variation inequalities on selected marginals would not establish sharpness if that dropped a required joint compatibility condition. Conversely, adding unstated restrictions could make the reported bounds too narrow for the proposed sensitivity model.
Do the total-variation constraints make the problem a linear program?

Total variation on finite categories can be represented using absolute-value inequalities, which may help in an optimization formulation. But the complete problem’s form depends on how the conditional distributions, their denominators, joint response types, and observable mapping are parameterized. The proposal does not establish that all of those pieces yield an exact linear program, nor that a particular numerical method finds global extrema. Computational convenience and model equivalence would need separate justification.
Could we treat the two conditional budgets as an additive allowance for total bias?

Not without a derived inequality for the actual policy-value contrast and the explicitly chosen comparisons. Treatment selection and recording act on related parts of one distribution; adding two budget numbers mechanically could ignore their dependence or exaggerate what is feasible. The proposed approach is to optimize over the *joint* distribution satisfying both restrictions, rather than assert an unproved additive bias formula.
What does the observable multinomial vector contain if some outcomes are missing?

It must distinguish the observable treatment and recording categories, and, when an outcome is recorded, its observed binary category, along with whatever other observable distinctions the analysis specifies. An unrecorded outcome does not create an observed zero-or-one cell; its possibilities live in the latent full-data model. The exact cell definitions and sampling scheme are not given in the proposal, and they are necessary for a particular multinomial inversion.
How does exact multinomial inversion work in this proposal?

For each proposed observable probability vector q, apply a multinomial test to the observed counts and retain q when its test does not reject. If each test rejects its true vector with probability at most 5% throughout the applicable multinomial parameter space, the inverted region C₉₅ contains the true vector with probability at least 95% uniformly. The proposal does not specify the test statistic or acceptance rule; those must be supplied to substantiate ‘exact.’
Is it enough to optimize the contrast at the empirical cell frequencies and attach the inverted region afterward?

No. Projection must range over every q retained in C₉₅ and every full-data distribution in F_TV(q). Symbolically, the projected contrast set is {Δ(P):q∈C₉₅, P∈F_TV(q)}. Its lower and upper endpoints reflect both sampling uncertainty in observable probabilities and the ambiguity allowed by the conditional total-variation model. A bound at empirical frequencies is a different, fixed-vector calculation.
Why should that projection cover the true policy gain with at least 95% probability?

Take any true distribution P in the stated sensitivity model, with observable vector q_P. If q_P is in the exact inverted region and the projection includes *every* distribution in F_TV(q_P), it includes P and hence Δ(P). Thus the observable-vector coverage event implies coverage of the true policy gain. A uniform at-least-95% guarantee for that event transfers to the projected contrast under those completeness and model assumptions. This is the intended coverage argument; the proposal alone does not verify its premises.
Would the projected set also cover the entire population identified interval?

On the event that the true observable vector q_P is retained, complete projection includes all of F_TV(q_P). It therefore includes the entire population range of contrasts at that vector, not merely the true contrast under one particular full-data distribution. That stronger confidence-set statement depends on retaining all compatible joint response-type distributions. It should be distinguished from covering a single true policy gain.
Does ‘exact’ mean coverage equals 95% for every allowable distribution?

No. The goal is *at least* 95% uniformly over the stated sensitivity model. Discrete multinomial tests and projection may yield more than 95% coverage. Exactness concerns justified control of the observable test’s rejection probability; it does not ensure that the projected confidence set is the narrowest possible one or that its actual coverage equals 95% at every distribution.
Suppose the conditional total-variation budgets are generous. Would exact coverage still give a useful improvement conclusion?

Coverage can hold even when the projected contrast set is wide. More permissive budgets generally allow more full-data possibilities, potentially including nonpositive policy gains, but the actual endpoints depend on the fully specified model and observable information. An exact confidence guarantee addresses reliability, not whether a candidate policy can be certified to improve.
What exactly is the certification rule?

Define value so that a positive Δ means the candidate policy improves on the historical policy. Then require the *lower endpoint* of the projected joint contrast set to be strictly greater than zero. If that condition holds and the region and projection carry the intended uniform at-least-95% coverage, it supports a confidence-based strict-improvement certificate under the stated total-variation budgets. An endpoint of zero or below does not certify strict improvement, even if some feasible contrasts are positive.
Could a negative lower endpoint establish that the candidate policy is worse?

No. It says the proposed bounds and confidence construction leave nonpositive gains possible. The set may also include positive gains. Establishing a strictly negative gain across the compatible set would require its *upper* endpoint to be below zero. Failure to certify improvement should not be turned into a conclusion of harm.
Does the proposal give us numerical budgets, bounds, or an improvement result?

No. It proposes conditional total-variation budgets for treatment confounding and selective recording, joint optimization over binary response types, and exact multinomial inversion. It does not state budget values, a particular policy or dataset, computed sharp endpoints, or a projected lower endpoint. Each of those would be needed to apply the certification rule to a specific clinical decision policy.
What is the careful one-sentence description?

“Specify conditional total-variation budgets for treatment confounding and selective outcome recording, jointly optimize binary response-type distributions for candidate-minus-historical policy value, and project an exact multinomial confidence region to obtain sharp improvement bounds and test whether its lower confidence endpoint exceeds zero.” Sharpness and coverage remain requirements for the proposed construction, not results established by this description.
Do separate conditional total-variation budgets permit sharp policy-gain bounds when treatment assignment and outcome recording share latent response types?

They can, but separate budgets alone do not guarantee sharpness. The key is to impose both budgets on distributions derived from one joint law for latent response types, treatment assignment, and outcome recording. Then optimize candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over exactly the joint laws allowed by the assumptions. If the calculation instead chooses a treatment-selection distribution and a recording-selection distribution independently, its extrema may describe combinations that no shared response-type distribution can produce.
What is the distinction between separate budgets and separate latent distributions?

Separate budgets mean there are two restrictions with different subjects: one limits a specified conditional distributional difference associated with treatment assignment, and the other limits one associated with recording. They need not have the same size. Separate latent distributions would go further: they would let each restriction be satisfied using its own independently chosen account of response-type frequencies. That would lose the requirement that both selection processes act within one possible full-data distribution.
What exactly has to be shared if the response types are binary?

The probabilities assigned to the joint potential-outcome types must belong to a single latent population. Within that population, treatment assignment and recording can each depend on response type in ways allowed by their respective budgets. For every candidate full-data law, its type probabilities, treatment probabilities, recording probabilities, and resulting observed cells must fit together. ‘Binary’ describes the possible outcome values; it does not make the unobserved response type known for anyone whose outcome was not recorded.
Does shared response type imply that treatment and recording select people in the same way?

No. They are distinct mechanisms and can select differently, subject to whatever conditional total-variation comparisons have been specified. Sharing means they are both described within one joint distribution over the same latent response types. It does not equate their conditional probabilities or make one budget a consequence of the other.
Can you state the sharp-bound question abstractly?

Let q denote the observable cell probabilities. Define F(q) as the set of all joint laws for binary response types, treatment, and recording that map to q and satisfy both precisely stated conditional total-variation budgets. For a candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, let Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The proposed sharp bounds are inf_{P∈F(q)}Δ(P) and sup_{P∈F(q)}Δ(P).

That notation does not establish sharpness by itself. F(q) must contain all and only the full-data laws allowed by the assumptions, and the extrema must be solved globally.
Why do the budgets have to be specified more precisely before answering yes or no?

A total-variation distance compares two distributions on a common set of categories. A *conditional* budget also requires a conditioning event. We need to know which response-type distributions the treatment budget compares, which distributions the recording budget compares, what information is held fixed in each comparison, and what limits apply. Different choices define different feasible sets, even if all are described informally as separate conditional total-variation budgets. The question does not give those definitions or numerical budget values.
Could both comparisons be valid separately but incompatible when put together?

If they are checked on independently selected distributions, yes: each comparison may satisfy its own budget without their proposed components assembling into one law with the required observable probabilities. If, instead, both comparisons are calculated from a single properly defined joint law, their coexistence is enforced by construction. The feasible set could still be empty for particular observable probabilities and budget definitions; an empty set is not a sharp policy-gain interval.
Is there a simple mathematical way to see why separately optimized selection effects might be too permissive?

Think of one vector of response-type probabilities that determines the candidate and historical values and contributes to both selection comparisons. Allowing the treatment calculation to use one vector and the recording calculation another gives two degrees of freedom that the intended joint law may not have. The optimization can then reach an extreme gain by pairing choices that cannot coexist. This is a structural possibility, not a claim that a particular pair of budgets has produced such a gap.
Does that mean the separate budgets themselves have to be replaced with one combined total-variation budget?

No. They may remain separate restrictions. The needed connection is a common full-data law from which the distributions in both restrictions are derived. Replacing them with a single budget would define a different sensitivity model unless an equivalence were proved. Keeping the two limits distinct can be useful, provided the optimization does not relax away their joint compatibility.
If both budgets are imposed on the same law, does that automatically give sharp bounds?

It addresses a necessary compatibility concern, but not every sharpness requirement. The representation must also account correctly for observed and unrecorded outcomes, include every permitted response-type configuration, and avoid imposing unstated constraints. The reported extrema must be global. A witness attaining a proposed endpoint, or admissible laws approaching it, helps show the bound cannot be tightened; a global inequality shows no law lies beyond it.
Could the sharp lower bound be an infimum that no joint law attains?

Yes, depending on the specified feasible set and its boundary rules. Admissible gains might approach an endpoint without a law that realizes it. In that case the infimum can still be sharp, but it should not be called an attained minimum. Conditional distributions can be undefined on zero-probability groups, so the model’s support conventions matter when deciding whether a boundary law is admissible.
What happens to a conditional total-variation constraint when its conditioning group has probability zero?

The corresponding conditional distribution is not ordinarily defined. A complete model must say whether that group is excluded by a positivity assumption, whether a limiting or unconditional form of the constraint is used, or whether the condition applies only when the group has positive probability. Different conventions can change both the feasible set and endpoint attainment. One cannot infer the appropriate convention from the phrase ‘conditional total-variation budget.’
Would evaluating candidate and historical values separately introduce another compatibility problem?

Potentially. Even if each value is optimized over the correct common set F(q), the candidate minimum and historical maximum may occur under different joint laws. Subtracting them gives a conservative lower bound, but it need not be the sharp lower bound for improvement. Optimizing Δ(P) directly preserves the shared response-type law for both policies as well as for treatment and recording.
Can you distinguish the two ways sharpness might be lost?

One loss occurs *inside the feasible set*: independently specified treatment and recording components may admit combinations that are not one valid joint law. Another occurs *after value optimization*: subtracting separate marginal policy-value extrema may pair values from different valid joint laws. The first concerns whether each candidate distribution is feasible; the second concerns whether two policy values can reach their separate extrema under the same feasible distribution. Direct contrast optimization addresses the second, but only an exact joint representation addresses the first.
Is a strict improvement claim possible if the resulting sharp lower gain bound is positive?

At the population-identification level, yes: a lower bound strictly above zero would mean every full-data law compatible with the observable distribution and both stated budgets gives the candidate policy a higher value than the historical policy. A lower bound at or below zero would not certify strict improvement. This is a conditional criterion, not a claim that any particular budgets or data yield a positive bound.
Would a sharp population bound also give the confidence statement automatically?

No. Sharpness describes what the observable *population* distribution and sensitivity assumptions allow. A confidence statement must also account for sampling uncertainty in the observable cells. One can project a suitably covered confidence region for those probabilities through the same exact joint-law feasible set. The coverage argument depends on the region covering the true observable probabilities and the projection retaining every compatible joint law; neither follows from sharpness alone.
What should we check if a computed lower bound looks unexpectedly high?

Check whether an admissible joint law can produce a gain below it. In particular, verify that all binary response types allowed by the model were represented, that unrecorded outcomes were not treated as observed, that both conditional budgets and the observable mapping use the same law, and that boundary cases were handled as stated. An admissible law below the computed lower bound would show that it is not a valid lower bound for that model, regardless of how the optimization was labeled.
And if the computed lower bound looks unexpectedly low?

Determine whether its extreme value comes from an admissible joint law or from a relaxation combining incompatible pieces. If it comes from a valid law, it is an attainable contrast; if it can only be approached, the limiting argument should be stated. A value below every attainable or approachable gain would be conservative but non-sharp. Its direction alone does not diagnose which possibility applies.
So what is the answer to the question as posed?

Separate conditional total-variation budgets *can* support sharp policy-gain bounds with shared latent binary response types, provided both restrictions are imposed on one exactly represented joint full-data law and the candidate-minus-historical contrast is optimized globally over all such laws. Merely checking the two budgets separately does not establish their joint compatibility, endpoint attainability, or sharpness. Those properties depend on the precise conditional comparisons and a proof or certificate for the resulting feasible set.

My hypothesis is that a single response-type distribution satisfying both conditional total-variation budgets yields attainable joint policy-gain extrema, unlike independently optimized margins. What exactly am I claiming?

You are proposing that the minimum and maximum candidate-minus-historical policy gains can each be realized by a joint full-data distribution over binary response types, treatment assignment, and outcome recording that satisfies *both* conditional total-variation budgets. The same distribution determines the two policy values within each contrast. The claim about independently optimized margins is that separately chosen extrema need not correspond to one such distribution. Attainability and any strict difference from marginal subtraction remain hypotheses, not established outcomes.
Does ‘a single response-type distribution’ mean the same distribution must attain both the minimum and maximum?

No. A different admissible distribution may attain each endpoint. ‘Single’ means that, for any one evaluated gain, its response-type probabilities, treatment selection, and recording mechanism belong to one coherent full-data law. It also means candidate and historical policy values are evaluated under that same law. It does not require one law to be both a minimizer and a maximizer.
Why is satisfying both budgets within one distribution stronger than satisfying them separately?

Each conditional total-variation budget limits a different comparison—one for treatment confounding and one for selective recording. If they are checked using independently chosen latent margins, those margins may not be compatible with the same underlying response-type frequencies or the same observed data. Imposing both within one distribution preserves that shared structure. It does not necessarily impose a smaller numerical budget; it rules out incompatible combinations.
Could you write the joint-extremum part symbolically?

Let q denote the observable probabilities, and let F_TV(q) be the full-data laws mapping to q and satisfying the two *precisely defined* conditional total-variation budgets on a common response-type distribution. For candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, define Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The hypothesis proposes admissible laws P_L and P_U such that Δ(P_L)=inf_{P∈F_TV(q)}Δ(P) and Δ(P_U)=sup_{P∈F_TV(q)}Δ(P).

Those equalities assert more than writing down infima and suprema: they say each endpoint is attained. Their validity depends on the actual budget definitions and feasible-set properties.
What needs to be defined before we can test the hypothesis?

Specify the observable categories, the binary outcome’s value coding, the candidate and historical policies, and how response types encode the potential outcomes relevant to those policies. For each budget, state the conditional distributions compared, the conditioning variables, its numerical limit, and how zero-probability conditioning events are handled. Then define one joint law linking response type, treatment, recording, and observable outcomes. The present hypothesis supplies none of those case-specific definitions or numbers.
Does the hypothesis assume that unrecorded binary outcomes are known once we define response types?

No. Response types enumerate possible joint potential-outcome patterns in the full-data model; they are latent. An observed, recorded outcome constrains which patterns can be associated with an observation, whereas an unrecorded outcome remains uncertain. Optimizing over admissible response-type distributions reflects that uncertainty rather than reconstructing individual missing outcomes.
What would show that the proposed joint endpoints are attainable?

For each endpoint, construct a full-data law satisfying the observable-data mapping and both conditional budgets, and show its candidate-minus-historical gain equals the claimed endpoint. A global bound is also needed to rule out any more extreme admissible gain. If the endpoint can only be approached by feasible laws, the bound may still be sharp as an infimum or supremum, but it would not satisfy this hypothesis’s stronger attainment claim.
Could compactness make attainment straightforward?

It could provide a route if the joint feasible set is nonempty and compact and the policy-gain functional is continuous on it. Conditional total-variation restrictions may involve conditional probabilities with denominators that vanish at boundaries, so closedness and continuity need to be established under explicit support conventions. One should not infer attainment simply from the fact that total variation is bounded.
What do ‘independently optimized margins’ refer to here?

They could mean separately optimizing candidate and historical policy values and subtracting their extrema, or separately optimizing the treatment- and recording-related latent margins before assembling a gain. Both can discard compatibility, but in different places. The hypothesis should specify which comparison is intended when tested. In either interpretation, the joint law is what ensures an evaluated gain is actually feasible.
Suppose we mean separate candidate and historical value bounds. What is the mathematical comparison?

Using the *same* F_TV(q), write C(P)=V_P(π) and H(P)=V_P(π₀). The joint lower gain bound is inf_P[C(P)−H(P)]. Marginal subtraction gives inf_P C(P)−sup_P H(P), which is no greater than the joint lower bound. For the upper endpoint, sup_P[C(P)−H(P)] is no greater than sup_P C(P)−inf_P H(P). The inequalities can be strict if the relevant marginal extrema cannot be reached together, but the hypothesis does not state that strictness occurs for every case.
If separate margins happen to attain their extrema under the same law, would they still be loose?

At that endpoint, they need not be. If one admissible law simultaneously attains the candidate minimum and historical maximum, marginal subtraction matches the joint lower bound. The analogous pairing governs the upper bound. The phrase ‘unlike independently optimized margins’ should therefore identify the risk of incompatibility, not assert that marginal subtraction is always strictly loose.
Could independently optimized treatment and recording margins produce a bound that is too low rather than too high?

Yes. Allowing combinations that no joint response-type law can realize may expand the feasible range, producing a conservative but non-sharp lower endpoint. Depending on how the independent pieces are assembled, an incorrect restriction could also omit admissible configurations and make a purported lower endpoint too high. The direction is not determined by the word ‘independent’; the precise relaxation or restriction must be examined.
What does it take to say that the joint gain extrema are *sharp*, in addition to attainable?

The feasible set must contain all and only distributions permitted by the stated observable constraints and both conditional budgets. A distribution attaining an endpoint shows that value is feasible; a global inequality over the full set shows it is extremal. If the formulation leaves out permitted response-type laws, an attained solver optimum can still be too narrow for the intended model. If it includes incompatible laws, it can be too wide. Attainment and exact representation are both needed for an attained sharp bound.
Do the two TV budgets have to use the same numerical limit?

No. They describe separate restrictions and can have different values if specified. ‘Single response-type distribution’ refers to their shared underlying full-data law, not equality of the budget limits. The hypothesis does not choose numerical budgets, so none should be inferred.
Would this hypothesis alone establish at least 95% confidence-set coverage?

No. It concerns the population gain extrema under conditional total-variation restrictions. A confidence statement additionally needs a suitably covered region for observable probabilities and complete projection through the joint-law feasible set. Exact multinomial inversion could supply the observable-region step if its test-size guarantee is established, but the attainability hypothesis does not itself provide a sampling guarantee.
Could the hypothesis itself certify that a policy improves?

No. Even attained sharp extrema could have a lower endpoint at or below zero. Population improvement requires a strictly positive lower candidate-minus-historical gain bound. An at-least-95% confidence-based certificate requires the *projected* lower endpoint to exceed zero under a valid coverage construction. The hypothesis supplies no endpoint value or sign.

“We hypothesize that, under precisely specified conditional total-variation budgets for treatment assignment and outcome recording, admissible joint distributions over binary response types attain both candidate-minus-historical policy-gain extrema, whereas separately optimized margins need not preserve that joint compatibility.”

They must be components of one full-data law. Its response-type probabilities, treatment mechanism, recording mechanism, and observable cell probabilities must fit together. What must the dual side establish?

For a lower endpoint, a valid dual certificate must bound the candidate-minus-historical gain from below for every full-data distribution allowed by the stated conditional-TV model. An upper certificate must establish the corresponding upper inequality. Would matching primal and dual solver outputs prove the TV bounds are sharp?

Only if the primal solution is genuinely feasible and the dual inequality applies to the entire intended model. Likewise, a dual check restricted to the configurations already considered by an optimizer would not rule out a more extreme admissible one. When the activity says ‘against independent margins,’ which comparison should we make?

If we compare separate policy-value bounds, what ordering should hold?

Over a common nonempty feasible set, the marginal-subtraction lower gain bound cannot exceed the directly optimized joint lower gain bound; the marginal-subtraction upper bound cannot be below the joint upper bound. The marginal interval is an outer interval because its extrema may come from different admissible laws. Equality is possible. Could independent margins be used as a valid comparison even though they might not be sharp?

What should ‘exact-95%’ mean in the benchmark?

For the observable test inversion, rejecting a true multinomial probability vector must have probability no greater than 5% across the stated parameter space. Inverting those tests then gives at least 95% coverage for the vector. If projection is complete for every distribution in the stated TV sensitivity model, that event yields at least 95% coverage for the true gain uniformly over that model. ‘Exact’ does not mean coverage equals precisely 95% everywhere, and an empirical audit on selected cases alone would not prove uniformity.

Not automatically. A fixed-table certificate applies to one observable probability vector. Certifying it requires a global bound for that larger collection, or a justified procedure that covers all its fixed-vector problems. The benchmark should distinguish the population sharpness check from certification of confidence-set endpoints.

A finding that the inverted test exceeds its allowed rejection probability, or that projection omits a gain from an admissible law at a retained observable vector, would challenge the intended guarantee. Could the extension certify improvement simply by obtaining sharp joint population bounds?

No. A sharp population lower gain bound above zero would certify improvement conditional on the observable population probabilities and the stated TV budgets. The activity supplies neither a population endpoint nor a projected one, so it makes no improvement claim.

Report equality for the endpoints and cases actually checked, subject to the precision of their certificates. The primal-dual and inversion checks remain necessary and should be reported separately.

I want to audit the nine TV-budget breaches using ΓTable v0.3 and MomentPolicy v1.0, specifically testing whether conditioning on outcome recording breaks shared-type feasibility. What is the question the audit should answer?

For each of the nine cases, the audit should ask whether the conditional total-variation (TV) constraints, as applied to recorded outcomes, can be satisfied by the *same* full-data distribution over latent binary response types, treatment assignment, and recording. If a calculation uses a conditional response-type distribution among recorded cases that cannot arise from its proposed underlying type distribution and recording mechanism, its apparent policy gain may not describe a feasible joint law. That is a possibility to test, not a diagnosis established by the activity.
What does shared-type feasibility mean here?

There must be one distribution assigning probabilities to the joint binary response types, together with treatment and recording behavior, that reproduces the specified observable probabilities and satisfies both stated TV budgets. The response-type distribution used to evaluate candidate and historical policy values must be consistent with the distributions used in the treatment and recording comparisons. Feasibility fails if those pieces cannot coexist in a single admissible law, even if separate marginal calculations look permissible.
Why focus on conditioning on recording?

Conditioning on whether an outcome was recorded changes the population whose response-type distribution is being described. The distribution among recorded cases is derived from the underlying type distribution *and* type-dependent recording probabilities. If a conditional TV restriction or an optimization treats the recorded-case distribution as freely choosable without that link, it may lose shared-type compatibility. The audit is meant to determine whether that happens in the nine cases; the activity does not say that it does.
Can you express that link in a simple general way?

If T is a latent response type and R indicates recording, then, where the conditioning event has positive probability, Pr(T=t | R=1) is proportional to Pr(R=1 | T=t)Pr(T=t). With treatment or other specified conditioning information, the same principle applies within the relevant conditional group. The conditional type frequencies are therefore consequences of one joint law, not parameters that can always be selected independently of the recording probabilities and underlying type frequencies.
Does conditioning on recording necessarily break feasibility?

No. Conditioning is a legitimate operation on an admissible full-data law. The concern is whether the *formulation* of a conditional TV budget or its implementation permits combinations of conditional and underlying distributions that cannot arise from one law, or excludes combinations that can. The audit tests that question for the nine cases; it should not assume the answer in advance.
What should we hold fixed when comparing the two tools?

But do those two tools automatically implement the same TV model?

What is the distinction between a recording constraint that uses response types and one that uses only observed outcomes?

A response type may include potential binary outcomes not revealed in the record. A distribution conditional on recording could therefore concern latent types even when only one realized outcome, if any, is visible. A restriction expressed solely in terms of recorded outcome frequencies may leave different type distributions compatible with the same observations. The audit must identify exactly which conditional distributions the recording TV budget compares; treating a latent-type restriction as though it were completely observed would change the model.
What would a concrete feasibility check do for one case?

It would seek a single nonnegative, normalized full-data distribution whose observable projection matches that case’s table. From that distribution, it would compute the response-type distributions in every conditional group used by the treatment and recording TV budgets and verify both restrictions. It would then compute both policy values and their difference under that same distribution. An explicit feasible witness supports a particular attainable gain, but it does not alone identify the global gain extremum.

Failure of a search to find one is not, by itself, proof that none exists. What would show specifically that conditioning on recording is responsible for a problem, rather than some other constraint?

And if a proposed extreme conditional distribution cannot be realized by any joint law?

Should I say that correcting those breaches proves the bounds are exact for every continuous-confounder model?

Which gain is compared with zero?

It is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value, with value defined so that a positive difference represents an improvement. It is not a test of whether a point estimate of the gain is positive.
Why use the projected lower endpoint rather than the sharp lower bound at the observed cell frequencies?

Observed cell frequencies are subject to sampling uncertainty. A bound calculated at those frequencies alone treats them as though they were the population probabilities. Does an exact-95% region guarantee that the projected set covers the policy gain?

That interpretation requires complete projection through the stated sensitivity model. When the region contains the true observable probability vector, the projection must also include every admissible full-data distribution compatible with that vector, including the one generating the true gain. With an exact region providing at least 95% coverage uniformly over the applicable model, that inclusion gives the corresponding confidence-set guarantee for the gain. A confidence region for observable cells alone cannot compensate for an incomplete latent optimization.
Does ‘exact-95%’ mean precisely 95% coverage at every distribution?

No. The relevant guarantee is *at least* 95% over the stated model; actual coverage can be greater. ‘Exact’ concerns the justification for the multinomial confidence procedure, not a promise that every distribution has coverage equal to 95.0% or that every projected interval has the same width.
Suppose the projected lower bound is exactly zero. Would we certify improvement?

No. The rule says the lower bound must *exceed* zero. An endpoint equal to zero does not rule out no gain. Likewise, a lower endpoint below zero fails to certify strict improvement, even if the projected set also includes positive gains.
Does failing that test mean the candidate policy is worse?

No. It means the corrected TV bounds and exact-95% projection do not establish strict improvement under the stated assumptions. If the lower bound is positive, does the decision make an unrestricted clinical claim?

A positive projected lower endpoint would support improvement over the historical policy across the distributions admitted by that stated sensitivity model, at the specified confidence level. It would not establish improvement under mechanisms outside the model.
Do the treatment and recording budgets still need to refer to one joint response-type distribution?

Yes. Retaining *corrected* joint TV bounds does not mean separately choosing a treatment-selection margin and a recording-selection margin and combining them freely. The two conditional budgets must be evaluated within a coherent distribution over response types, treatment, and outcome recording. Both policy values must also come from that same distribution when a candidate-minus-historical gain is evaluated.
Could we certify improvement using the independently optimized marginal interval instead?

A valid, appropriately covered marginal-subtraction lower bound above zero could also establish improvement, despite being conservative. Does the decision report a positive projected lower endpoint for any candidate?
