I want to propose optimizing joint policy-gain bounds under shared-latent KL budgets of 0.05 nats for assignment and 0.05 nats for recording, then certifying positive exact-95% lower bounds. What is the core idea?

Define a sensitivity model in which treatment assignment and outcome recording are both linked to one latent full-data distribution. Impose a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence budget of 0.05 nats on a precisely defined assignment comparison and a separate budget of 0.05 nats on a precisely defined recording comparison. Then minimize and maximize candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over the full-data distributions satisfying both budgets and the observable constraints.

For a confidence-based improvement claim, project an exact-95% confidence region for the observable probabilities through that same model. Certify strict improvement only if the projected *joint* lower policy-gain bound is greater than zero. This is a proposal, not a reported bound or certificate.
Does ‘shared-latent’ mean the assignment and recording processes have to be identical?

No. Assignment and recording are different processes and may depend differently on latent information. ‘Shared-latent’ means their specified distributions and divergences must be derived from one compatible full-data law. They cannot each use independently chosen latent-population weights and then be combined as though they described the same population.
What exactly is a KL budget of 0.05 nats?

For distributions P and Q on an appropriate common space, KL divergence in one direction is D_KL(P‖Q)=∫log(dP/dQ)dP when that expression is defined. For finite categories it is ΣⱼPⱼ log(Pⱼ/Qⱼ). ‘Nats’ indicates the natural logarithm. A 0.05-nat budget would require the *specified* divergence to be at most 0.05.

That statement is not yet a complete sensitivity assumption: we still need to define P, Q, their direction, and any conditioning. The number 0.05 cannot be interpreted without those choices.
Is 0.05 nats one combined allowance for both sources of selection?

The proposal states a 0.05-nat budget for assignment and a 0.05-nat budget for recording. They are two restrictions, not an asserted single 0.05-nat limit on their sum. Nor does having equal numerical limits make the two processes equivalent. Both budgets must hold within each admissible shared-latent distribution.
Why do we have to state the direction of the KL divergence?

Because D_KL(P‖Q) generally differs from D_KL(Q‖P). A constraint of at most 0.05 nats in one direction can admit a different set of distributions from the reverse-direction constraint. To make the policy-gain bounds meaningful and reproducible, the assignment and recording assumptions must each identify their reference and selected distributions in the intended order.
What could the assignment comparison be without committing to one in advance?

As a conceptual example, it might compare a response-type distribution among recipients of a decision with a reference response-type distribution in a stated target group, conditional on specified observed information. The divergence could then limit how strongly assignment changes that distribution. But that is only an illustration: the proposal has not selected those distributions, the treatment choices, or the conditioning groups. Calling the budget ‘for assignment’ does not supply them.
And for recording?

A recording restriction would identify which distribution among patients whose outcomes are recorded is compared with which underlying reference distribution, and under what conditioning. If recording depends on a latent outcome or response type, that possibility must be represented consistently in the full-data law. The recording KL limit should constrain the precise selection mechanism intended; it must not silently turn selectively observed outcomes into outcomes assumed missing at random.
Can I simply impose each KL inequality on a separately estimated margin?

That would not by itself enforce the proposed shared-latent model. The margins used in the assignment and recording inequalities must be derived from a single candidate full-data distribution that also reproduces the observable probabilities. Two individually permissible margins could fail to coexist in such a distribution. Optimizing over independently assembled pieces would answer a different, potentially looser feasibility question.
Does shared-latent coupling also apply to the two policy values?

Yes. Every evaluated gain is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value under one admissible distribution. The candidate’s unfavorable value cannot be taken from one latent law and the historical policy’s favorable value from another and treated as an attainable contrast. That policy-value compatibility is related to, but distinct from, ensuring assignment and recording share the latent law.
How would you write the joint policy-gain bounds?

Let q represent the observable probability vector, and let F_KL(q) be all full-data laws compatible with q and both fully specified shared-latent KL restrictions, each with its respective 0.05-nat limit. For candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, write Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The proposed population bounds are L(q)=inf_{P∈F_KL(q)}Δ(P) and U(q)=sup_{P∈F_KL(q)}Δ(P).

These expressions define the optimization target. They do not assert that F_KL(q) has been specified in full, that its extrema are attained, or that numerical values have been obtained.
Why optimize the difference rather than first bound both policy values?

Direct optimization keeps the two values on the same admissible shared-latent law. Subtracting a separately optimized historical upper value from a candidate lower value gives a conservative lower gain bound if the marginal bounds are valid, but the extrema may come from incompatible laws. That subtraction need not be sharp for improvement. A positive conservative lower bound can still be useful, but the proposal targets *joint* gain bounds.
What assumptions about outcomes are implied by the 0.05-nat limits?

Neither limit alone specifies an outcome scale, outcome distribution, or clinical utility. They constrain designated distributional comparisons for assignment and recording. To evaluate policy value, one must separately define the outcome or utility, the policies, and the target population. The proposal does not state whether outcomes are binary, continuous, favorable when high, or coded in any particular way.
Does a small KL budget mean unmeasured confounding is absent?

No. A budget of 0.05 nats permits differences up to the specified limit between the distributions being compared. Its substantive strength depends on that comparison and direction. Nor is 0.05 an estimate of confounding or recording selectivity from observed data; it is a proposed sensitivity restriction to state and assess conditionally.
Are there support issues with KL that would matter for sharp bounds?

Yes. In D_KL(P‖Q), assigning positive P mass where Q has zero mass generally makes divergence infinite. Conditional KL may also be undefined if its conditioning event has zero probability. The model has to state its support and boundary conventions. Those choices determine which full-data laws are feasible and can affect whether an endpoint is realized or only approached.
If both separate 0.05-nat inequalities hold, is the full-data model automatically nonempty?

No. The two restrictions must also coexist with each other and with the observable distribution under a single latent law. For some specified comparisons and observable probabilities, there might be no compatible full-data distribution. An empty feasible set should be identified as a model-compatibility issue, not treated as evidence of a positive policy gain.
What would it take to call the joint bounds sharp?

The formulation must include every full-data law permitted by the observable constraints and both shared-latent 0.05-nat budgets, and exclude laws those assumptions forbid. One must then find the global infimum and supremum of the gain over that exact set. An admissible law attaining an endpoint—or admissible laws approaching an unattained endpoint—shows why it cannot be tightened. The words ‘joint optimization’ and ‘KL budget’ alone do not provide that demonstration.
Does the KL formulation guarantee that each extremum is attained?

No. Attainment depends on the defined feasible class, support conventions, and the policy-value functional. For example, whether a boundary law is included can matter. A sharp infimum can be approached without being attained. The proposed bounds should be stated as infima and suprema until an existence or attaining-witness argument is established.
What does ‘exact-95% lower bound’ mean here?

It refers to a lower confidence endpoint obtained by projecting an observable confidence region with the required exact 95% guarantee through the shared-latent KL model. It is not merely the population lower bound evaluated at observed frequencies, and ‘95%’ is not a numerical precision tolerance for the optimization. The proposal has not specified a particular observable sampling model or confidence-region construction.
How would projection be expressed?

If C₉₅(N) is an exact-95% confidence region for observable probabilities based on data N, the projected gain set is D(N)={Δ(P): q∈C₉₅(N), P∈F_KL(q)}. Its lower endpoint is the infimum over *both* the retained observable vectors and all full-data laws compatible with each vector. Optimizing only at one estimated vector and attaching a 95% label would not perform this projection.
Why should the projected set have at least 95% coverage uniformly?

Take any true full-data law P in the stated sensitivity model, with observable vector q_P. If the confidence region includes q_P and the projection includes every law in F_KL(q_P), then D(N) includes Δ(P). Thus a region that covers q_P with probability at least 0.95 for *every* admissible P transfers that at-least-95% guarantee to the gain. Complete projection also includes the entire identified gain set at q_P on the same event. These are conditions the proposed procedure must satisfy, not guarantees supplied by the KL label alone.
Does exact-95% mean coverage must be exactly 95% for every admissible distribution?

No. The target is coverage of *at least* 95% uniformly over the stated model. An exact observable procedure and the subsequent projection can be conservative. What matters is a justified uniform lower coverage guarantee, not equality to 95% at each distribution.
Would a valid observable confidence region compensate if the KL optimization omitted a possible latent law?

No. If the true observable vector is retained but an admissible full-data law is excluded from the projection, that law’s gain need not be covered. Conversely, adding incompatible laws may widen the set and lose population sharpness. The coverage and sharpness claims both depend on representing the shared-latent 0.05-nat constraints faithfully.
What exactly certifies a positive gain?

Define policy value so that Δ>0 means the candidate improves on the historical policy. Then require inf D(N)>0: the *projected exact-95% joint lower gain bound* must be strictly positive. An endpoint equal to zero does not certify strict improvement, and a positive point estimate is insufficient. Even if this rule is met, the conclusion remains conditional on the specified assignment and recording KL comparisons and their two 0.05-nat budgets.
If the projected lower bound is negative, does that show the policy is harmful?

No. It means the proposed confidence and sensitivity analysis does not rule out a nonpositive gain. Positive gains might remain in the projected set. Establishing that every retained gain is negative would instead require an upper endpoint below zero. Failure to certify improvement is not a finding of harm.
Does this proposal give any numerical gain bound or say that a policy passes the test?

No. Its numerical commitments are the proposed 0.05-nat KL budget for assignment, the separate 0.05-nat budget for recording, and the exact-95% confidence target. It supplies no observable data, fully specified KL comparisons, computed policy-gain endpoints, or positive projected lower bound. It therefore proposes a way to seek a certificate, not an achieved certification.
How would you state the proposal succinctly while preserving all those qualifications?

“Specify shared-latent KL sensitivity restrictions of 0.05 nats each for treatment assignment and outcome recording, optimize candidate-minus-historical policy gain jointly over compatible full-data laws, and use an exact-95% projected confidence lower bound to certify strict improvement only when that bound exceeds zero.” Sharpness and uniform coverage must be justified for the specified model and projection.
Can shared-latent KL constraints yield attainable policy-gain extrema when outcome recording depends on unobserved potential outcomes?

They can, but neither shared-latent coupling nor a KL bound guarantees attainment by itself. The model would need to permit that dependence explicitly: a candidate full-data law must jointly describe potential outcomes, treatment assignment, and whether the realized outcome is recorded. The sharp gain bounds are the infimum and supremum of candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over all such laws compatible with the observations and the stated KL constraints. To call an endpoint *attainable*, one must also show that an admissible law actually realizes it.
Does allowing recording to depend on an unobserved potential outcome mean that outcome has been inferred for an individual?

No. It means the full-data model permits dependence that the observed records cannot directly reveal. An admissible law assigns probabilities to possible potential outcomes and recording events; it does not identify any patient’s missing outcome. The optimization considers every jointly compatible law, including different possibilities for outcomes that are never recorded.
Should recording depend only on the potential outcome under the treatment received?

That is a modeling choice that must be stated. The realized outcome under the received treatment can be unobserved when it is not recorded. A model could permit recording to depend on that outcome, or it could permit dependence on a broader latent response type containing outcomes under other treatments. Those choices define different feasible classes. The question as posed does not select one, so an attainability argument cannot quietly assume either.
What does sharing the latent structure require if recording can depend on those outcomes?

Each admissible candidate must be one joint law for the latent information, the potential outcomes, treatment assignment, and recording. The distributions used in the assignment KL comparison and the recording KL comparison must be derived from that law. One cannot optimize assignment with one latent mixture and recording with another, then treat their combination as an attainable policy gain. The candidate and historical policy values must also be evaluated under that same law.
Are the assignment and recording KL restrictions identical because they share a law?

No. They can constrain different conditional distributional comparisons, and recording may depend on potential outcomes in ways assignment does not. Sharing a law establishes compatibility; it does not equate the two mechanisms, their reference distributions, or their KL divergences.
What needs to be specified before we can reason about whether an extremum exists?

Define the potential-outcome and policy-value scales, the observable-data mapping, and exactly which full-data laws are admitted. For each KL constraint, specify the two distributions compared, the direction of divergence, any conditioning information, and the treatment of zero-probability events and support mismatches. If recording may depend on latent outcomes, say which outcomes it may depend on and how that dependence enters the joint law. Existence of an optimizer depends on those details, not just on the phrase ‘shared-latent KL.’
Why does KL direction matter to attainment rather than merely to the numerical bound?

KL divergence is asymmetric: D_KL(P‖Q) and D_KL(Q‖P) can define different feasible sets. Its direction also determines which support mismatches have infinite divergence. Those choices affect whether a sequence of feasible laws can approach a boundary law and whether that boundary law remains feasible. Thus direction and support conventions can affect both the endpoint’s value and whether it is attained.
Could a recording rule that nearly never records one latent outcome cause an endpoint to be approached but not reached?

Possibly, depending on the stated support and conditioning rules. A sequence might drive a recording probability toward zero while remaining admissible, yet the limiting law might be excluded by a strict positivity condition or leave a conditional KL comparison undefined. Then the gain could approach an infimum without any admissible law attaining it. If the boundary law is included and satisfies every constraint, attainment may instead be possible. This is a general illustration, not a finding about a specified recording rule.
If the gain approaches an endpoint, isn’t the bound still sharp?

It can be. A sharp infimum cannot be increased if admissible gains come arbitrarily close to it, even when no single law attains it. But ‘sharp’ and ‘attainable’ are different claims. The question asks the stronger existence question: is there an admissible law at the endpoint, rather than merely a sequence approaching it?
Would a KL constraint by itself make the set of admissible laws compact?

Not as an unconditional statement. Compactness depends on the underlying spaces, reference distributions, topology, additional constraints, and how conditional KL is defined at boundaries. One would also need the observable constraints and shared-latent relationships to remain closed under the relevant limits. A claim of compactness must be established for the fully specified feasible class, not inferred from the presence of a KL budget.
What is the standard existence argument if those properties can be shown?

Show that the admissible set of full-data laws is nonempty and compact in a topology under which the policy-gain functional is continuous. Then the gain has a minimum and maximum on that set. If continuity fails, one needs the appropriate semicontinuity for the endpoint at issue or a different argument. Conditional selection constraints involving low-probability groups make it especially important to check the premises rather than simply invoke an existence theorem.
Can you write the optimization without assuming attainment?

Let F(q) be the set of full-data laws mapping to observable probabilities q and satisfying the fully specified shared-latent KL constraints, including the permitted outcome-dependent recording mechanism. For a candidate policy π and historical policy π₀, write Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). Then L(q)=inf_{P∈F(q)}Δ(P) and U(q)=sup_{P∈F(q)}Δ(P). Attainment would require laws P_L and P_U in F(q) with Δ(P_L)=L(q) and Δ(P_U)=U(q), respectively. Different laws may attain the two endpoints.
Does joint optimization of that difference settle the shared-latent issue?

It settles one part: within each evaluation, the candidate and historical values come from the same proposed law. But the law itself must be coherent. In particular, its assignment and recording components must be compatible with the same latent outcomes and probabilities, and its KL comparisons must be computed from that law. A joint objective over an incorrectly relaxed set could still produce an unattainable endpoint for the intended model.
Would modeling only the realized but unrecorded outcomes be sufficient?

Only if those variables contain everything needed to evaluate the policies and state the sensitivity assumptions. A candidate policy may assign decisions other than the one observed, so its value generally involves the relevant potential outcomes under those decisions. If recording is allowed to depend on a broader response type, that dependence also has to be represented. Which components are necessary follows from the explicitly chosen policy and full-data model; an observed-outcome table alone need not suffice.
If recorded and unrecorded people have the same observable cells, can their latent potential outcomes still differ?

Yes. Agreement on observable probabilities does not identify the distribution of unobserved potential outcomes. Outcome-dependent recording is precisely a mechanism under which the recorded cases need not represent the unrecorded ones. The KL assumptions restrict the distributions specified in their comparisons, but they do not make latent potential outcomes observed.
Could we prove attainment by constructing a feasible extremizing distribution rather than proving compactness?

Yes. For a lower endpoint, an explicit admissible law attaining value b and a global inequality Δ(P)≥b for every P∈F(q) establish an attained minimum. The upper endpoint needs an analogous witness and inequality. The construction must reproduce the observable probabilities and satisfy *both* KL constraints with the stipulated outcome-dependent recording relationship. A witness without the global inequality proves only that its gain is feasible.
Would a dual certificate provide the needed global inequality?

It could, if its validity extends to every law in the stated shared-latent model, including laws where recording depends on the specified unobserved potential outcomes. Matching that inequality with a feasible attaining law would certify the endpoint. A dual derived for a model that assumes outcome-independent recording, or one that lets assignment and recording use incompatible latent distributions, would not certify this question’s target.
What if primal and dual optimal values agree, but no feasible optimizer is exhibited?

Agreement can establish the sharp infimum or supremum under a correctly formulated duality result, but it does not automatically establish attainment. The primal optimum might be a limit of admissible gains. To answer the attainability question, one still needs an attaining law or an existence theorem whose assumptions hold for the relevant feasible class.
Could a finite atomic law be an attaining witness even though the confounder is allowed to be continuous?

Possibly. An unrestricted latent class can include finite atomic distributions, in which case a feasible atomic law and a global bound over the *whole* class could certify an attained extremum. But a fixed finite approximation is not automatically exhaustive. One must show the atomic law satisfies the outcome-dependent recording and both KL restrictions; proving a universal finite-support reduction would be a separate, broader result.
What if the latent law reproduces the recorded outcomes but violates the recording KL budget only among unrecorded potential-outcome types?

Then it is not an admissible witness under a model whose recording KL comparison covers those types. Reproducing the recorded cells is necessary but not sufficient. The feasibility check must use the full latent distribution required by the stated comparison, including unobserved potential-outcome information wherever the model makes it relevant. The exact reference and conditioning for that KL comparison must be specified before a violation can be assessed.
Could the feasible set be empty for a given observable distribution?

Yes. The observable probabilities, shared-latent structure, and KL restrictions might be incompatible. If F(q) is empty, its formal optimization expressions do not provide meaningful attainable policy-gain extrema, and emptiness is not an improvement certificate. Compatibility should be checked before interpreting a bound.
If the extrema are attainable, are they necessarily sharp?

An attained minimum and maximum *over an exactly specified full-data feasible set* are sharp for that set. But attainment of an optimizer in a computational representation does not show that the representation includes every law allowed by the intended sensitivity model or excludes incompatible laws. For a sharp policy-gain claim, model equivalence and global optimization still have to be established.
How does this relate to certifying improvement over the historical policy?

Attainability clarifies whether the extreme gains correspond to actual admissible laws. Population-level strict improvement requires the valid lower candidate-minus-historical gain bound to exceed zero, whether the infimum is attained or only approached. A confidence-based claim additionally needs an appropriately projected lower confidence bound above zero with the required coverage. Neither positivity nor a confidence result follows just from establishing attainment.
Does an exact-95% observable confidence region prove that the extrema exist?

No. Exact confidence coverage concerns sampling uncertainty in observable probabilities. Attainment concerns the geometry and boundary behavior of the latent full-data feasible set at a given observable vector, or across a projected region if that is the optimization target. The two properties require separate arguments.
So what is the careful answer to the original question?

Yes, shared-latent KL constraints *can* yield attainable policy-gain extrema even when recording depends on unobserved potential outcomes, if the permitted dependence is encoded in one coherent full-data law and the resulting feasible class admits optimizers. But separate KL inequalities, a jointly written objective, or a matching dual value do not by themselves prove attainment. The answer for a particular model requires its precise KL comparisons and boundary conventions, plus feasible endpoint laws or a valid existence argument.

My hypothesis is that a shared response-type distribution satisfying both 0.05-nat KL budgets attains the policy-gain extrema even when outcome recording depends on unobserved potential outcomes. What would that claim require?

It would require an admissible full-data distribution at each endpoint of the candidate-minus-historical policy-gain range. Within each distribution, the response types, treatment assignment, and outcome recording must be jointly compatible; the specified KL divergence for assignment must be no more than 0.05 nats, and the separate specified divergence for recording must also be no more than 0.05 nats. Recording may depend on the unobserved potential outcomes in the way the model expressly allows. The hypothesis is that such distributions *attain* the gain extrema, not merely that gains can approach them.
Does ‘a shared response-type distribution’ mean the same distribution must minimize and maximize gain?

No. A lower-extremum distribution and an upper-extremum distribution can differ. ‘Shared’ means that within either candidate law, the response-type probabilities used for treatment selection, recording selection, and both policy values belong to one coherent distribution. It does not require a single law to attain both endpoints.
What are response types in this claim?

They encode the potential outcomes relevant to the policies under the treatment choices being considered. A response type may contain outcomes that are not seen because a different treatment was received or because the realized outcome was not recorded. The hypothesis concerns a *distribution* over such types; it does not say that an individual’s missing potential outcomes can be recovered from the observable data. The proposal does not specify the outcome categories or treatment choices, so those would have to be defined in a concrete model.
How can outcome-dependent recording be compatible with a shared type distribution?

A full-data law can specify, for each response type and other relevant information, probabilities of treatment assignment and of recording the realized outcome. Recording can vary with a potential outcome permitted by the model, while the overall type weights remain those of the same underlying population used for policy evaluation. The observed records then arise by marginalizing that law. Compatibility means the type weights and conditional mechanisms jointly generate the observables and satisfy both KL budgets; it does not mean recording is independent of latent outcomes.
Could assignment and recording use different selected-type distributions while still sharing an underlying one?

Yes. Different selection mechanisms can produce different type distributions among treated and recorded groups. Those conditional distributions must, however, be derived from the *same* underlying response-type law and its assignment and recording probabilities. The hypothesis rules out assembling independently chosen conditional type distributions that cannot coexist under one full-data law; it does not require the selected groups to have identical compositions.
What do the two 0.05-nat constraints actually compare?

The hypothesis identifies their roles and numerical budgets—0.05 nats for assignment and 0.05 nats for recording—but it does not identify the reference and selected distributions, KL directions, or conditioning groups. Those must be stated to define a testable sensitivity model. KL is asymmetric, so reversing either comparison could change the feasible distributions. The hypothesis cannot be verified simply by checking that two unspecified divergences are small.
Are those two budgets combined into a single allowance of 0.10 nats?

No. The claim is that the shared distribution satisfies *both* separate 0.05-nat limits. It does not assert an additive 0.10-nat constraint, nor that one mechanism can exceed 0.05 nats if the other uses less. Any trade-off rule would be a different assumption and would need to be stated.
Why is attainment a stronger claim than sharpness?

A bound can be sharp as an infimum or supremum even if no admissible distribution reaches it, provided admissible gains approach it arbitrarily closely. Attainment requires a specific admissible full-data distribution at the endpoint. The hypothesis asserts that stronger property for the gain extrema, so a sequence of closer and closer feasible gains would not by itself verify it.
Can you express that difference in symbols?

Let F_KL(q) be the full-data laws compatible with observable vector q, the outcome-dependent recording model, and both specified 0.05-nat KL constraints. Define Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀). The bounds are L=inf_{P∈F_KL(q)}Δ(P) and U=sup_{P∈F_KL(q)}Δ(P). The hypothesis asserts the existence of P_L,P_U∈F_KL(q) with Δ(P_L)=L and Δ(P_U)=U. Merely having sequences with Δ(P_n)→L or U would support limiting sharp bounds, not those existence equalities.
What would prove the lower endpoint is the minimum rather than just an attainable gain?

One needs both a feasible law P_L attaining the stated lower value and a global inequality showing Δ(P) is at least that value for every P in F_KL(q). A valid dual certificate over the full shared-latent model could provide the inequality. The attaining law must reproduce the observable probabilities, satisfy both 0.05-nat comparisons in their specified directions, and implement the permitted outcome-dependent recording. A witness alone cannot rule out a lower gain.
Would the upper endpoint need a separate witness?

Yes. One needs a feasible law reaching the proposed maximum and a global inequality ruling out higher gains. It need not be the same law as the lower-endpoint witness. A lower-bound certificate does not establish an upper extremum, even though both use the same model definition.
What if the recording KL constraint is conditional on a group with zero recording probability?

Then the relevant conditional distribution may be undefined. The model must specify whether that boundary law is excluded, whether the KL restriction applies only for positive-probability groups, or whether another formulation handles it. The choice affects whether an extreme gain is feasible or only approached. A proof of attainment has to use the same boundary convention as the stated sensitivity model.
Could the 0.05-nat KL limits themselves guarantee that boundary problem cannot arise?

Not without knowing the directions, reference supports, conditioning groups, and any positivity conditions. KL can exclude certain support mismatches, but a numerical limit alone does not define all conditional probabilities or settle whether recording can vanish in a group. It would be unsound to infer endpoint existence solely from the two 0.05-nat figures.
Is compactness a plausible proof strategy?

Conditionally, yes. If the precisely defined feasible class of shared response-type laws is nonempty and compact and the gain functional is continuous, both extrema are attained. But conditional KL and outcome-dependent recording may complicate closedness or continuity at boundary events. A proof must establish those properties for the actual model, or instead construct feasible endpoint laws directly. The hypothesis supplies neither proof yet.
Could we restrict the response-type distribution to finitely many types and then invoke compactness?

If the model has a finite set of response types and its constraints define a closed subset of the associated probability simplex, compactness may help. But one still has to handle conditional KL properly and show that the finite response-type representation covers every full-data law relevant to the policies and recording dependence. A compact *restricted* formulation may attain its own extrema without attaining the extrema of the intended model.
Does the hypothesis imply the policy-gain bounds are sharp for any observable table?

No universal quantifier over all tables is stated. Even for a given table, attainment must be paired with an exact representation of the admissible laws and a global-extremum argument to call the bounds sharp. The hypothesis proposes existence of shared, budget-compliant extremizers despite outcome-dependent recording; it does not supply a theorem for every possible observed distribution.
What if there is no distribution consistent with the observed probabilities and both budgets?

Then the feasible set is empty, so it contains no attaining extremizer. That is a compatibility issue to address, not a policy-improvement certificate. The hypothesis requires nonempty feasibility wherever it is claimed to apply; it cannot turn inconsistency between the observables and sensitivity restrictions into an endpoint.
Do the two policy values need to be optimized separately to check the hypothesis?

No. The target is the *joint* gain Δ(P), evaluated under one admissible law. Separately optimizing the candidate and historical values could combine incompatible extrema and produce an outer interval. It would not test whether a single shared response-type distribution attains the minimum or maximum of their difference.
Could a duality result prove the hypothesis by itself?

A duality result might identify the optimal values and furnish global bounds, but equality of primal and dual values does not necessarily show that a primal optimizer exists. To establish this attainment hypothesis, the proof must produce admissible endpoint laws or establish an existence theorem for the precisely defined feasible class. Duality and primal attainment should be stated separately.
Would attaining extrema automatically certify clinical improvement?

No. An attained lower gain extremum could be zero or negative. Population-level strict improvement requires the valid lower gain bound to exceed zero. An exact-95% confidence-based certificate requires a projected lower bound above zero with the stated uniform coverage guarantee. The attainment hypothesis provides neither an endpoint value nor a confidence statement.
How would you state the hypothesis without presenting it as proved?

“We hypothesize that, under a fully specified shared-response-type model allowing outcome-dependent recording, admissible distributions satisfying both the assignment and recording KL budgets of 0.05 nats attain the minimum and maximum candidate-minus-historical policy gains.” The KL comparisons, feasibility, and endpoint proofs remain to be supplied.
I want to derive shared-latent KL primal-dual bounds, construct attaining response-type distributions, and project exact-95% multinomial confidence regions. How do those parts fit together?

First, define the full-data distributions permitted by the shared-latent KL sensitivity model and the observed probabilities. Optimize candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value over that class, then derive dual inequalities that bound the same contrast globally. Next, construct admissible response-type distributions whose gains meet the proposed lower and upper bounds; a dual inequality alone does not establish attainment. Finally, project an exact-95% multinomial confidence region through the admissible distributions so the bounds account for sampling uncertainty in the observed probabilities. These are steps to carry out, not results already established.
What does ‘shared-latent’ need to mean in the primal problem?

Each feasible point must describe one coherent full-data law. Its response-type distribution, treatment-assignment mechanism, and outcome-recording mechanism must jointly generate the observable data. Assignment and recording can behave differently, including recording dependence on potential outcomes if the model permits it, but their KL comparisons must be calculated from that same law. Both policies’ values must also be evaluated under that law whenever their difference is calculated.
Do the assignment and recording KL budgets remain separate?

Yes. The established proposal has one 0.05-nat budget for assignment and a separate 0.05-nat budget for recording. Sharing a latent distribution does not combine them into one allowance or require the two mechanisms to have identical probabilities. To turn either budget into a constraint, the derivation must still specify the compared distributions, KL direction, conditioning, and support conventions.
What should the primal objective be if the question is improvement over the historical policy?

Define Δ(P)=V_P(π)−V_P(π₀), where π is the candidate policy, π₀ is the historical policy, and both values refer to the same target population and admissible full-data law P. At a fixed observable probability vector q, minimize and maximize Δ(P) over the laws consistent with q and both specified KL budgets. Those are the proposed population improvement bounds. Their values and signs are not supplied by the plan.
Why not establish primal-dual bounds for each policy value and subtract them?

That can yield a conservative interval if the separate bounds are valid, but the minimizing law for the candidate value need not maximize the historical value. Deriving primal and dual bounds for Δ directly preserves which pairs of policy values can coexist. It also keeps the bound being certified aligned with the improvement criterion, which concerns the sign of the candidate-minus-historical contrast.
What exactly would a lower dual certificate say?

For a specified observable vector q, it would give a number b and a valid argument that Δ(P)≥b for *every* full-data law P admitted by the shared-latent KL model at q. An upper certificate would establish Δ(P)≤b for every such P. The dual derivation must cover the permitted outcome-dependent recording mechanisms as well as assignment; an inequality proved only for a restricted set of response types would not certify the proposed full-model bound.
If we derive both inequalities, have we established sharp bounds?

Not necessarily. Globally valid dual inequalities establish bounds, but either may be conservative. To show a lower bound is sharp, an admissible law must attain its value or admissible laws must approach it arbitrarily closely; the same applies at the upper endpoint. Because this plan specifically calls for *attaining* response-type distributions, its intended result is stronger than merely showing sharp infima and suprema.
Would matching primal and dual values by itself establish attainment?

No. Agreement of optimal values, if proved, addresses duality, but the primal optimum might still be an infimum no feasible law reaches. Constructing an attaining distribution is a separate task. An explicit feasible endpoint law together with a globally valid matching dual inequality would establish both attainment and optimality for that endpoint.
Does one response-type distribution need to attain both endpoints?

No. A lower-endpoint distribution and an upper-endpoint distribution may differ. ‘Shared’ means that within each one, response types, assignment, recording, and both policy values form a single compatible law. It does not mean one law must simultaneously minimize and maximize gain.
What must an attaining distribution demonstrate besides producing the desired numerical gain?

It must reproduce the specified observable probabilities, define the response types needed for both policy values, satisfy the assignment and recording KL restrictions in their stated directions, and implement the permitted dependence of recording on potential outcomes. Its probabilities must describe one full-data law. A numerical gain from a distribution that fails one of those checks is not an attainable gain under the proposed model.
If recording depends on an outcome that is never seen, how can we check an extremizing distribution?

The check concerns the distribution’s internal feasibility, not recovery of individual missing outcomes. A proposed full-data law specifies latent outcomes and their relationship to recording, then implies observable probabilities by marginalization. We can ask whether those implied probabilities match the observed-data target and whether the specified recording KL restriction holds. Different admissible laws may pass those checks; the optimization searches among them without declaring a patient’s unobserved outcome known.
Could a dual argument accidentally assume recording is independent of potential outcomes?

Yes, if the derivation silently restricts its feasible laws. The plan should explicitly state which potential outcomes recording may depend on and verify that the lower and upper dual inequalities hold for every law permitted by that specification. A certificate for outcome-independent recording would not automatically apply to a model that allows outcome-dependent recording.
What role do KL support and zero-probability events play in this plan?

They help determine the feasible set and whether an extremum can be attained. KL divergence is directional, and a support mismatch can make a specified divergence infinite. A conditional comparison can also be undefined when its conditioning group has probability zero. The primal constraints and dual proof must use the same explicit boundary conventions. A sequence approaching an excluded boundary could yield a sharp infimum without supplying the attaining law this plan seeks.
Would a finite collection of response types make the existence proof automatic?

Not automatically. Even with finitely many response types, conditional KL constraints can involve denominators and boundary cases whose treatment affects whether the feasible set is closed. One route would be to prove that the feasible set is nonempty and compact and that gain is continuous on it; another would be to construct endpoint laws directly. Either route must apply to the exact shared-latent model, not just a convenient restricted optimization.
What if a numerical primal–dual match is close but not exact?

Report the tolerance and what is certified on each side. A feasible gain and a global dual bound separated by a small amount bracket the extremum to that amount; they do not establish exact equality. Likewise, an approximately extremizing response-type distribution does not prove that the mathematical endpoint is attained unless the remaining gap is resolved by an exact argument.
Before doing inference, what does the population result have to cover?

It must characterize candidate-minus-historical gain over all full-data laws compatible with a specified observable probability vector and both KL restrictions. A faithful primal representation, globally valid dual bounds, and endpoint constructions each address a different part of that characterization. The intended confidence projection then varies the observable vector, so a population result at one vector alone cannot settle every projected endpoint.
How is the exact-95% multinomial region constructed conceptually?

Specify the observable multinomial cells and a family of tests for candidate cell-probability vectors. Retain vectors their tests do not reject. If the probability of rejecting a true vector is at most 5% at every vector in the stated parameter space, the inverted region contains the true vector with probability at least 95% uniformly. The plan calls for projecting such a region; it does not specify the test statistic, acceptance rule, or cell definitions.
What precisely is projected through the KL model?

For every observable vector q retained in the confidence region, take every shared-latent, KL-admissible full-data law compatible with q and evaluate its gain Δ(P). The projected confidence set is the collection of those gains. Its lower endpoint minimizes over both q and P in that compatible collection, not merely over distributions matching the observed cell frequencies. A vector in the region with no compatible law contributes no gain.
Would a fixed-q dual certificate remain valid for that entire projection?

Not without further argument. Its inequality may depend on q. A projected lower-bound certificate must hold across *all* observable vectors retained by the region and every compatible law at each vector, or be obtained by a justified optimization over their collection. Likewise, an attaining law at one q does not necessarily attain the projected endpoint when q is allowed to vary.
Does the plan call for attained projected endpoints as well as attained population endpoints?

It calls for constructing attaining response-type distributions and projecting confidence regions. The attainment claim should identify which optimization it covers. If it is made for fixed-q population extrema, it should not silently be extended to projected extrema; the projected feasible collection also varies q and needs its own existence or witness argument. A confidence set can be defined using infima and suprema without asserting projected attainment.
How does exact-95% observable coverage transfer to the policy gain?

For any true law in the stated sensitivity model, if the inverted region contains its observable probability vector, complete projection includes that law and therefore its candidate-minus-historical gain. Uniform coverage of the observable vector at a level of at least 95% then gives at-least-95% coverage of the true gain, provided no admissible laws are omitted. Complete projection also includes the entire population identified gain range at the true observable vector on that same event. Those implications depend on the precise model and correct projection, not on duality alone.
Can primal-dual sharpness compensate for an inaccurate multinomial confidence region?

No. Primal-dual arguments address the range of gains allowed at observable probabilities; multinomial test inversion addresses sampling uncertainty about those probabilities. Accurate population extrema cannot supply a missing coverage guarantee. Conversely, an exact observable region cannot make an omitted latent law feasible in a purportedly complete projection. Both parts need their own justification.
When would the projected analysis certify improvement?

Only when its lower confidence endpoint for joint candidate-minus-historical gain is strictly above zero, with policy value oriented so positive means improvement. The certificate is conditional on the specified shared-latent KL model and the exact-95% projection’s coverage guarantee. An attained population minimum, even if established, does not alone say whether that projected endpoint is positive.
If that lower endpoint equals zero, do we certify anything about the candidate?

It does not certify *strict* improvement over the historical policy. A confidence set whose lower endpoint is zero may still contain positive gains, so failure to pass the threshold does not establish that the candidate is worse. The plan supplies no endpoint sign in any event.
How can I describe the plan without presenting any of its claims as completed?

“We will derive primal and dual bounds for joint policy gain under a shared-latent KL model, construct response-type distributions attaining the extrema, and project exact-95% multinomial confidence regions through the admissible laws to assess improvement over the historical policy.” The duality, attainment, uniform coverage, and any positive projected lower bound remain to be established.

For this activity, implement KL-constrained shared-type optimization at 0.05 nats and compare primal-dual certificates with exact-95% projections on 200 outcome-dependent-recording tables. What are we evaluating?

The activity evaluates whether the shared-type optimization produces defensible joint policy-gain bounds for those 200 tables and whether its bounds are carried correctly into exact-95% confidence projections. A primal witness and a globally valid dual inequality address an optimization endpoint at specified observable probabilities. Projection additionally varies those probabilities over an exact multinomial confidence region. The activity gives no certificate gaps, projected endpoints, coverage findings, or improvement decisions.

The stress test should check that the optimizer’s representation and dual certificates cover the continuous-confounder laws being claimed, rather than assuming a finite response-type calculation is automatically equivalent.
How would we test attainment of a lower endpoint?

For a proposed lower gain L, verify a full-data law under the continuous-confounder model whose gain equals L, while satisfying the observable constraints and both shared-latent KL restrictions. Then verify a global lower inequality Δ(P)≥L for every law in that model. If the witness and global bound meet only to a stated numerical tolerance, describe agreement to that tolerance. A sequence of feasible gains approaching L would support a sharp infimum, but not attainment by a single law.
And would the upper endpoint need the same treatment?

Yes. A feasible law realizing the greatest candidate-minus-historical gain and a global upper inequality address that endpoint. The lower and upper extremizers may be different laws. Evidence for one endpoint should not be extended to the other unless the corresponding checks have been done.
Why might low recording affect attainment rather than just interval width?

If extremal gains are approached by making recording of a particular latent type increasingly rare, an endpoint’s existence can depend on whether the limiting law is allowed and whether conditional KL quantities remain defined there. The same low recording rate may also leave many latent outcome distributions compatible with the observed cells, widening bounds. These are possible mathematical effects to investigate, not findings from the stress test.
Does positive 1% overall recording guarantee every conditional KL comparison is defined?

No. An overall rate of 1% can coexist with zero recording probability for some relevant conditional group, unless the model imposes support conditions that rule it out. Conditional distributions given such an event would be undefined in the usual sense. The stress test must use an explicit convention for those groups, consistent across the primal constraints, dual derivation, and confidence projection.
What is a feasible primal witness in a continuous-confounder case?

It is a complete admissible distribution: latent confounder and response-type probabilities, assignment and recording mechanisms, and the implied observable outcomes, all consistent with the tested model. It must reproduce the specified observable probability vector, respect the 1% recording condition as defined there, and satisfy the assignment and recording KL limits in their specified directions. Its candidate-minus-historical gain is then an attainable value, though not necessarily the global extremum.
Could KLPolicy v0.1 report a primal–dual match but miss a continuous-confounder distribution?

That is something the stress test must check. Primal–dual agreement proves little about a distribution omitted from the feasible representation if the dual inequality also applies only to the represented class. To certify the intended continuous model, the dual bound must hold across all of its admissible laws, and the proposed primal witness must belong to that model. A finite or restricted representation cannot be assumed complete merely because its own optimization converges.
What is the confidence set being checked at the exact-95% stage?

Exact multinomial inversion first yields a region for observable cell probabilities. Projection through every compatible shared-latent KL law yields a set of possible candidate-minus-historical gains. The intended at-least-95% coverage claim concerns the true gain under the stated sensitivity model, or the entire identified gain set if that stronger target is specified. The stress test should identify which event it checks.
Why is projecting only the observable region insufficient to claim gain coverage?

An observable probability vector can be compatible with several latent confounder and outcome distributions that imply different policy gains. The projection must include those admissible gains. If it omits a law that becomes important when recording is only 1%, covering the true observable vector would not necessarily cover that law’s gain. Complete projection is the link between an exact observable region and a policy-gain confidence set.
Could an exact multinomial region still lead to undercoverage of the gain?

Yes, if the gain projection is incomplete or uses a feasible class narrower than the stated sensitivity model. The exact region’s guarantee is for observable probabilities. A claim about the gain also depends on the latent-model representation. The activity tests this in a low-recording setting; it does not report that undercoverage occurs.
What does uniform at-least-95% coverage require here?

For every full-data distribution admitted by the stated shared-latent KL model with the specified recording condition, the projected set must contain the true policy gain with probability at least 95% under its observable sampling distribution. Exact multinomial test inversion can give a uniform coverage event for the true observable vector if its size is controlled across all relevant vectors. Complete projection must then transfer that event to the gain for every admissible law, not only the continuous-confounder examples examined.
Would checking a collection of continuous-confounder examples prove that uniform guarantee?

No. Examples can reveal failures or support an implementation audit in the tested settings, but uniformity quantifies over an entire stated model. An all-vector test-size result and an all-law projection argument are still needed. The activity specifies no number of tested models or empirical coverage rates, so none should be inferred.
What if the projected confidence lower bound is negative because recording is sparse?

Then it would not certify strict improvement, even if coverage is valid. Sparse recording may limit informativeness, but the sign of the projected endpoint is an output, not determined by the 1% rate alone. A negative lower endpoint does not establish the candidate policy is worse; it leaves nonpositive gain among the compatible possibilities.
Could the 1% stress test establish improvement over the historical policy?

Only if a particular candidate’s correctly projected exact-95% lower gain bound is strictly above zero under the stated sensitivity model. The stress-test description reports no such endpoint, no policy definition, and no improvement decision. Attainability and coverage checks are necessary to interpret a positive certificate, but they do not supply its sign.
How should the result of this activity eventually distinguish a sharpness issue from a coverage issue?

Report whether feasible continuous-confounder witnesses and global dual bounds agree for each endpoint, with any numerical gap and whether an optimum is attained or merely approached. Separately report whether the inverted multinomial region has its exact-95% guarantee and whether projection includes all KL-admissible gains at covered vectors. A small primal–dual gap does not establish coverage, and a covered observable vector does not establish sharpness.
What would be a concise, non-result statement of the activity?

Stress-test KLPolicy v0.1 under continuous-confounder models with 1% outcome recording, assessing whether reported policy-gain extrema are attainable and globally certified and whether exact-95% multinomial inversion yields the intended coverage after complete projection. No success or failure is implied by the activity itself.
What happened in the continuous-confounder stress test with 1% outcome recording?

Feasible shared-type policy gains approached −0.12, but no feasible gain attained −0.12. The extremizing sequences had recording propensities that vanished. The result distinguishes a limiting gain from a gain realized by an admissible distribution; it does not report an exact-95% coverage outcome.
What does ‘approached −0.12’ mean here?

It means there were feasible shared-type configurations with gains progressively closer to −0.12. The reported finding says none of them attained that value. Numerical closeness should therefore not be described as an admissible configuration whose gain equals −0.12.
Does this make −0.12 an attained minimum?

No. An attained minimum requires a single feasible shared-type distribution whose gain is −0.12. The finding explicitly says that did not occur. An endpoint reached only as a limit may still serve as a sharp infimum if a global lower-bound argument rules out smaller feasible gains, but the statement about approaching it should not be turned into an attainment claim.
Why do vanishing recording propensities matter?

They describe what happens along the extremizing sequences: some recording probabilities tend toward zero as the gains approach −0.12. Whether the limiting configuration is admissible depends on the model’s support and conditional-KL conventions. If a relevant conditional distribution ceases to be defined at zero recording probability, taking the limit need not produce a feasible endpoint law. The evidence identifies vanishing propensities; it does not provide a more detailed account of which constraint excludes an endpoint.
But outcome recording was 1%. How can a recording propensity vanish?

A 1% outcome-recording condition does not, by itself, say that every latent type or conditional group has recording probability bounded away from zero. Propensities in an extremizing sequence can vanish for some part of the latent population while the stated overall recording condition is maintained. The result does not identify which groups have vanishing propensities or how the 1% recording is distributed among them.
Does ‘never attained’ mean no feasible gains were close to −0.12?

Quite the opposite: the feasible gains *approached* −0.12. The distinction is between being arbitrarily close along an admissible sequence and having an admissible member of that sequence—or another admissible distribution—at exactly −0.12. The reported finding asserts closeness without attainment.
Could I describe −0.12 as a sharp lower bound?

The approaching feasible gains show that a valid lower bound could not be raised above −0.12 without excluding gains in those sequences. To assert that −0.12 is the sharp lower bound, one also needs to establish that no admissible gain falls below it. The finding reports the extremizing sequences and nonattainment, but does not spell out a separate global certificate, so I would keep any sharpness claim tied to whatever global bound has actually been established.
Could we report a distribution with gain −0.12 by taking the limit of the sequence?

Not on this evidence. A limiting probability law need not satisfy the same feasibility requirements as every member of a sequence, particularly where recording propensities vanish and conditional quantities may become undefined. More directly, the reported result says −0.12 was never attained. It is appropriate to report the limit of feasible gains, not an endpoint distribution that the finding says does not exist.
Does this say anything about the greatest feasible policy gain?

No. The stated result concerns feasible gains approaching −0.12 and the failure to attain that limiting value. It gives no corresponding upper endpoint, upper extremizing sequence, or attainment result for the maximum.
Can we conclude that outcome-dependent recording caused the nonattainment?

The stress test is in the shared-type, low-recording setting, and the reported extremizing sequences had vanishing recording propensities. That identifies the feature accompanying the limiting behavior. It does not isolate outcome dependence itself as the cause or specify which modeling convention makes the limit inadmissible.
What does this mean for an attainable-extremizer claim in the 1% recording setting?

For the reported −0.12 limit, the claim cannot be supported by an attaining witness: feasible shared-type gains approach it but never reach it. A correct statement must allow for a limiting extremum rather than insist on a feasible distribution at that value. That conclusion is about the reported setting and endpoint, not every possible recording rate or KL specification.
Does a failure of attainment mean we cannot bound policy gain?

No. Bounds are naturally expressed as infima and suprema, which need not be attained. If −0.12 is globally established as the infimum, it remains a meaningful population lower bound even though no admissible law realizes it. The key is to distinguish a justified limiting bound from an attainable minimum; nonattainment alone does not make a bound unusable.
Would a gain limit of −0.12 certify improvement over the historical policy?

No. A lower gain limit at −0.12 is negative and cannot establish that all admissible candidate-minus-historical gains are positive. That does not show the candidate policy’s actual gain is negative; no true gain or full identified interval is reported. A confidence-based improvement certificate would require a correctly projected lower endpoint strictly above zero.
Did the stress test find that exact-95% coverage failed?

No coverage result is given in this finding. It reports feasible gains approaching −0.12 without attaining it, and vanishing recording propensities along the extremizing sequences. Attainability of a population endpoint and repeated-sampling coverage of a projected confidence set are separate questions; we should not infer a coverage success or failure from this result alone.
Does exact multinomial inversion require an attaining distribution at the lower endpoint?

Not inherently. A confidence projection can be defined using the infimum of gains over compatible distributions, including an infimum approached only by feasible sequences. Its coverage argument concerns whether the true observable probabilities are retained and whether all admissible gains are included. An implementation that requires an endpoint witness would need to handle the nonattained limit carefully, but the nonattainment finding by itself does not decide the coverage question.
How should I state the result without overstating sharpness or coverage?

“With 1% outcome recording, feasible shared-type policy gains approached −0.12 but did not attain it; the extremizing sequences had vanishing recording propensities. No exact-95% coverage outcome is reported in this finding.”

Could imposing recording propensity ≥0.005 move the lower policy-gain bound?

Yes. If it removes previously admissible laws while leaving a nonempty feasible set, the infimum of the same gain cannot decrease; it may stay the same or increase. The added constraint can therefore change the population bound as well as its attainment status. There is no numerical change in policy gain stated here, and restoring attainment should not be conflated with preserving the original infimum.
Does that mean the positivity condition is merely a computational convenience?

No. If adopted as an assumption, it is a substantive restriction on which recording mechanisms the sensitivity model permits. Its possible mathematical benefit—preventing certain limiting behaviors—does not make it innocuous. A bound obtained under the 0.005 floor would have to be labeled conditional on that floor, as well as on the 0.05-nat KL assumptions.
Why might a positive propensity floor help with attainment?

A plausible route is that keeping the specified recording probabilities away from zero prevents an extremizing sequence from escaping through a zero-recording boundary at which a conditional recording distribution becomes undefined or a feasibility requirement ceases to hold. If, *in addition*, the complete constrained feasible set is nonempty and compact in a suitable topology and the gain is continuous, an existence argument could yield a minimizer.

The floor alone does not prove those other premises. It may leave other boundary or noncompactness issues untouched, particularly in a model with an unrestricted latent distribution.
Could the assignment mechanism still create a nonattained limit after imposing the recording floor?

Possibly. A 0.005 lower bound on recording propensity addresses the recording probabilities to which it applies; it does not automatically bound treatment-assignment probabilities away from zero or settle every KL support condition. The restoration-of-attainment claim must account for the whole shared-latent feasible class, not only one possible boundary mechanism.
Does the hypothesis require the confounder to have finite support?

No finite-support condition is stated. The existence question can be posed over the full admissible latent-distribution class. A finite-support attaining law might be one way to prove the claim if it can be constructed and shown admissible, but imposing a fixed atomic approximation without justification would answer a narrower question.
How does outcome-dependent recording fit with a propensity floor?

Recording may still depend on the latent potential-outcome information permitted by the shared-response-type model. The proposed floor limits how small the specified conditional recording probabilities may become; it does not require recording to be independent of outcomes. Assignment, recording, response types, and both policy values must continue to belong to one coherent full-data law satisfying the KL restrictions.
If recording propensities can be exactly 0.005, is the lower boundary included?

The symbol ‘≥0.005’ includes equality. That may matter for attaining an extremum at the boundary. But inclusion of that numerical boundary does not by itself establish that every other constraint remains defined and closed there. The KL directions, reference supports, conditioning events, and observable-data mapping still need consistent boundary conventions.
What would be a convincing proof that the propensity restriction restores attainment?

One route would show that the 0.005-constrained feasible class is nonempty and compact, that its KL and observable constraints are preserved under relevant limits, and that the policy-gain functional has the continuity needed to achieve its infimum. Another route would construct an admissible shared-response-type law at the proposed endpoint and pair it with a globally valid lower-bound certificate.

Either proof must apply to the precise 0.05-nat model with the stated recording floor. Finding a feasible law close to a solver endpoint would show approximate feasibility, not necessarily attainment of the mathematical infimum.
Could we prove nonattainment in the no-floor model just by showing one sequence of propensities going to zero?

No. Such a sequence might show that a particular gain is approachable, but it does not rule out some *other* admissible law attaining the same gain. Nor does it establish that no feasible law has an even lower gain. Nonattainment of a sharp infimum calls for a global bound, a sequence approaching it, and an argument excluding every feasible endpoint law under the model’s stated boundary conditions.
Would the 0.005 floor guarantee attainment of the upper gain bound too?

That is not asserted by this hypothesis. It specifically says sharp gain *infima* need not be attained and proposes restoration of attainment when recording propensity is at least 0.005. A claim about upper extrema would need its own existence argument or endpoint construction. Likewise, a proof for one policy contrast does not automatically cover every possible candidate policy.
How does this affect a claim of improvement over the historical policy?

The criterion remains a strictly positive lower bound on candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value. The no-floor model may have a sharp lower infimum even without an attaining law; its sign is still meaningful for that criterion. Under a 0.005 floor, a potentially different attained minimum would be interpreted relative to the *restricted* sensitivity model. Neither part of the hypothesis supplies the lower bound’s value or shows that it exceeds zero.
Does an attained population minimum give an exact-95% improvement certificate?

No. Population attainment concerns the feasible gain range at given observable probabilities. An exact-95% certificate also requires a suitably covered confidence region for those probabilities, complete projection through the specified sensitivity model—including the 0.005 floor if that model is used—and a projected lower gain endpoint strictly above zero. The attainment hypothesis does not establish that coverage or positivity.
If a projected lower bound under the 0.005 floor is positive, can I claim the same result without the floor?

Not without a separate bound for the no-floor model. The floor may exclude distributions that lower the candidate-minus-historical gain, so a positive lower endpoint under the restricted model need not remain positive when the floor is removed. A certificate must identify which sensitivity assumptions support it.
What is a careful formulation of the revised hypothesis?

“At the shared-latent 0.05-nat KL sensitivity setting, the sharp lower policy-gain bound may be an unattained infimum; we hypothesize that requiring the specified recording propensities to be at least 0.005 yields an attained lower extremum for the resulting restricted model.” That keeps the possible nonattainment and the proposed restoration separate, without asserting that the two models have the same bound or that improvement has been certified.
I want to add a recording-propensity floor of 0.005, prove compactness and existence of policy-gain extremizers, and then rerun the sparse-recording coverage tests. How should I sequence that work?

Does 0.005 constrain the overall fraction of outcomes recorded?

Not merely by being called a propensity floor. The plan calls for a lower bound on recording propensities, which are conditional recording probabilities. Should I describe the floor as 0.5%?

Yes: a probability of 0.005 equals 0.5%. Keep the statement tied to the specified conditional recording propensities, though. Saying only that at least 0.5% of outcomes are recorded overall would state a different condition.
What needs to stay shared when the floor is added?

Treatment assignment, outcome recording, the latent response types, and the potential outcomes relevant to policy value must still form one admissible full-data distribution. Candidate-policy and historical-policy values are evaluated under that same distribution when their difference is optimized. The floor cannot be checked using recording probabilities taken from an unrelated latent mixture.
If recording can depend on an unobserved potential outcome, does the floor rule out that dependence?

No. A lower probability limit does not require recording to be independent of potential outcomes. The plan needs to define those conditional propensities without treating unrecorded outcomes as though they had been observed.
Would adding the floor leave the policy-gain bounds unchanged?

That is not guaranteed. The floor may exclude full-data distributions that were otherwise admissible. If the restricted feasible set is nonempty, its infimum for the same candidate-minus-historical gain cannot be lower than the infimum over the larger set, but it could remain equal or move upward. The plan is to prove existence for the model *with* the 0.005 floor; it does not state an endpoint value or claim the bounds stay the same.
What would the compactness proof be about, exactly?

It would concern the set of full-data distributions satisfying the observable constraints, the shared-latent KL restrictions, and the specified recording-propensity floor. To call that set compact, the proof must say in what topology distributions are considered and show both the required relative compactness and that permissible limits remain in the set. The fact that recording probabilities cannot fall below 0.005 may help with one boundary issue, but it does not establish compactness of the whole class by itself.
Why isn't closing off the zero-recording boundary enough?

Other aspects of the feasible class may still matter: support and conditioning rules for KL comparisons, limits of the latent distributions, the mapping to observable probabilities, and the behavior of assignment probabilities. A sequence could satisfy the recording floor yet fail to have an admissible limit for another reason. The proof needs to check the full joint set, not just the recording condition.
Would we also have to show that the feasible set is nonempty?

Yes, for any instance for which an extremizer is claimed. Compactness of an empty set does not supply a minimum or maximum policy gain. The observable probabilities, KL restrictions, and 0.005 floor must be jointly compatible with at least one full-data distribution. If they are not, emptiness should be identified rather than interpreted as a policy-value result.
What must hold for compactness to imply existence of extremizers?

A standard route is a nonempty compact feasible set and a continuous policy-gain functional on it. Then the candidate-minus-historical gain reaches its minimum and maximum. The plan must establish those premises for the actual outcome and policy-value definitions; it cannot infer continuity just from compactness. If a different existence argument is used, its conditions must likewise apply to the fully specified shared-latent model.
Does the plan promise existence of both a minimum and a maximum?

It calls for proving extremizer existence. A full policy-gain interval has lower and upper endpoints, so a claim about both would need an admissible minimizer and an admissible maximizer, potentially different distributions. Any completed proof should say which endpoints it covers rather than assuming a lower-endpoint argument automatically applies to the upper one.
Could a numerical optimizer finding a feasible table replace the existence proof?

A verified feasible distribution proves that its own gain is attainable. It does not show that it realizes the global minimum or maximum, nor that an optimizer exists for every instance covered by a general claim. To certify an endpoint in a particular case, one would also need a valid global inequality meeting the feasible value; to prove existence more broadly, the argument must apply across the stated class.
Where do the KL constraints enter the compactness argument?

They are part of the feasible set whose limits must remain admissible. Do we have to define the policy-gain target before proving continuity?

Yes. Write the gain as candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value on a common target population, with an explicitly defined outcome or utility scale. What would distinguish a proof for a fixed observable probability vector from one needed for confidence projection?

In sparse-recording cases, the rerun can check whether the implemented projection and its boundary treatment follow the stated 0.005-floor model. No. The floor is a restriction on admissible recording mechanisms, intended here to support an extremizer-existence argument. Coverage is a repeated-sampling property of the confidence procedure. Four out of 80 is 5% of the tables in this stress test. That is a fraction of the evaluated tables, not an estimate of how frequently nonattainment occurs across every KL-constrained policy problem.

It distinguishes the endpoint of the feasible gain range from a feasible gain at that endpoint. A lower bound on recording probabilities does not, by itself, bound treatment probabilities away from zero. Does nonattainment make −0.11 an invalid lower bound?

No. A lower bound can be a certified infimum without being a minimum. The result explicitly calls the −0.11 gain infima certified and unattained. Its point is the distinction between a justified endpoint value and the existence of a distribution at that value.

What can we conclude about the other 76 tables?

Only that they are not among the four tables described by this particular finding. It does not report their endpoint values, whether their infima were attained, or whether their extremizer certificates passed. We should not infer success for all 76 from the count alone.
Does the finding say anything about the upper gain bounds?
No. It concerns certified *infima* of −0.11 in 4/80 tables. There is no reported upper endpoint or upper-endpoint attainment result.
Can the candidate policy be certified to improve in those four cases?

Does a negative infimum imply that the candidate is harmful?

No. It means the feasible gain range has a negative lower limit under the stated comparison. Did exact-95% coverage hold in these 80 tables?

No coverage outcome is stated in this finding. The reported result concerns nonattainment of four certified gain infima and vanishing treatment propensities despite the recording floor. It should not be recast as either a coverage success or a coverage failure.
Could exact confidence projection still be defined with an unattained infimum?

Yes, conceptually. A projected gain set and its lower endpoint can be defined using an infimum even when no admissible distribution realizes that endpoint. The confidence question remains whether the observable region has its stated coverage and whether projection includes all admissible gains. Nonattainment alone does not settle those questions.
What is the narrow conclusion about the 0.005 recording floor?

In these 4/80 tables, the 0.005 recording-propensity floor did **not** ensure attainment of the certified −0.11 gain infima: treatment propensities vanished instead. That conclusion is confined to the reported cases and lower endpoints; it does not characterize every model using the floor.
