“In 4/80 floor-active tables, certified candidate-minus-historical gain infima of −0.11 were unattained as treatment propensities vanished despite the 0.005 recording-propensity floor.”

Does 0.005 mean a treatment probability of at least 0.5%?

Does KLPolicy v0.2 already have a propensity floor?

It includes a 0.005 *recording*-propensity floor. This activity adds a separate 0.005 *treatment*-propensity floor. They constrain different events, even though the numerical thresholds are equal. Both must be evaluated within one admissible shared-response-type distribution.
Would the treatment floor replace either the recording floor or a KL restriction?

No. It is an additional constraint, not a substitute for the recording floor or the stated KL sensitivity restrictions. What should remain joint when both floors are imposed?

One full-data law must determine the response types, treatment assignment, outcome recording, and both policy values. Treatment and recording may depend differently on latent information, but their propensities and KL comparisons must come from that same law. The gain being minimized is candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value under one admissible law, not a subtraction of values selected from different laws.
Can you show formally why the lower bound might move?

Let F_rec(q) be the distributions compatible with observable probabilities q and the existing model, including its recording floor. Could adding the floor make one of the four cases infeasible?

Possibly. Its observable probabilities and other restrictions might not admit any distribution satisfying the additional treatment floor. What would certify attainment in a nonempty case?

If a solver gives a gain very close to its dual bound, can we call the endpoint attained?

Report exactly what is supported. A verified feasible law attains *its own* gain, and a valid dual bound can bracket the mathematical infimum. If attainment is proved for the new model, does that show −0.11 is now attained?

This activity does not report an upper-endpoint finding.
What does exact-95% coverage refer to in the retest?

It refers to a confidence procedure based on an exact multinomial region for observable probabilities and its projection to candidate-minus-historical gains. Testing attainment at fixed observable probabilities and testing confidence coverage after projection are different tasks.
Why can’t we simply reuse a confidence projection for a model without the treatment floor?

A projection’s target and interpretation depend on the feasible class used. What has to hold for observable multinomial coverage to transfer to gain coverage?

Whenever the exact region contains a true observable probability vector, projection must include every full-data law compatible with that vector and both floors under the stated KL assumptions. It then includes the true law’s gain. If the observable region has at least 95% coverage uniformly over the applicable parameter space, and that projection implication holds throughout the stated sensitivity model, the gain set inherits the at-least-95% guarantee.
Could treatment propensities exactly equal 0.005 in an attaining distribution?

Yes, if the condition is written as ≥0.005, equality is included. A boundary witness would still need to satisfy the other constraints, including any conditional KL definitions, and its gain would need a global optimality certificate. The retest should use the same boundary convention in optimization and projection.
Would successful checks on all four tables prove uniform coverage?

No. Four case checks can assess those implementations, while a uniform confidence guarantee ranges over every distribution in the stated sensitivity model. That guarantee requires an applicable exact multinomial test-size argument and complete projection across the model. Any empirical coverage measured in the four cases should be labeled as empirical, not promoted to a uniform proof.
Could exact-95% coverage hold even if one new infimum were unattained?

Yes. Coverage of a projected gain set does not require a distribution at its lower endpoint; it requires inclusion of the gains of admissible distributions when their observable probabilities are covered. An unattained infimum can still define a confidence-set endpoint. Attainment and coverage should therefore be reported separately even if the same four tables are used to examine both.
What would a positive policy-gain certificate require after the retest?

The lower endpoint of the correctly projected exact-95% *joint* candidate-minus-historical gain set would have to be strictly greater than zero. Any such claim would be conditional on the specified KL restrictions and both 0.005 propensity floors. Attainment of a population endpoint, or confirmation of coverage alone, would not establish that its projected lower bound is positive.
What should we report without presuming the activity succeeds?

For each of the four cases, report whether the new feasible set is nonempty, its certified lower endpoint, whether a law attains that endpoint, and how it compares with −0.11. Separately report the exact-95% coverage check for projection through the model with both floors. The activity supplies no new endpoint, attainment, coverage, or improvement result.
What did rechecking the four −0.11 cases reveal?

Should I say the extremal policy gains were all exactly −0.11?

Does an inactive treatment floor mean the constraint is unnecessary everywhere?

No. The result is specific to four rechecked −0.11 cases. It says the recording floor alone sufficed for attainment *there*. Whether that holds for other shared-latent KL models, observable distributions, or policy contrasts is not answered by this finding.

Can I summarize the recheck without adding an endpoint gap or coverage percentage?

Does the decision specify a new version of KLPolicy or a new numerical bound?

Give me a concise statement of the decision.

What does the 0.005 floor restrict?

What does ‘attainable sharp bounds’ mean here?

Sharpness means the lower and upper policy-gain bounds delimit the values permitted by the stated observable information and sensitivity assumptions, rather than merely enclosing them in a wider interval. Why is the joint gain the relevant quantity for certification?

Improvement is a comparison: candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value. Bounding that difference directly preserves which values can coexist under one admissible distribution. Does the decision give the value of the lower gain bound?

How does the exact-95% part relate to the population bounds?

Does ‘exact-95%’ promise coverage equal to precisely 95% everywhere?

When does that projected result certify improvement?

An empty feasible set cannot furnish an attainable extremum or a positive-gain certificate. Compatibility has to be addressed rather than interpreting emptiness as evidence that a candidate policy improves.
Does this decision establish the same bounds without the 0.005 recording floor?

No. The decision specifically retains KLPolicy v0.2 *with* that floor. Removing it would change the feasible full-data class and could change whether endpoints are attained or what their values are. A certification under the retained formulation should not be restated as one for a model without the floor.
What is a concise way to state the decision without implying a positive gain has been observed?

Retain KLPolicy v0.2 with its 0.005 recording-propensity floor for attainable sharp policy-gain bounds and exact-95% improvement certification; certify a particular policy only if its projected lower gain bound exceeds zero.
Which approaches are we selecting for policy-gain bounds and improvement certification?

Select ΓTable v0.3, MomentPolicy v1.0, corrected TV bounds, and KLPolicy v0.2. Reject finite-atom shortcuts. For improvement over the historical policy, use a jointly evaluated candidate-minus-historical gain and certify strict improvement only when its projected exact-95% lower bound is positive. This decision selects the approaches and the certification threshold; it does not say that a particular candidate policy has cleared that threshold.
Are those four names meant to describe one combined sensitivity model?

No combined sensitivity model is specified by the decision. They identify selected approaches. A particular analysis must state the sensitivity assumptions and feasible full-data distributions for the approach it uses, then compute and project the corresponding gain bounds. Results under different assumptions should not be combined into a single certificate without defining and justifying that combined model.
What exactly are we rejecting when we say ‘finite-atom shortcuts’?

The rejection is of treating a convenient finite collection of latent atoms as though it automatically captures the full set of gains permitted by the stated model. A finite-atomic representation can still be useful if its adequacy for the relevant extrema is justified and its bounds are globally certified. What is not acceptable is replacing that justification with an unsupported support limit or a solver output.
So is every calculation using finitely many atoms excluded?

No. ‘Finite-atom shortcuts’ is narrower than ‘finite atoms.’ An admissible finite-support distribution can witness an attainable gain. To use a finite representation for a sharp bound, however, one must also establish that more extreme admissible distributions outside the representation have not been missed. The decision rejects skipping that step, not finite support as a mathematical tool.
Why optimize policy gain jointly?

Candidate-policy value and historical-policy value must be evaluated under the same admissible full-data distribution for their difference to be a feasible gain. Separately optimizing the two values and subtracting their marginal endpoints may combine values from different distributions. That subtraction can be a conservative comparison, but it need not characterize the sharp gain bound. The certification target is the jointly feasible difference.
What does ‘positive exact-95% lower bound’ mean operationally?

Let Δ be candidate-policy value minus historical-policy value, with value oriented so that a higher value is better. Form a confidence set for Δ by projecting an exact-95% region for the observable probabilities through all full-data distributions allowed by the stated sensitivity model. The improvement criterion is that the projected set’s lower endpoint be *strictly greater than zero*. A positive point estimate, or a population bound evaluated only at observed frequencies, is not that lower confidence bound.
Would a projected lower endpoint of exactly zero qualify?

No. ‘Positive’ means strictly above zero. An endpoint at zero leaves no gain compatible with the lower-limit claim and therefore does not certify *strict* improvement. Failure to certify does not establish that the candidate is worse than the historical policy.
Does exact-95% imply that coverage equals exactly 95% in every case?

No. The confidence requirement is coverage of at least 95% over the stated sensitivity model; actual coverage can be higher. For the gain, that interpretation depends on both a suitably covering observable confidence region and complete projection through the model’s admissible full-data distributions. The 95% level describes repeated-sampling coverage, not optimization precision or the magnitude of a policy gain.
What does complete projection require?

For every observable probability vector retained by the confidence region, include every gain arising from a full-data distribution compatible with that vector and the sensitivity assumptions. If the true observable vector is covered, the true admissible distribution and its gain must remain in the projected set. Restricting the projection to a point estimate, or to an unjustified finite selection of latent configurations, would not support the stated confidence interpretation.
If a lower bound is above zero, is the conclusion robust to any amount of confounding or missing outcomes?

No. A certificate applies to the treatment-assignment, outcome-recording, and latent-outcome possibilities admitted by the *stated* sensitivity model. Selective observation and unmeasured confounding are addressed only to the extent that model permits them. A positive lower bound should be reported alongside the assumptions under which it was computed.
Do all four selected approaches have to give the same numerical gain interval?

The decision does not say that. The approaches can express different sensitivity assumptions or bound constructions, and their numerical intervals cannot be expected to coincide without a common target, observable distribution, and feasible model. Nor does the decision supply intervals to compare. Each reported bound should identify the approach and assumptions that give it meaning.
What if an approach gives a sharp population lower bound but the projected lower bound is not positive?

Then that projected confidence set does not certify strict improvement under this decision rule. Population sharpness concerns the tightest gain bound at specified observable probabilities; exact-95% projection also accounts for uncertainty in those probabilities. A sharp population calculation does not guarantee that its confidence lower endpoint clears zero.
Could a conservative method still certify improvement?

A valid, appropriately covered conservative lower bound that is strictly positive would also rule out nonpositive gains under its stated model. The decision nevertheless selects the named approaches and rejects *unjustified finite-atom shortcuts*. Its certification criterion is positivity of a valid projected exact-95% lower bound, not narrowness by itself.
Does selecting these approaches mean we have a positive certificate for a particular clinical decision policy?

No. The decision states which approaches to retain and what threshold a certificate must meet. It gives no candidate-specific projected lower endpoint, so there is no basis here to say that any particular policy improves on the historical policy with exact-95% confidence.
How should I state the decision concisely?

Select ΓTable v0.3, MomentPolicy v1.0, corrected TV bounds, and KLPolicy v0.2; reject unjustified finite-atom shortcuts; and certify improvement over the historical policy only when the projected exact-95% joint policy-gain lower bound is strictly positive.
